pool.q: A consult is placed for a newborn infant. Clinical evaluation of the infant shows a microphthalmic left eye and a normal right eye. What is the next step in the treatment for this condition?
pool.rationale: Microphthalmic eyes have hypoplastic orbits and most have no potential for vision. As such, treatment focuses on achieving a cosmetically acceptable appearance that is reasonably symmetrical. Treatment begins shortly after birth and consists of socket expansion with progressively larger conformers, which are used until the patient can be fitted with a prosthesis. An enucleation and evisceration is not usually necessary, and it is ordinarily avoided because it may worsen the bony hypoplasia. Orbital volume may be augmented with dermis-fat grafts; however, the first step is to use progressively larger conformers.

pool.q: A 57-year-old patient was recently diagnosed with a low-grade isolated orbital lymphoma. What is the preferred treatment?
pool.rationale: The most common type of orbital lymphoma is extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma, which is a low-grade malignancy. The typical treatment is external beam radiotherapy, with 10-year survival rates of 92%. A surgical cure usually is not possible because of the infiltrative nature of lymphoid tumors. Corticosteroids can decrease the size of an orbital lymphoma but are not adequate treatment. Chemotherapy such as carboplatin sometimes is used in cases of systemic lymphoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What structure(s) most closely co-localize with the axial position of the cribriform plate?

options.a: superior border of the cartilaginous nasal septum

pool.rationale:
The skull base, which separates the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses from the intracranial cavity, is composed of the cribriform plate (roof of the nasal cavity) and the fovea ethmoidalis (roof of the ethmoid air cells). The boundary between these 2 structures is the root of the middle turbinate. The axial level of the skull base is best approximated by the frontoethmoidal suture and the 2 (anterior and posterior) ethmoidal foramina found along the medial orbital wall.
The medial canthal tendon lies well below (7-10 mm) this level. The cartilaginous portion of the nasal septum is also found below and anterior to the skull base; the roof of the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, a more posterior and superior segment of the nasal septum, abuts the skull base.
The anterior clinoid process is found intracranially, behind the fovea ethmoidalis and cribriform plate.
Note that these landmarks are approximations. Some patients have naturally low-lying skull base anatomy which, on occasion, can approach the level of the medial canthal tendon. Furthermore, certain craniofacial anomalies, most notably Crouzon syndrome, feature a low-lying skull base.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What produces the majority of the lipid layer of the precorneal tear film?
pool.rationale: The tear film comprises 3 layers: the lipid layer (anterior), aqueous layer, and mucin layer (posterior). The lipid layer is secreted by the meibomian glands, and to a lesser extent, the glands of Zeis. The aqueous layer is secreted from the lacrimal glands. Mucin is secreted by the conjunctival goblet cells.

pool.q: An afebrile 17-year-old patient presents with periorbital edema, no eyelid lesions, and minimal erythema. Imaging demonstrates an ill-defined anterior orbital process with clear sinuses. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.d: admit for intravenous (IV) antibiotics and blood culture

pool.rationale: The clinical scenario presented is not consistent with orbital cellulitis. Most cases of orbital cellulitis occur secondary to an extension of acute or chronic bacterial sinusitis. Other diagnostic possibilities such as sarcoidosis, ruptured dermoid cyst, leukemic infiltrate, or idiopathic orbital inflammation. Surgical intervention is the next appropriate step to obtain the diagnosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What structure of the upper eyelid is analogous to a component in the lower eyelid retractors?
pool.rationale:
The lower eyelid anatomy may be considered a simplified or primitive analog of the upper lid. In the lower lid, 2 retractors are present: the capsulopalpebral fascia and the inferior tarsal muscle. Because both of these structures are rudimentary and essentially inseparable surgically, they are usually coupled together as the "lower lid retractors."
The capsulopalpebral fascia component of the lower lid retractors is analogous to the levator aponeurosis of the upper lid. Similarly, the inferior tarsal muscle component of the lower lid retractors is analogous to the Müller muscle.
The preseptal orbicularis lies posterior to the skin and anterior to the septum.
The orbital septum can be considered a multilamellar fascial extension of the periosteum, emanating from the orbital rim.
The preaponeurotic fat pad lies between the orbital septum anteriorly and the levator aponeurosis posteriorly and serves as a reliable anatomic landmark intraoperatively.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What surgical procedure may result in continued orbital expansion in a child born with a microphthalmic eye?
pool.rationale: Dermis-fat grafting, when placed at an early age, may continue to grow with the child, resulting in progressive orbital expansion and minimizing hypoplasia of the orbit. A large implant, with or without enucleation, may improve the hypoplastic orbit in the short term, and maintain the volume, but it will not expand over time. An enophthalmic wedge may be used in an adult to correct enophthalmos from microphthalmos, but is not recommended in a child.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An 85-year-old diabetic inpatient reports new-onset right-sided orbital pain and blurred vision. An ear-nose-throat (otolaryngologist) colleague has noted a necrotic eschar in the nasal cavity with overlying focal tissue necrosis. The patient was initially admitted for cancer chemotherapy. What would be the most likely diagnosis?

options.c: granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), formerly known as Wegener granulomatosis

pool.rationale: In patients with metabolic acidosis, diabetes mellitus, or malignancies, or patients who are undergoing treatment with antimetabolites or steroids, it is necessary to consider zygomycosis (also known as phycomycosis or mucormycosis) fungal disease. These fungi extend into the orbit from an adjacent sinus or the nasal cavity. Orbital involvement can present with proptosis and orbital apex syndrome (internal and external ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, decreased corneal sensation, and decreased vision). They invade blood vessel walls, leading to a thrombosing vasculitis. Diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy of the necrotic-appearing tissues in the nasopharynx or involved sinus or orbit. On histology, zygomycosis shows nonseptate large branching hyphae.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most appropriate treatment for a 75-year-old male with chronic, unilateral, lower lid chalazia and eyelid induration?
pool.rationale:
The presentation is suspicious for sebaceous gland carcinoma masquerading as chronic unilateral blepharitis. Although this neoplasm is more common in women, asymmetric eyelid margin disease in an elderly patient should prompt the examiner to look for other signs of malignancy (eyelash loss, eyelid thickening). In this situation, the most appropriate treatment is margin-controlled excisional biopsy.
Topical 5-fluorouracil may be used in the management of conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia and actinic keratosis but is not suitable for sebaceous gland carcinoma.
Temporary use of topical steroid ointment and intralesional steroid injections may be useful adjunctive treatment for chronic blepharitis, but malignancy must be ruled out first in this situation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 42-year-old woman complains of eyelid asymmetry and has 2 mm of left upper lid ptosis. Her pupils, ocular motility, and levator function are normal. What clinical test would help confirm whether she is a candidate for transconjunctival Müller muscle resection?
pool.rationale: The patient likely has involutional ptosis, which could be treated via external levator advancement or transconjunctival Müller muscle resection. If instillation of 2.5% phenylephrine restores the normal position of the lid, it suggests the patient would respond favorably to transconjunctival Müller muscle resection. Edrophonium (Tensilon) testing and ice testing are useful to diagnose myasthenia gravis. Tropicamide does not have a role in this setting.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What vascular structure passes through the optic canal?
pool.rationale: The ophthalmic artery passes through the optic canal adjacent to the optic nerve. The recurrent branch of the middle meningeal artery, and the superior ophthalmic vein, pass through the superior ophthalmic fissure. The inferior ophthalmic vein passes through the inferior ophthalmic fissure.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 58-year-old woman presents to the office unhappy with the appearance of her eyelids. She wants her eyelids to appear more youthful. What would be the most appropriate surgical approach?

options.a: suturing of the sub-brow tissue to the frontal bone periosteum
options.c: resection of upper eyelid skin with advancement of the levator aponeurosis.

pool.rationale:
The figure shows a patient with dermatochalasis, mild brow ptosis on the left side, and blepharoptosis. Surgical treatment should be aimed to correct the dermatochalasis and ptosis. An upper blepharoplasty is the best surgical approach and includes the resection of upper eyelid skin, with varying amounts of orbicularis, and preaponeurotic fat resection. If there is concurrent ptosis, this can be addressed with the same anterior eyelid incision through advancement of the levator aponeurosis. Dermatochalasis is redundancy of eyelid skin that occurs in middle-aged to elderly individuals. Preoperative examination should include a visual field test to document any superior visual field defects, if present. Brow ptosis includes age-related involutional changes of forehead skin that cause drooping of the eyebrows.
Patients often have chronic contraction of the frontalis muscle in an attempt to elevate the eyebrows/eyelids, and this is observed as forehead wrinkling. Treatment is usually a browpexy (sub-brow tissue sutured to the frontal bone periosteum). A frontalis sling is often used to treat blepharophimosis syndrome or ptosis with poor levator function.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: On computed tomography (CT) imaging, what is the expected appearance of allergic aspergillosis of the sinus and orbit?

options.a: orbits with enhancement of the fascial planes and bulla formation
options.b: orbits with unilateral fusiform enlargement of the levator complex
options.c: mottled areas of increased attenuation on nonenhanced images
options.d: orbit and sinus involvement and thrombosis of the cavernous sinus

pool.rationale:
Aspergillus can affect the orbit and sinus in a couple different manners, including as an acute or chronic infection causing orbital signs. Allergic aspergillosis sinusitis is another condition that affects immunocompetent individuals with nasal polyposis and chronic sinusitis. Patients often have serum eosinophilia or high serum IgE. CT imaging shows thick mucin within the sinus as mottled increased signal on non-enhanced images. Bone erosion and remodeling is often present but does not signify tissue invasion.
Sinus biopsy shows thick, green mucus with eosinophils and fungal hyphae. Treatment is surgical debridement often with oral corticosteroids. CT imaging with fusiform enlargement of the recti muscles or levator complex is found with thyroid eye disease. CT with spread of infection along preseptal fascial planes is consistent with necrotizing fasciitis. Zygomycosis may result in thrombosing vasculitis and cavernous sinus thrombosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with a right lower lid lesion that is elevated and poorly demarcated, with superficial scaling. Pathology from a biopsy is performed and shows squamous cell carcinoma confined to the epidermis, without invasion of the dermal epidermal junction. What is the most appropriate management for this lesion?
pool.rationale:
The disease process described is squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the skin, this is also known as Bowen disease. Lesions are typically elevated, nonhealing, and erythematous. They may present with scaling, crusting, or pigmented keratotic plaques. Pathologically, the lesions demonstrate full-thickness epidermal atypia without dermal invasion. In 5% of patients, it may progress to vertically invasive squamous cell carcinoma; therefore, complete surgical excision is advised. Nonsurgical options may be available; depending on the location and size of the lesion, some of these may include cryotherapy, topical 5 fluorouracil, and imiquimod.Topical hydroquinone is used to treatment skin dyschromias.
Topical trichloroacetic acid is a chemical peel to exfoliate the skin and treat fine lines, superficial rhytids, and photo damaged skin. It may also improve dilated pores, superficial scars, and pigmentary dyschromias.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 60-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presents with a relative afferent pupillary defect on the right eye, mild swelling of the right eyelid, proptosis, and severely restricted motility. He has a black eschar in his nose. He has been on oral antibiotics for sinusitis for 2 days, without improvement in his symptoms. Imaging confirms orbital inflammation in his right eye. What is the next appropriate step in management?

options.a: admission to hospital for intravenous vancomycin
options.b: switching to an oral antibiotic with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) coverage
options.d: biopsy of necrotic tissue, aggressive surgical debridement, and treatment with intravenous amphotericin B

pool.rationale:
In this setting, zygomycosis (also termed phycomycosis or mucormycosis), which is the most common and devastating fungus of the orbit, is suspected. Patients present with an orbital apex syndrome with sinusitis. The fundus directly invades blood vessels, causing vessel thrombosis (even central retinal artery occlusion in rare cases). The tissue appears necrotic and a black eschar may be seen. Predisposing conditions include metabolic acidosis, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, organ transplantation, renal failure, immunosuppression, and malignancies (such as lymphoma/leukemia). Microscopically nonseptate, large branching hyphae that stain with hematoxylin and eosin (unlike most fungi) are seen. Treatment is aggressive surgical debridement with intravenous amphotericin B. Even with aggressive treatment, outcomes can be poor.
Intravenous antibiotics such as vancomycin, nasal decongestants, and consultation with an otolaryngologist are indicated for possible MRSA, or orbital cellulitis not responding to oral antibiotics, but the symptoms, the predisposing factor of uncontrolled diabetes, and the presence of an eschar require more aggressive action.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 35-year-old patient presents with an acquired pigmented area involving the majority of the lower eyelid. The lesion has variable pigmentation and irregular borders. The ophthalmologist suspects possible melanoma because of a central area of elevation. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.a: incisional biopsy to incorporate some nonpathologic tissue to demonstrate the transition area
options.b: incisional biopsy incorporating the maximum thickness of the lesion
options.d: observation for change in appearance or thickness

pool.rationale:
The patient described has a presentation worrisome for malignant melanoma. It is important to biopsy the area of maximum thickness to determine if there is vertical invasion, and to obtain Breslow thickness. Because tumor thickness has strong prognostic implications, a biopsy taken through the full depth of the tumor should be performed on these lesions. Regional lymph node dissection or sentinel lymph node (SLN) biopsy may be performed in patients with Breslow thickness greater than 1 mm. Complete preoperative metastatic workup is indicated for tumors with thickness greater than 1.5 mm.
A biopsy that includes the transition area can be helpful in certain cutaneous lesions, but not in malignant melanoma. Wide surgical resection can be required, but biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis before proceeding with resection of the entire lid. Observation is not appropriate at this point, since there is already a worrisome area of thickening present.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: During patient evaluation, the ophthalmologist attempts to digitally elevate the margin of the lower eyelid to the superior corneal limbus with the eye in primary position. The inability to perform this maneuver suggests what diagnosis?
pool.rationale: In cicatricial ectropion, there is a vertical shortage of the anterior lamella, preventing manual repositioning of the eyelid. Potential causes include thermal or chemical burns, mechanical or surgical trauma (tumor removal or blepharoplasty), chronic actinic sun damage, rosacea, atopic dermatitis, eczematous dermatitis, herpes zoster, and ichthyosis. In spastic and involutional entropion and involutional ectropion, one can return the eyelid to a normal position using digital traction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is an example of a condition where orbital exenteration would be an appropriate initial management?

options.b: Merkel cell carcinoma of the eyelid
options.c: extraocular extension of choroidal melanoma in a patient with lung metastasis

pool.rationale:
Exenteration is an extensive surgical procedure defined by removal of the soft tissue contents of the orbit. A subtotal exenteration is basically an enucleation with removal of the adjacent lesion, leaving the periorbita and most or all of the eyelids. In a total exenteration, all intraorbital soft tissue is removed, usually including the eyelids. An extended exenteration involves removal of all orbital soft tissue, as well as adjacent bony structures, such as the paranasal sinuses and/or the skull base. Exenteration should be considered for any aggressive tumor within the orbit that is not responsive to radiation or is too large to be removed entirely with excision. Intraocular tumors that extend into the orbit should be considered for exenteration if no systemic metastasis is found.
Merkel cell carcinoma of the eyelid is a neuroendocrine tumor that presents as a painless, red nodule with overlying telangiectatic blood vessels. The tumor should be excised with or without chemotherapy/radiation. There is a high rate of tumor recurrence and metastasis. Mortality is high, at around 38%.
Rhabdomyosarcoma was traditionally treated with exenteration in the past. However, the most recent guidelines recommend chemotherapy and radiation as first-line treatment. Exenteration is considered for recurrent cases.
Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a highly malignant tumor for which exenteration is often indicated. Median age of presentation is 40 years, and that carcinoma is more common in women. The tumor often erodes bone and invades nerves. Histologically, the tumor has a "Swiss cheese" appearance (cribriform pattern). Other types include basaloid, comedo, sclerosing, and tubular. The basaloid pattern has the worse prognosis. Severe orbital fungal infections are another indication for exenteration.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the term for adhesions between conjunctival surfaces due to inflammation, trauma, or previous surgery?
pool.rationale: Symblepharon refers to adhesion of conjunctival surfaces. Entropion refers to an inward turning of the lid margin. Euryblepharon refers to vertical shortening and horizontal lengthening of the affected eyelid. Trachoma is one of several causes of symblepharon.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An 8-year-old girl complains of excessive mattering from the right eye. Four years ago, following ocular trauma, she had an enucleation and placement of an implant. The right socket is shown in the figure. What is appropriate treatment for this condition?

options.d: placement of a scleral patch graft

pool.rationale:
Complications of the anophthalmic socket include exposure and extrusion of implants. Exposed or extruded implants should be repaired via scleral patch graft or autogenous tissue graft to assist in conjunctival closure.
When implants are deeply seeded with infection, removal of the implant is usually required; however, there is no evidence of infection in this case. Artificial tears are not adequate treatment for an exposed implant. Amniotic membrane may be used to treat some corneal epithelial defects but is not indicated for an exposed implant.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the primary treatment regimen for orbital rhabdomyosarcoma?
pool.rationale:
Prior to 1965, the standard treatment for orbital rhabdomyosarcoma was orbital exenteration, and the survival rate was poor. Since 1965, orbital radiation and systemic chemotherapy have been the mainstays of primary treatment for orbital rhabdomyosarcoma. With radiation and chemotherapy, survival rates are better than 90% if the orbital tumor has not invaded or extended beyond the bony orbital walls.
Although biopsy is indicated for diagnostic purposes, surgical excision is not adequate treatment for orbital rhabdomyosarcoma, which may have microscopic cellular metastases.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 15-year-old boy presents with 2 pearly ulcerated lesions with rolled edges on his face. The patient also has lesions on the palms of his hands. Further examination shows multiple cystic lesions of the mandible, bifid ribs, and several pit-like lesions on the soles of his feet. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Basal cell nevus syndrome, also known as Gorlin syndrome, affects 0.7% of patients with basal cell carcinoma. This autosomal dominant syndrome results in multiple nevoid BCC in young patients aged 10 to 30 years old. The syndrome also causes odontogenic jaw cysts, skeletal abnormalities, palmar and plantar pits, neurologic abnormalities, and endocrine disorders.
Sudden onset of multiple seborrheic keratoses is known as the Leser-Trélat sign and is associated with systemic malignancy, usually a gastrointestinal adenocarcinoma.
Muir-Torre syndrome encompasses visceral carcinoma, usually colon, and multiple sebaceous gland neoplasms. Muir-Torre is caused by a defect in the MSH2 DNA mismatch repair gene.
Cowden disease causes multiple hamartomas, especially facial trichilemmomas, and is associated with breast or thyroid cancer.

pool.q: What type of repair is preferred for a patient with a moderately large upper eyelid margin defect (30% margin loss) and healthy periocular skin and moderate eyelid laxity?

options.a: advancement of subbrow orbicularis and skin graft
options.b: direct closure after lateral canthal release
options.d: medial canthal tendon release and nasal flap

pool.rationale:
In a patient with healthy skin that has not undergone significant involutional change, direct closure can be performed in an eyelid defect of about 20%. Beyond that, other techniques are required. By contrast, patients with significant involutional changes, including medial and lateral canthal laxity, can often undergo direct closure for defects involving up to one-third of the eyelid.
In this case, a lateral canthal release should provide enough laxity to advance the intact lateral eyelid as a full-thickness flap to close the defect, and it is the easiest solution, using only 1 step.
A Hughes tarsoconjunctival flap is typically reserved for a large defect of the lower eyelid. Although this technique can occasionally be used for upper eyelid defects, it is usually avoided simply because of the shorter vertical tarsal dimension in the lower eyelid, which may not provide enough structural stability to the upper eyelid. In such cases, a full-thickness Cutler-Beard flap is used instead, as a reasonable lid-sharing reconstruction.
A medial canthal release with a nasal rotational flap will also work. However, medial canthal incision and release should be avoided when at all possible, since this will typically result in unacceptable telecanthus and will in all likelihood permanently damage the canaliculi, causing chronic epiphora.
Advancement of the subbrow orbicularis introduces a counterproductive upward vertical vector on the upper eyelid, which will almost invariably result in lid retraction and lagophthalmos. One of the major advantages of lid-sharing reconstructions (eg, Hughes procedure, Cutler-Beard procedure) is that the affected eyelid is pulled toward the visual axis and away from the orbital rim, allowing for a better final success and hopefully avoiding retraction and lagophthalmos.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When repairing a deep upper eyelid laceration with fat in the wound, it is generally advisable to avoid suturing what structure?
pool.rationale:
An upper eyelid laceration with fat in the wound describes an injury where the orbital septum is involved. The orbital septum arises from the periosteum over the superior and inferior orbital rims at the arcus marginalis. In the upper eyelid, the orbital septum fuses with the levator aponeurosis.
When repairing such an injury, the levator muscle, levator aponeurosis, and tarsal plate should all be repaired. Suturing the orbital septum can lead to vertical shortening, with subsequent lagophthalmos and tethering of the lid to the superior orbital rim.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common ocular finding in an infant with a unilateral small orbit and no visible eye?
pool.rationale: Microphthalmia is defined by the presence of a small eye with axial length that is at least 2 standard deviations below the mean axial length for age. Microphthalmia is much more common than anophthalmia, and the vast majority of microphthalmic eyes have no potential for vision. Although no visible eye may be present, most of these patients actually have a microphthalmic globe. The defect can be isolated or occur with a constellation of abnormalities as part of a syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 17-year-old trapeze artist has noticed increased left-sided, deep orbital pain and occasional loss of vision when performing upside down for a prolonged period of time. Clinical findings include normal visual acuity and intraocular pressures. What imaging modality is most likely to delineate the orbital disorder?
pool.rationale:
Gravity-dependent changes, which can be observed during examination, are most frequently secondary to orbital varices. These venous malformations are a result of vascular dysgenesis and are low-flow vascular lesions, as opposed to arteriovenous malformations (AVMs), which are high-flow anomalies. It is important to evaluate these patients with contrast-enhanced radiologic imaging, such as contrast-enhanced rapid spiral computed tomography (spiral CT) or contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which will show engorgement of veins during Valsalva maneuver.
Echography and computed tomography with fat suppression are not as ideal for delineating venous malformations. Due to the risk of hemorrhage of these lesions, biopsy should be avoided and thus appropriate imaging is important in order to manage these patients appropriately.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What procedure that is used to correct punctal ectropion involves a horizontal fusiform excision of conjunctiva and eyelid retractors 4 mm inferior to the puncta?
pool.rationale:
In cases of mild medial ectropion with punctal eversion, a medial spindle procedure can be performed. The procedure involves a horizontal fusiform excision of conjunctiva and eyelid retractors 4 mm inferior to the puncta, followed by inverting sutures for closure. In cases with associated horizontal eyelid laxity, lateral canthal tightening may be used in conjunction with this procedure.
In the lateral tarsal strip procedure, the tarsus is sutured directly to the lateral orbital rim periosteum. The goal of this procedure is to correct the position of the eyelid while maintaining the horizontal dimension of the palpebral fissure and a sharp, correctly positioned lateral canthal angle.
Punctoplasty changes the size of the puncta and does not alter the punctal position relative to the globe.
Rotational suture techniques are used as temporizing measures for involutional entropion; however, when these techniques are used in isolation, recurrence is anticipated.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most appropriate surgical repair for severe lower lid cicatricial entropion with retraction?
pool.rationale:
When assessing eyelid malposition, it is important to determine the eyelid lamellae that are involved in the pathologic process. The anterior lamella includes the skin and orbicularis oculi muscle, and anterior lamella shortening results in ectropion. The posterior lamella is the conjunctiva and tarsus, and shortening of this lamella results in entropion. Scarring and fibrosis are key factors that lead to either posterior or anterior lamellar deficiencies.
This patient has posterior lamellar shortening leading to entropion. The proper approach for repair is to lengthen the posterior lamella, which can be accomplished with a hard-palate spacer graft or other autologous or alloplastic graft. A full-thickness skin graft would be helpful to repair a cicatricial ectropion. Eyelash ablation would help relieve ocular irritation from lash-cornea touch, but would not fix the eyelid malposition. Likewise, a Quickert everting suture may temporarily reposition the lower lid but is not a definitive treatment for entropion, especially in the setting of severe scarring and lower lid retraction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The repair of a symptomatic punctal ectropion should include what procedure?
pool.rationale: Although thermal cautery of the conjunctiva can help to improve punctal ectropion, it is often not long-lasting and results in recurrence. A more permanent solution is the medial spindle procedure. This entails excision of the conjunctiva and retractors inferior to the puncta, with inverting sutures to correct the eyelid and punctal ectropion. If the eyelid ectropion is more extensive with horizontal eyelid laxity, then a lateral tarsal strip may be indicated. Quickert sutures are used to reinsert the retractors for repair of entropion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with diffuse actinic changes and a history of renal transplantation presents with progressive external ophthalmoplegia and forehead numbness that has progressed over several months. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.a: orbital spread of a bacterial sinusitis
options.d: perineural spread of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma

pool.rationale:
A perineural spread of a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) along the facial sensory nerves into the skull base (orbital apex and cavernous sinus) should be suspected in any patient with actinic changes or a history of facial cutaneous malignancies who presents with progressive periocular sensory and motor changes. SCC has a propensity for sensory nerves, and it occurs much more frequently in individuals with chronic immunosuppression (eg, those who have undergone renal transplantation).
Bacterial sinusitis typically occurs in a fulminant fashion, and orbital involvement usually manifests with external eyelid changes (eg, erythema, edema) and proptosis. However, more indolent fungal sinusitis, especially aspergillosis, may occur in a slowly progressive manner. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is an ill-defined cavernous sinus inflammation that presents with explosive pain and responds to systemic corticosteroids. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, because other pathologies may mimic its symptoms. Microvascular cranial neuropathy typically affects only 1 cranial nerve and typically resolves within 100 days. It does not usually affect sensory nerves.

pool.q: What is a contraindication to laser resurfacing techniques for eyelid or periocular skin surface irregularities or rhytids (skin wrinkles)?

pool.q: Where is the valve of Hasner located?
pool.rationale: The valve of Hasner is located at the distal end of the nasolacrimal duct. It represents a mucosal flap over the distal ostium of the nasolacrimal duct (NLD) below the inferior turbinate of the nose. The persistent membrane at the valve of Hasner is a common site of congenital NLD obstruction. The junction of the common canaliculus and lacrimal sac represents the valve of Rosenmüller.

pool.q: A 75-year-old man presents with a left lower eyelid lesion. He reports that the lesion appeared suddenly 3 weeks ago and has been rapidly growing in size. On examination, the ophthalmologist notes a 1.5 cm dome-shaped lesion with a central crater. What is the appropriate treatment for this lesion?

options.a: Perform a fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNAB) of the contents of the central crater.
options.b: Perform a shave biopsy to improve cosmesis.
options.c: No treatment is necessary, as this lesion will spontaneously involute.
options.d: Perform an incisional biopsy, followed by complete surgical excision.

pool.rationale: Keratoacanthoma is a rapidly growing epithelial proliferation occurring over weeks to months. It appears clinically as a dome-shaped nodule with a keratin-filled crater. Histologically, keratoacanthoma appears as well-differentiated squamous cells forming a cup-shaped lesion. The rapidly proliferating epithelial cells undermine adjacent skin. Mitotic activity and cellular atypia may occur at the deep margin, which can make the distinction from squamous cell carcinoma difficult. There is evidence suggesting that keratoacanthomas are a variant of well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. These entities express similar proliferation markers and oncoproteins (mutated p53). Some have replaced the term keratoacanthoma with well-differentiated keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma because of the possibility of deep invasion, perineural spread, and distant metastasis. Although the natural history of these lesions is typically spontaneous involution over several months, incisional biopsy followed by complete surgical excision is recommended. Intralesional methotrexate or 5-fluorouracil may be options for patients who are not surgical candidates.

pool.q: Why is a conformer placed in the fornices after a routine enucleation with orbital implant?

Placing extraocular muscles in their normal anatomical positions also minimizes shortening of the fornices. It is recommended that the patient wear a conformer in the immediate postoperative period to maintain soft-tissue anatomy and minimize conjunctival shortening. Conformers and prostheses should not be removed for periods greater than 24 hours. The prosthesis can be removed and cleaned, especially in the presence of infection, but should be replaced promptly after irrigation of the socket.

pool.q: A 41-year-old man presents at a clinic with spontaneous right eye enophthalmos, a deep superior sulcus, and mild upper eyelid retraction that occurred 1 week ago. He has just returned from vacation in Australia, where he went scuba diving for the first time. Since his return, he has had intermittent diplopia in upgaze. On examination, he is alert, oriented, and afebrile; all cranial nerves are intact. He is somewhat tender over the right maxillary sinus with percussion. What is the most likely cause of the spontaneous enophthalmos?

options.d: new cranial nerve palsy from progression of pseudotumor cerebri

pool.rationale:
Silent sinus syndrome results from chronic subclinical sinusitis, which causes thinning of the bone of the involved sinus, leading to enophthalmos due to collapse of the orbital floor. The spontaneous collapse often occurs in association with a recent significant change in atmospheric pressure, for example in airplane travel or scuba diving. Upper eyelid ptosis, deepening of the superior sulcus, and occasionally diplopia may occur. Patients can present with either eyelid retraction or ptosis. Treatment includes restoration of maxillary sinus aeration and reconstruction of the orbital floor. The entrapped maxillary sinus secretions are often sterile in nature.
Osteoma is a nonepithelial tumor that can invade the orbit from the sinuses, nose, and facial bones. It is not typically spontaneous nor rapid in progression; thus, time to diagnosis may be slow. At the time of diagnosis, there may be extensive orbital involvement, a palpable orbital mass, and ocular muscle restriction. Plexiform neurofibromas are tumors formed by diffuse proliferation of Schwann cells within nerve sheaths. They are often associated with von Recklinghausen disease (neurofibromatosis 1), in which hamartomas may develop in the skin, eyes, central nervous system, and viscera. The most common orbital finding associated with plexiform neurofibromatosis is infiltration of the lateral upper eyelid, which causes an S-shaped contour to the eyelid margin and possible proptosis. Pseudotumor cerebri (also known as idiopathic intracranial hypertension) can cause cranial nerve VI palsy, which causes horizontal deviations, not vertical deviations.

pool.q: What subtype of rhabdomyosarcoma has the worst prognosis?
pool.rationale: Rhabdomyosarcoma arises from pluripotential mesenchymal cells, not from extraocular muscles. There are 4 different variants of rhabdomyosarcoma. Alveolar accounts for only 9% of orbital rhabdomyosarcomas and is the most malignant form. It has a tendency to develop in the inferior orbit. Embryonal is the most common type and accounts for more than 80% of cases. It has a predilection for a superonasal location in the orbit and has a very high survival rate (94%). Pleomorphic is the rarest form. It is also the most well-differentiated form and consequently has the highest survival rate (97%). The botryoid variant of rhabdomyosarcoma is quite rare. It is unique in that it does not occur as a primary orbital tumor, but rather invades the orbit from the adjacent paranasal sinuses or from the conjunctiva. Treatment of rhabdomyosarcoma requires both chemotherapy and radiation.

pool.q: A patient has a small, painless, pink, pedunculated mass on the lower lid shown in the image. The area does not have any ulceration or discharge. What management is appropriate in this case?

options.a: cryotherapy or excision to eliminate the lesion and minimize the risk of viral spread
options.c: observation with spontaneous resolution in 2 weeks
options.d: timolol ophthalmic gel 0.5% applied topically twice daily

They are usually asymptomatic and, because they are contagious, patients may have multiple lesions. The lesions may resolve spontaneously. Cryotherapy or excision may also eradicate the lesion and reduce the chance of spread.

pool.q: In a young person with corneal neovascularization and the lesion below, what condition should be suspected?
pool.rationale:
Photos show a firm, raised, pearly nodule with central ulceration that is characteristic of basal cell carcinoma. Young patients with basal cell carcinoma should be evaluated for systemic associations such as xeroderma pigmentosum and basal cell nevus syndrome (Gorlin syndrome). Xeroderma pigmentosum is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by extreme sun sensitivity and defective repair of UV light-induced damage in skin cells. It often causes multiple skin cancers including basal cell carcinoma, as well as causing inflammation of the conjunctiva and cornea, which can lead to corneal neovascularization.
Gorlin syndrome, or basal cell nevus syndrome, is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple basal cell carcinomas and skeletal anomalies. Gorlin syndrome does not affect the cornea. Muir-Torre syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition of sebaceous tumor involving the gastrointestinal, endometrial, or urologic systems. Neither Muir-Torre syndrome nor HIV is associated with basal cell carcinoma.

pool.q: Examination of a 70-year-old patient discloses loss of eyelashes in conjunction with a thickened eyelid. Appropriate management consists of what procedure?
pool.rationale:
This clinical scenario typifies the ominous "masquerade syndrome" of sebaceous carcinoma (also termed sebaceous gland carcinoma, sebaceous cell carcinoma, sebaceous adenocarcinoma, meibomian gland carcinoma), which is a highly malignant and potentially lethal tumor that arises from the meibomian glands of the tarsal plate, the glands of Zeis associated with the eyelashes, or the sebaceous glands of the facial skin, eyebrow, or caruncle. Early in the course of the disease, patients can present with nonspecific findings of blepharitis, madarosis, and eyelid thickening. Since sebaceous carcinoma can arise from the tarsal plate or the eyelid margin, superficial shave biopsies may miss the underlying tumor, and a full-thickness biopsy is recommended for diagnosis.
The treatment of sebaceous carcinoma is wide excision or Mohs micrographic surgery. Because skip areas and pagetoid spread are common in sebaceous carcinoma, map biopsies of the conjunctiva may be considered. If pagetoid spread is present, then adjuvant cryotherapy may be used. External beam radiotherapy is not recommended for treatment of sebaceous carcinoma, as these tumors are relatively radioresistant.

pool.q: What approach is preferred for managing malignant melanoma of the eyelid?

options.a: wide surgical resection with permanent histological evaluation of resected margins
options.b: surgical excision with frozen section cytological evaluation of the resected margins
options.c: cryotherapy consisting of at least 3 freeze-thaw cycles of 30 seconds each

pool.rationale:
Two tissues do not freeze well for frozen section control: pigmented tissue and fat. Therefore, of the myriad malignancies that affect the ocular adnexa, 2 are not amenable to this technique: melanoma and sebaceous cell carcinoma. Both of these tumors are excised using permanent sectioning technique with rapid turnaround. Unfortunately, this can require multiple excisions over sequential days/weeks before reconstruction can be performed. Wide margins are recommended for melanoma. Some experts also recommend sentinel node biopsy.
Cryotherapy is typically reserved for a variety of conjunctival malignancies, and not eyelid melanoma. Topical 5-FU may be used to treat actinic keratoses and occasionally squamous cell carcinomas, but is not used in the management of cutaneous malignant melanomas.

pool.q: What muscle causes glabellar folds?
pool.rationale: The corrugator supercilii muscles cause glabellar folds. The frontalis causes transverse forehead rhytids. The orbicularis oculi muscles close the eyelids and depress the eyebrows. The nasalis muscle functions to compress the nasal cartilages.

pool.q: A full-thickness upper eyelid blepharotomy is created 13.5 mm above the eyelid margin in a 45-year-old woman with no surgical history and an upper eyelid crease of 9 mm above the eyelid margin. Through what structures does this incision pass, from anterior to posterior?

options.a: skin, orbicularis oculi, orbital septum, orbital fat, levator aponeurosis, Müller muscle, conjunctiva
options.b: skin, orbicularis oculi, orbital septum, capsulopalpebral fascia, Müller muscle, conjunctiva
options.c: skin, orbicularis oculi, retro-orbicularis oculi fat, orbital septum, levator muscle, Müller muscle, conjunctiva
options.d: skin, orbicularis oculi, orbital septum, orbital fat, levator aponeurosis, Müller muscle, tarsus, conjunctiva

pool.rationale:
"Skin, orbicularis oculi, orbital septum, capsulopalpebral fascia, Müller muscle, conjunctiva" is incorrect because the capsulopalpebral fascia is a lower eyelid structure and the levator aponeurosis is left out here. "Skin, orbicularis oculi, retro-orbicularis oculi fat, orbital septum, levator muscle, Müller muscle, conjunctiva" is incorrect because retro-orbicularis oculi fat is superior to the incision, and the levator muscle has already become the levator aponeurosis at the level of the incision. "Skin, orbicularis oculi, orbital septum, orbital fat, levator aponeurosis, Müller muscle, tarsus, conjunctiva" is incorrect because the lid incision is superior to the tarsus.
The skin on the eyelids is the thinnest skin in the body, lacking subcutaneous tissue. Posterior to the skin lies the orbicularis oculi muscle, divided into pretarsal, preseptal, and orbital portions. The pretarsal portion sits anterior to the tarsus, as the name would suggest, from the lid margin superiorly about 10 mm, to the superior edge of the tarsus near the lid crease. Superior to the upper lid crease, the orbicularis lies anterior to the orbital septum, an extension of periosteum from the arcus marginalis at the orbital rim.
Posterior to the orbital septum lie 2 orbital fat pads in the upper eyelid and the lacrimal gland laterally. The fat pads are just anterior to the levator muscle and aponeurosis. In white patients, the orbital septum fuses with the levator aponeurosis superior to the superior tarsal border. This marks the first time the anterior levator fibers are not bordered anteriorly by orbital fat and septum; as a result, their anterior extensions through the pretarsal orbicularis form the lid crease, which is 7-10 mm superior to the margin in the non-Asian eyelid.
Müller muscle, the other upper eyelid retractor, originates from the posterior surface of the levator muscle 14 mm superior to the superior tarsal border, approximating Whitnall ligament. This muscle inserts on the superior tarsus. Posterior to Müller muscle lies the conjunctiva, which extends inferiorly on the posterior side of the tarsus to the lid margin. In Asian eyelids, the septum fuses with the pretarsal levator aponeurosis and the orbital fat approaches the eyelid margin as a result, explaining the location of the Asian lid crease several millimeters from the eyelid margin.

pool.q: A 2-year-old child is brought into the clinic because the mother notes tears constantly running down the child’s face. There is no reflux on palpation of the lacrimal sac and there is no increased tear film height. There is a small tuft of eyelashes a few millimeters lateral to and above the eyelash line. The absence of discharge or increased tear film suggest that this symptom is not a result of an obstruction of the lacrimal system, a condition that could improve with either probing or probing and intubation of the lacrimal system. pool.q: What is the typical mode of spread of adenoid cystic carcinoma of the lacrimal gland?
pool.rationale: Although all of the modes listed (hematologic metastasis, lymphatic metastasis, local invasion only, perineural invasion) are possible for adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) of the lacrimal gland, the typical mode is perineural spread. One of the classic symptoms of ACC is pain or headache in the area of the tumor. ACC (as well as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma) harbors a particular neurotropism for sensory nerves, traveling along the nerve to gain entry into the skull base. Local spread through bone erosion may also occur. Regional lymphatic spread is uncommon, but distant metastasis, usually to the lung, eventually occurs in a significant number of patients.

pool.q: A 17-year-old adolescent boy reports experiencing left orbital pain and diplopia on upgaze for 3 days. His visual acuity and the results of his ocular examination are otherwise normal. He started taking oral antibiotics 24 hours prior, and a computed tomography (CT) scan shows a left superior subperiosteal abscess. What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.a: careful observation with monitoring for 48 hours
options.c: careful observation with monitoring for 24 hours

pool.rationale:
Although in this case surgical drainage is the best option, not all subperiosteal abscesses (SPAs) require surgical drainage. Isolated medial or inferior SPA in children younger than 9 years with underlying isolated ethmoid sinusitis, intact vision, and only moderate proptosis typically responds to medical therapy.
In addition, management may consist of careful observation unless any of the following criteria are present:
  • patient aged 9 years or older
  • presence of frontal sinusitis
  • non-medial SPA location
  • large SPA
  • suspicion of anaerobic infection (eg, presence of gas in abscess on CT)
  • recurrence of SPA after prior drainage
  • evidence of chronic sinusitis (eg, nasal polyps)
  • acute optic nerve or retinal compromise
  • infection of dental origin (anaerobic infection more likely)

pool.q: What are the primary contributing factors in the development of involutional entropion of the lower eyelid?

options.a: vertical laxity, tarsal conjunctival scarring, and orbicularis weakness
options.b: horizontal laxity, disinsertion of lower eyelid retractors, and orbicularis weakness
options.c: horizontal laxity, disinsertion of lower eyelid retractors, and orbicularis override
options.d: horizontal laxity, tarsal conjunctival scarring, and orbicularis override

pool.rationale:
Involutional entropion is primarily due to horizontal laxity and vertical instability, owing to disinsertion of the lower lid retractors. Orbicularis override is also a common feature, either due to soft tissue laxity or secondary to a spastic component. Keratopathy from entropion leads to a secondary orbicularis spasm as a protective measure for the cornea. However, because of the horizontal and vertical instability, the preseptal tarsus "overrides" the pretarsal orbicularis, resulting in exacerbation of the entropion and more keratopathy, creating a vicious cycle that may broken by placement of a rotational (Quickert) suture.
Tarsal conjunctival scarring (as seen in Stevens-Johnson syndrome, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, trachoma, etc.) certainly results in entropion, but this is classified as cicatricial rather than involutional. Orbicularis weakness would be more likely to cause ectropion, as is the case of paralytic ectropion.

pool.q: The risk of what condition is thought to be minimized by the enucleation of NLP (no light perception) eyes within 14 days of penetrating injury?
pool.rationale: Immune system sensitization to choroidal antigens is less likely if the inciting tissues are removed within 14 days of exposure. Therefore, some recommend enucleation of NLP (no light perception) eyes within 2 weeks following visually unrecoverable penetrating ocular injury to prevent sympathetic ophthalmia. Proliferative vitreoretinopathy may occur following penetrating injury, but its management with enucleation is not time-dependent. Similarly, bacterial endophthalmitis and/or phacoantigenic uveitis can be managed medically or by enucleation, and if surgical removal is necessary, it can be performed when required for medical management or cosmesis.

pool.q: During evaluation of a patient for lower lid blepharoplasty, the ophthalmologist realizes that the patient's lid problem is compounded by a descended midface. To resuspend the midface, the ophthalmologist recommends vertical support. To achieve the best result, what structure will require surgical suspension?
pool.rationale: The suborbicularis oculi fat (SOOF) plays an important role in the aging process of gradual gravitational descent of the midface soft tissues. Studies and surgical procedures suggest that elevation of the SOOF into its previous anatomical position restores more youthful contours in the lower eyelid and midfacial soft tissues. Conservative transconjunctival fat removal or redistribution may be utilized concurrently to achieve a more cosmetically desirable appearance. pool.q: A 5-year-old boy presents for evaluation of unilateral tearing for the past 2 months. In what population would the dye disappearance test (DDT) be best used?
pool.rationale:
The dye disappearance test (DDT) is used to assess lacrimal drainage outflow. This is a very good test in children, as it does not require probing or irrigation of the drainage system. This test is especially useful in the analysis of unilateral epiphora. Fluorescein dye is placed in the conjunctival fornices of both eyes, and a cobalt blue light is used to evaluate the tear film. Special attention is paid to the symmetry or asymmetry between the tear films of both eyes. The tear film is evaluated for 5 minutes. At this point, a well-functioning lacrimal drainage system should have cleared the dye from the tear film. Presence of dye or significant asymmetry indicates an obstruction or dysfunction of the drainage system.
The Jones I and II tests are also used to evaluate epiphora and lacrimal drainage. The Jones I test (primary dye test) evaluates lacrimal drainage under normal physiologic conditions. Fluorescein dye is placed into the conjunctival fornix and the dye is recovered by placing a cotton tipped applicator inside the nostril at the site of the nasolacrimal duct (NLD) ostium. This is tested at both 2 minutes and 5 minutes after initial application of dye in the conjunctival fornix. If dye is observed, then the NLD system is patent. If no dye is observed, then this may indicate an anatomic obstruction or dysfunction. However, there are many false negatives associated with this test, and thus, it is not frequently used.
The Jones II test is a nonphysiologic test and is performed if the Jones I test indicates a possible obstruction or dysfunction of the lacrimal drainage system. After the Jones I test is completed, the conjunctival fornix is irrigated to remove all dye. Next, the lacrimal drainage system is irrigated with saline only. A cotton-tipped applicator is again placed inside the nostril at the ostium of the NLD. If dye is detected, then this indicates a partial obstruction of the lower lacrimal sac or distal NLD. If only saline is retrieved, then no dye made its way into the lacrimal drainage system, thus indicating punctal or canalicular stenosis or physiologic dysfunction.

pool.q: What foramina and associated vessels are an ophthalmologist most likely to encounter while performing a decompression of the medial orbital wall?
pool.rationale:
The anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina (which contain the ethmoidal arteries and sensory nerves) penetrate the superior edge of the lamina papyracea at the frontoethmoidal suture and are therefore frequently encountered during medial orbital decompression. The ethmoidal foramina also serve as a reasonable anatomic landmark for the skull base. It is prudent for the orbital surgeon to dissect below the level of the foramina to avoid intracranial penetration.
The zygomaticofacial and zygomaticotemporal foramina are located in the lateral orbital wall. They are most often encountered during lateral orbital decompression, lateral orbitotomy, or tripod fracture repair.
The supraorbital foramen is found along the orbital roof and carries sensory input from the forehead.

pool.q: A surgeon approaches an inferior intraconal lesion through a lower lid medial orbitotomy. What nerve may be damaged in the intraconal space?
pool.rationale:
Both the trochlear (CN-IV) and supratrochlear (a sensory nerve branching from the frontal nerve) are located in the superior orbit and would be spared during an inferomedial orbitotomy. Of note, both travel in the extraconal space. The infraorbital nerve is protected within its canal along the lateral orbital floor and is also extraconal.
The oculomotor nerve (CN-III) is found in the intraconal space. It divides into a superior and inferior division either in the cavernous sinus or in the orbital apex, and arborizes significantly in the orbit to supply the medial, superior, and inferior rectus muscles, the inferior oblique muscle, and the levator muscle. It also carries parasympathetic supply to the globe.
In this particular scenario, CN-III would be the most likely nerve damaged during an inferomedial orbitotomy to explore the intraconal space.

pool.q: A new patient is diagnosed with right hemifacial spasm and treated with botulinum toxin. One month later, the patient complains that the left upper eyelid is retracted. pool.q: A 42-year-old woman has chronic epiphora, pain, and mucus discharge with palpation over the lacrimal sac. After 7 days of antibiotics, her symptoms have resolved. The patient described is an adult with a complete nasolacrimal duct obstruction, and history of recurrent dacryocystitis. The treatment of choice is dacryocystorhinostomy, which can be performed endoscopically and thereby achieve her goal of avoiding a visible scar. Lacrimal probing is not typically effective in adult patients with nasolacrimal duct obstruction.

pool.q: What abnormality is characteristic for cicatricial ectropion of the lower eyelid?
pool.rationale: Anterior lamellar deficiency is a hallmark of cicatricial ectropion. Lower eyelid laxity is a common pathologic change seen in patients with involutional ectropion. This laxity can involve the medial or lateral canthal tendon or both. Lower eyelid retractor disinsertion may also be a component of involutional ectropion and is typically manifested by tarsal ectropion, in which the palpebral conjunctival surface is outwardly rotated.

pool.q: What is the most common cause of pseudoptosis?
pool.rationale: The most common cause of pseudoptosis is dermatochalasis, which is redundant upper eyelid skin that hangs over the lashes and reduces the margin-reflex distance. Brow ptosis and enophthalmos can also cause reduction in the margin-reflex distance, but are not as common as dermatochalasis. Graves disease typically causes lid retraction, not ptosis.

pool.q: Darkly pigmented skin increases the risk of what complication of laser skin resurfacing?
pool.rationale: In the 1990s, an ultrapulsed carbon dioxide laser was developed that allowed skin resurfacing without the side effect of thermal-induced skin damage and scarring. Pauses between the pulses of the laser allow cooling of the tissue to minimize thermal damage. The CO2 laser can shrink skin and tighten collagen and is useful as an adjunct to blepharoplasty. Complications include eyelid retraction, exposure keratopathy, lagophthalmos, and ectropion. The CO2 laser is contraindicated in patients who have taken isotretinoin (Accutane) within the past 12 months, because skin healing is delayed. In addition, the CO2 laser is contraindicated in patients with active collagen vascular disorders, such as lupus. Caution must be used in patients with darker skin pigmentation, due to the risk of postoperative inflammatory hyperpigmentation. If patients have a history of herpes simplex, they are often treated preoperatively with antiviral medications to prevent an outbreak postoperatively that may result in scarring.

pool.q: Increased risk and severity of thyroid eye disease in patients with Graves hyperthyroidism are more likely in what group of patients?

options.c: patients with a high serum T4 level
options.d: patients in their 3rd decade of life

pool.rationale:
Thyroid eye disease (TED) disease is 6 times more common in women than in men. Peak incidence rates occur in age groups 40 to 44 years and 60 to 64 years in women, and 45 to 49 years and 65 to 69 years in men. Smoking is associated with increased risk and severity of TED. 
Patients can be hypothyroid, euthyroid, or hyperthyroid. Severity of TED usually does not parallel serum levels of T4 or T3. TED is associated with hyperthyroidism in 90% of patients, but 6% may be euthyroid.

pool.q: What historical characteristic of a lacrimal gland tumor is most suggestive of adenoid cystic carcinoma?

options.d: persistence of symptoms for longer than 1 year

pool.rationale: Adenoid cystic carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor of the lacrimal gland. This highly malignant tumor may cause pain because of perineural invasion and bone destruction. Proptosis, ptosis, and persistent symptoms for longer than 1 year are typical of the most common benign tumor of the lacrimal gland, pleomorphic adenoma.

pool.q: What orbital mass is most likely to change in size within minutes?
pool.rationale:
Orbital varices are low-flow vascular lesions resulting from vascular dysgenesis. At rest, the lesions are not engorged, and patients may exhibit enophthalmos. However, when the patient's head is in a dependent position or after a Valsalva maneuver, proptosis may occur. Characteristic enlargement of the varices may be seen on contrast-enhanced rapid spiral computed tomography (CT) during a Valsalva maneuver. Treatment is conservative and surgery is reserved for patients with vision-threatening compressive optic neuropathy or significant pain.
Capillary hemangiomas present at birth or in the first few weeks after birth. They may enlarge dramatically over the first 6-12 months of life and involute after the first year. Approximately 75% of lesions resolve in the first 4-5 years of life. They do not enlarge over the course of minutes. Capillary hemangiomas may be superficial involving the skin, presenting as a bright red, soft mass with dimpled texture, or they may be subcutaneous and blue in color. When hemangiomas are deeper within the orbit, they may present as a progressively enlarging mass without any overlying skin change. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is helpful in distinguishing capillary hemangiomas from other vascular malformations by demonstrating characteristic fine intralesional vascular channels and high blood flow. Orbital inflammatory syndrome and thyroid eye disease can demonstrate proptosis that is slowly progressive and does not fluctuate within minutes.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What bone is among those that make up the medial wall of the orbit?
pool.rationale:
The medial orbital wall is made up of 4 bones from anterior to posterior: the ascending process of the maxilla, the lacrimal bone, the ethmoid bone, and a portion of the sphenoid bone. There is a mnemonic for this: "SMELl with your nose" (S - sphenoid, M - maxilla, E - ethmoid, L - lacrimal, your nose - medial wall)
The palatine bone makes up a small portion of the posterior orbital floor. The zygoma, along with the greater wing of the sphenoid, makes up the robust lateral orbital wall. The nasal bone does not contribute to orbital bony anatomy.

pool.q: A patient presents with progressive monocular vision loss. Orbital computed tomography (CT) reveals narrowing of the optic canal and diffuse hyperostotic bones of the orbit, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicates absence of dural enhancement. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Fibrous dysplasia is a bone tumor in which normal cancellous bone is replaced by immature woven bone and fibrous cystic tissue. Involvement of the optic canal can lead to vision loss. CT imaging shows hyperostotic bone, and MRI shows lack of dural enhancement. Meningiomas typically show dural enhancement. Neurofibromatosis is associated with absence of the sphenoid rim, but not bony tumors. Although osteomas are bone lesions with hyperostosis, they typically have well-defined margins.

pool.q: The medial orbital wall includes what orbital bones?

options.a: frontal and lesser wing of sphenoid
options.c: greater wing of sphenoid and zygomatic
options.d: lesser wing of sphenoid, maxillary, ethmoid, lacrimal

pool.rationale: The medial orbital wall is composed of 4 bones: the sphenoid (lesser wing), maxillary, ethmoid, and the lacrimal (mnemonic: SMEL, since the medial wall is close to the nose). The palatine, maxillary, and zygomatic bones make up the orbital floor (mnemonic: PaM-Z). The greater wing of the sphenoid and the zygomatic bones make up the lateral orbital wall (mnemonic: great Z). The frontal bone and lesser wing of the sphenoid make up the orbital roof (mnemonic: "front-less").

pool.q: A patient with thyroid-related orbitopathy that has been stable for 2 years presents to her ophthalmologist to request help in improving her cosmetic appearance. She has prominent bilateral proptosis and an obvious large-angle esotropia and lid retraction in her right eye. In what order should the surgeries applicable to her condition be performed?

options.a: Eyelid surgery should be performed first, then decompression surgery, and then strabismus surgery.
options.b: Decompression surgery should be performed first, then strabismus surgery, and then eyelid surgery.
options.c: Decompression surgery should be performed first, then eyelid surgery, and then strabismus surgery.
options.d: The order does not necessarily matter; the most severe problem should be addressed first.

pool.rationale: As a general rule, surgery for thyroid eye disease should be delayed until the disease reaches a stable state for at least 6 to 9 months. Urgent surgery may be indicated when disease is so severe that the patient is at risk of compressive optic neuropathy or has severe corneal exposure refractory to medical management. When surgeries are undertaken, the order is very important. Orbital decompression procedures can alter the position of the globe and thus affect extraocular motility; they should be done before strabismus surgery. It is important to note that a balanced decompression can help minimize a change in strabismus. Likewise, muscle surgery can impact eyelid position, and thus, eyelid surgery should be performed last.

pool.q: A 24-year-old woman is referred for evaluation of the clinical finding seen in the figure. It has been present since birth. What condition is this patient at increased risk of developing?
pool.rationale: The patient described has oculodermal melanocytosis, also known as nevus of Ota. Although malignant transformation may occur, especially in white patients, no prophylactic treatment is recommended. Ten percent (10%) of patients with oculodermal melanocytosis also have glaucoma and pigmentation of the trabecular meshwork. There is no relationship with this condition to cataract formation. Multiple eyelid lentigines, which are flat, pigmented spots larger than ephelides, may be associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, which is associated with intestinal polyposis, with increased risk of colon cancer. Approximately 0.25% of patients with oculodermal melanocytosis develop a uveal melanoma, but there is no known relationship to the development of uveitis.

pool.q: What cranial suture are orbital dermoid cysts most commonly adjacent to?
pool.rationale: Orbital dermoid cysts are congenital choristomas lined by keratinized epithelium and dermal appendages (as opposed to epidermoid cysts, which are lined by only epidermis and do not contain dermal appendages). Usually recognized in childhood, they present as a mass in the superotemporal or superomedial quadrant of the orbit. Of the 2, the superotemporal quadrant along the frontozygomatic suture is most common. Less commonly, they may occur at the suture between the frontal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla. Dermoid cysts can be freely mobile or attached to the underlying periosteum.

pool.q: What clinical scenario is best for temporary (Quickert) sutures to correct lower lid entropion?

options.d: when a more definitive procedure cannot be performed

pool.rationale: Quickert suture is indicated as a temporizing solution for involutional, acute spastic entropion, and when a more definitive procedure cannot be performed. Quickert suture, as the name implies, can be performed quickly, but a downside is entropion recurrence when the suture is used as the sole intervention. If the lower lid retractor complex is disinserted, retractor advancement surgery is required. Cicatricial entropion requires addressing the underlying cause and often requires a tarsal fracture operation (mild to moderate cicatricial changes) or a tarsal plate graft (severe cicatricial changes).

pool.q: The histology shown in the figure is from a cystic lesion on the eyelid of a 30-year-old woman. The specimen was stained with H&E and is shown at 250x. The cytoplasm of the endothelial cells contains pigment that stains positive with periodic acid-Schiff. What is the diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The apocrine and eccrine glands of the eyelid are sweat glands. Any of these glands may give rise to one or multiple cysts. The histopathology of an apocrine hidrocystoma demonstrates endothelium composed of tall eosinophilic cells with characteristic apical snouts or decapitation secretion, which is evident in the image shown here. The cytoplasm of these cells contains granules of lipofuscin pigment that is PAS positive. Clinically, apocrine hidrocystomas often contain a brown fluid stained by this pigment.
Eccrine hidrocystomas appear clinically as soft, cystic lesions filled with a clear fluid that readily transilluminate. Histology shows a multilocular lumen that appears empty. The epithelial lining consists of a dual layer of cuboidal cells. Epidermal inclusion cysts are filled with laminated eosinophilic keratin and lined by keratinized squamous epithelial cells. Dermoid cysts are histologically similar to epidermal inclusion cysts but contain skin adnexal structures such as hair follicles and sebaceous glands.

pool.q: What is a characteristic finding in blepharophimosis–ptosis–epicanthus inversus syndrome (BPES)?
pool.rationale: The typical features of BPES, also known as blepharophimosis syndrome, are telecanthus, epicanthus inversus, and severe ptosis, usually with limited levator function. Hypertelorism, ectropion, and hypoplasia of the superior orbital rims can also occur. Dermatochalasis is not a typical finding in BPES.

pool.q: In what clinical scenario would a Müller muscle resection be an appropriate surgical approach to treating ptosis?

options.a: 3 mm ptosis, normal levator function, persistence of ptosis with instillation of a drop of 2.5% phenylephrine hydrochloride
options.b: 5 mm ptosis, poor levator function, 3 mm residual ptosis with instillation of a drop of 2.5% phenylephrine hydrochloride
options.c: 1 mm ptosis, normal levator function, resolution of ptosis with instillation of a drop of 2.5% phenylephrine hydrochloride
options.d: 1 mm ptosis, poor levator function, persistence of ptosis with instillation of a drop of 2.5% phenylephrine hydrochloride

pool.rationale: Müller muscle resection may be indicated when sympathetic innervation to Müller muscle has been damaged, as with Horner syndrome. Good candidates include those with mild ptosis (< 2mm), normal levator function, and resolution of ptosis with instillation of 2.5% phenylephrine hydrochloride. With significant ptosis or poor levator function, the surgeon should use accessory elevators of the eyelid in the repair.

pool.q: A 35-year-old woman with drooping upper eyelid skin associated with recurrent swelling has what condition?
pool.rationale:
Blepharochalasis is a rare familial variant of angioneurotic edema. It typically occurs in younger persons, most commonly young females, and is characterized by idiopathic episodes of inflammatory edema of the eyelids. As a result of recurrent bouts of inflammation and edema, the eyelid skin of a patient with blepharochalasis becomes thin and wrinkled, simulating the appearance of dermatochalasis. In addition, true ptosis, herniation of the orbital lobe of the lacrimal gland, atrophy of the orbital fat pads, and prominent eyelid vascularity may be associated with blepharochalasis. Surgical repair of the eyelid-skin changes and the ptosis that result from blepharochalasis may be complicated by repeated episodes of inflammation and edema, causing recurrence of the ptosis and other eyelid changes.
Dermatochalasis refers to redundancy of eyelid skin and is often associated with orbital fat prolapse. Benign essential blepharospasm (BEB) is a bilateral focal dystonia that is characterized by increased blinking and involuntary spasms of the periocular protractor muscles. Meige syndrome is a lower facial dystonia associated with BEB.

pool.q: An anophthalmic patient stopped wearing his 15-year-old prosthesis for 2 years. He has now tried to starting wearing it again, but is unable to retain it and complains that it feels "tight." On examination, he has shortened fornices. What intervention is recommended?

options.c: temporarily discontinue the use of the prosthesis

pool.rationale:
The patient has a contracted socket. Causes of contracted sockets include radiation treatment, extrusion of enucleation implants, severe initial injury (alkali burns or extensive lacerations), poor surgical technique, multiple socket operations, and removal of the conformer or prosthesis for prolonged periods. Orbital implant exchange will not solve this issue and may cause more difficulty for the patient wearing the prosthesis. Discontinuance of prosthesis use is also counterproductive, because the fornix may further contract if the prosthesis is left out for an extended period of time. Temporary tarsorrhaphy also does not alter the forniceal contraction that has caused the problem.
The best course of action in this case is forniceal reconstruction, usually with a mucosal graft (either buccal mucosa or contralateral conjunctiva). Stiffer graft with banked fascia, hard palate, ear cartilage, etc, may be used if significant lower lid retraction is also present and will help with deepening of the fornix.

pool.q: What medial orbital wall landmark most closely corresponds to the level of the cribriform plate?
pool.rationale: The anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina are located at the superior border of the ethmoid bone, at the expected level of the cribriform plate. The other choices listed (base of the lacrimal fossa, posterior margin of optic foramen, and orbital roof) do not correspond to this landmark.

pool.q: Incomplete development of what structure accounts for most cases of nasolacrimal duct blockage in infants?
pool.rationale: The valve of Hasner, at the distal end of the nasolacrimal duct, under the inferior turbinate, is the last part of the duct to develop. It causes obstruction in 5% of infants at birth, but patency usually occurs within several months of life. Infants may not be symptomatic initially, as normal lacrimation does not typically occur until around 6 weeks of age.

pool.q: What is the most common pathogen associated with canaliculitis?
pool.rationale:
Actinomyces israelii

Infection within the canaliculus is caused by a variety of bacteria, viruses, and mycotic organisms. The most common pathogen is a filamentous gram-positive rod, Actinomyces israelii. The other pathogens listed (Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa) can cause canaliculitis, but are not the most common causes.

pool.q: In the management of tarsal ectropion, what procedure should be added to horizontal tightening of the eyelid?

options.c: reformation of the lateral canthal angle
options.d: reattachment of the lower lid retractors

pool.rationale:
Involutional lower eyelid malpositions (ectropion and entropion) are caused by 2 main eyelid changes--horizontal and vertical laxity. In a typical involutional ectropion, horizontal tightening (typically by a lateral tarsal strip procedure) suffices. However, if retractor laxity, disinsertion, or dehiscence is present (known as tarsal ectropion), advancement and reattachment of the lower lid retractors provides vertical stability.
Reformation of the lateral canthal angle is an aesthetic maneuver to give the patient a sharp lateral canthal angle.
A medial spindle procedure shortens the posterior lamella of the medial eyelid and is a good option for punctal ectropion.
Skin grafting is used in cases of cicatricial ectropion to lengthen a shortened anterior lamella.

pool.q: What is the most common malignant tumor derived from the paranasal sinuses?
pool.rationale: Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common epithelial tumor secondarily invading the orbit. These malignancies usually arise within the maxillary sinuses, followed by the nasopharynx or the oropharynx. It is very uncommon for the other tumors listed (sebaceous cell carcinoma, melanoma, and basal cell carcinoma) to arise in the sinus.
