pool.q: A 35-year-old patient presents for follow-up after biopsy-proven lentigo simplex. How should the ophthalmologist respond to questions about the prognosis of the lesions?

options.a: Malignant transformation is more likely with adult onset.
options.b: The lesions do not progress to melanoma.
options.c: The lesions often progress to melanoma.
options.d: Malignant transformation is more likely with childhood onset.

pool.rationale: Simple lentigines are flat, pigmented spots larger in diameter than ephelides (freckles). They are benign and do not require treatment. Lentigo maligna is a different skin disorder that confers a higher risk of malignant melanoma. Lentigo maligna lesions are characterized by irregular shape and uneven pigmentation in older persons.

pool.q: The lacrimal sac sits proximate to what nasal structure?
pool.rationale:
The lacrimal fossa and lacrimal bone are located just anterior to the insertion of the middle turbinate. When viewing the lacrimal sac at an intranasal perspective, the lacrimal sac corresponds to the lateral nasal wall just anterior to the middle turbinate.
The nasolacrimal duct opens into the nose through an ostium under the inferior turbinate.
The uncinate process, a sickle-shaped process of bone on the medial wall of the ethmoidal labyrinth below the middle concha, is often removed during dacryocystorhinostomy to allow proper exposure of the superior aspect of the lacrimal passage.
The nasal cavity is divided into 2 nasal fossae by the nasal septum.

pool.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 1-week history of increasing proptosis. A computed tomography (CT) scan demonstrates a mass between the superior and medial recti. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary orbital malignancy of childhood. The average age of presentation is usually between 5 and 7 years, with sudden onset and rapid progression of unilateral proptosis. There is a marked adnexal response with edema and discoloration of eyelids. Ptosis and strabismus may also be present. Rhabdomyosarcomas arise from undifferentiated pluripotential mesenchymal elements in orbital soft tissues but not from the extraocular muscles themselves. The embryonal form is by far the most common type and has a predilection for the superonasal quadrant of the orbit.

pool.q: Histopathologic analysis of the affected tissue in this ocular condition would most likely demonstrate what finding?

options.c: immunofluorescent staining of basement membrane zone
options.d: admixture of acute and chronic inflammatory cells with numerous capillaries

pool.rationale:
Floppy eyelid syndrome (FES) is characterized by a flaccid upper tarsus that is easily everted and rubbery. This condition is often associated with a chronic papillary conjunctivitis. Due to the strong association with obstructive sleep apnea, the patient should be referred for appropriate sleep study.
Histopathologically, floppy eyelid syndrome demonstrates a marked decrease in elastin fibers in the tarsus. Elastotic or elastoid degeneration refers to actinic changes in pterygia and pingueculae with degenerated collagenous tissue demonstrating elastin staining, but it does not truly represent a decrease in elastin fibers. A mix of acute and chronic inflammatory cells with capillaries refers to the granulation tissue of pyogenic granuloma, which is neither pyogenic nor granulomatous.

pool.q: In a patient with insidious onset of an esotropia and hypotropia associated with lid retraction, what is the most likely etiology of the ocular misalignment?
pool.rationale:
The restrictive strabismus of thyroid eye disease (TED) most often causes hypotropia and esotropia from involvement of the inferior and medial recti muscles, respectively. Eyelid retraction is the most common clinical feature of TED (present in more than 90% of patients at some point in their clinical course), and TED is the most common cause of eyelid retraction.
A partial CN III palsy can cause ptosis and exotropia as well as hypotropia. Carotid cavernous fistula can produce multiple cranial nerve palsies but not eyelid retraction. Orbital inflammatory syndrome usually has a more rapid course and almost always is painful.

pool.q: What is the most common form of basal cell carcinoma?
pool.rationale:
Nodular BCC is the most common form of basal cell carcinoma. It presents as a firm, raised, pearly nodule that may have telangiectasias and central ulceration.
Morpheaform is less common and behaves more aggressively than the nodular form. Multicentric, or superficial, BCC can silently spread across the eyelid margin and mimic blepharitis. Central ulceration is a classic feature of basal cell carcinoma, but it is not a specific type. BCC lesions are most often located on the lower lid, and are typically painless. Conjunctival extension can occur, but it is not a typical feature of basal cell carcinoma.

pool.q: During the biopsy of a presumed lymphoma involving the conjunctiva, what should the pathologist ideally receive?
pool.rationale: During the biopsy of a lymphoma, the pathologist should ideally receive fresh tissue to be sent for cytogenetic/gene rearrangement/immunohistochemical studies to look for polyclonality (benign lymphoid hyperplasia) or monoclonality (lymphoma). While the concept that polyclonality denotes benignity and monoclonality signifies malignancy does not apply rigidly to ocular adnexal lymphoid lesions, it can be a useful prognostic tool. A portion of the tissue is later placed in a paraffin block for histologic sections. Conjunctival scraping is not indicated, electron microscopy is not performed routinely, and culture is not helpful.

pool.q: What is the cellular origin of lesion finding shown in the figure?
pool.rationale: A blue nevus is a dark blue-gray to blue-black, slightly elevated lesion that may be congenital or develop during childhood. It arises from dermal melanocytes. It has a very low malignant potential, but the lesions are routinely excised. Keratinocytes are epidermal cells that produce keratin. Chondrocytes are cells that contribute to collagen production. Keratocytes are corneal fibroblasts found in the corneal stroma. They are not pertinent to blue nevi.

pool.q: Biopsy of the nasopharyngeal mucosa in a patient with orbital apex syndrome reveals nonseptate, large branching hyphae on hematoxylin-eosin staining. What organism is responsible for the infection?
pool.rationale: Zygomycetes cause zygomycosis (also known as mucormycosis). Mucormycosis is the most common and devastating fungus infection of the orbit. Patients present with an orbital apex syndrome with sinusitis. The fungus directly invades blood vessels, causing vessel thrombosis (even central retinal artery thrombosis in rare cases). The tissue appears necrotic and a black eschar may be seen. Predisposing conditions include metabolic acidosis, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, organ transplant, renal failure, immunosuppression, and malignancies (such as lymphoma/leukemia). Microscopically nonseptate large branching hyphae are seen that stain with hematoxylin and eosin (unlike most fungi). Treatment is aggressive surgical debridement with intravenous amphotericin B. Even with aggressive treatment, outcomes can be poor. Serum eosinophilia is often seen with aspergillosis, and corticosteroids are sometimes indicated in the treatment of allergic aspergillosis sinusitis.

pool.q: What is the most likely cause of cicatricial entropion?
pool.rationale: Cicatricial entropion can have horizontal and vertical laxity as associated clinical findings; however, shortening of the posterior lamella is the initial inciting event. Conditions that can lead to cicatricial entropion include mucous membrane pemphigoid, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, trachoma, herpes zoster, and trauma (including surgery) affecting the conjunctiva. Trichiasis is usually a secondary process of cicatricial entropion and results in ocular irritation.

pool.q: Medial canthal reconstructions should be attached to what structure in order to maintain globe apposition?
pool.rationale: Reconstruction of the medial canthus is challenging due to the presence of the lacrimal outflow apparatus and the need for proper 3-dimensional positioning of the medial canthal tendon. The reconstruction must include attachment to the posterior lacrimal crest to restore the proper posterior curvature of the lid and avoid poor globe apposition. Attachment to the anterior lacrimal crest or to the nasal bone would be too anterior and not restore the proper antero-posterior position. Care must be taken to avoid damage to the lacrimal sac.

pool.q: A 32-year-old man is involved in a motor vehicle accident. He is intubated and sedated. His ophthalmic examination is limited, but the ophthalmologist detects an afferent pupillary defect of the right eye with normal intraocular pressure. Orbital and brain imaging shows no evidence of fractures, retrobulbar stranding, or intracranial abnormalities. What is the next step in management?
pool.rationale: The patient presents with an indirect traumatic optic neuropathy of the right eye, based on the afferent pupillary defect of the right eye without a history of eye problems before injury. There is no evidence of a direct traumatic optic neuropathy from bone fracture and no evidence of a retrobulbar hemorrhage (no retrobulbar stranding). Therefore, the patient has an indirect traumatic optic neuropathy. Studies have not shown that administration of high doses of intravenous methylprednisolone is superior to observation alone. Therefore, conservative observation is an appropriate course of action. Intracranial hemorrhage does not typically cause an afferent pupillary defect.

pool.q: A 54-year-old woman presented with pain, including left-eye enophthalmos and diplopia. Imaging revealed the following lesion with infiltration of the left orbit (see figures). What past medical history would be helpful in making the diagnosis?

options.d: travel to the Ohio River Valley

pool.rationale: Although virtually any cancer of the internal organs, hematopoietic system, or skin can metastasize to the orbit, most orbital metastases derive from lung, breast, and prostate tumors. The presence of pain, proptosis, inflammation, bone destruction, and early ophthalmoplegia suggests the possibility of metastatic carcinoma. Some 75% of patients have a history of a known primary tumor, but orbital metastasis is the presenting sign of cancer in 25% of patients. The extraocular muscles are frequently involved because of their abundant blood supply. The second most common site is the bone marrow space of the sphenoid bone because of the relatively high volume of low-flow blood in this area. Lytic destruction of this part of the lateral orbital wall is highly suggestive of metastatic disease. Elevation of serum carcinoembryonic antigen levels also may suggest a metastatic process. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy can be performed in the office and may obviate the need for orbitotomy and open biopsy.

pool.q: What is the first-line treatment for patients with symptomatic, acquired, complete nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO)?
pool.rationale: A DCR is the treatment of choice for most patients with acquired NLDO. Surgical indications include recurrent dacryocystitis, chronic mucoid reflux, painful distention of the lacrimal sac, and bothersome epiphora. A CDCR can be performed when one or both canaliculi are severely obstructed. The CDCR creates a complete bypass of the lacrimal drainage system. A canaliculodacryocystorhinostomy can be performed for total obstruction of the common canaliculus or if the lacrimal sac is sclerotic. These are not first-line treatments for acquired NLDO. Intubation and stenting is only effective for partial stenosis of the nasolacrimal duct and should not be attempted for complete NLDO.

pool.q: Over a 2-year interval, a patient's trichiasis of the left lower lid is treated 4 times with electrolysis and cryotherapy. For the past several months, his eye has become increasingly irritated. What possible sequela of treatment most likely explains these symptoms?
pool.rationale: Trichiasis is an acquired misdirection of the eyelashes. Management options include mechanical epilation, electrolysis, radiofrequency, cryotherapy, argon therapy, or full-thickness pentagonal resection. Cicatricial entropion is caused by vertical tarsoconjunctival contracture and internal rotation of the eyelid margin, resulting in irritation of the globe. Traumatic scarring, such as that caused by electrolysis, radiofrequency, or cryotherapy burns from trichiasis treatment, can lead to cicatricial entropion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A physician is asked to examine a patient with periorbital trauma. What would be the best way to determine whether there has been an avulsion of the medial or lateral canthal tendon?

options.a: pulling the eyelid and palpating the insertions of the tendon
options.b: observing the contour of the eyelids and the position of the puncta
options.c: reviewing the medical history and the mechanism of the trauma
options.d: probing and irrigating the lacrimal outflow

pool.rationale: Although observing the contour of the eyelids and the position of the puncta, reviewing the medical history and the mechanism of the trauma, and probing and irrigating the lacrimal outflow may all provide some information about the status of the canthal tendons and their possible need for repair, the integrity of the inferior and superior limbs of the medial or lateral canthal tendon can be assessed definitively by grasping each eyelid with toothed forceps and tugging away from the injury while palpating the insertion of the tendon. Medial canthal tendon avulsion should be suspected when there is rounding of the medial canthal angle and acquired telecanthus. Probing and irrigation assess tear outflow, which could be affected by a medial canthal injury.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A well-circumscribed orbital mass is noted in an otherwise asymptomatic 42-year-old man who is undergoing magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for workup of chronic headaches. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The most common primary orbital tumor in adults is cavernous venous malformation [formerly cavernous hemangioma]. Cavernous venous malformation is a benign, very slow-moving tumor with characteristic features on MRI. It is well tolerated and well circumscribed on imaging. The most common malignant orbital tumor in adults, depending on the clinical series, is non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma; metastatic and secondary tumors rival lymphoma in incidence in patients older than 60 years.
Dermoid cyst is a congenital tumor that typically occurs either superolaterally or superonasally in the orbit in the area where 2 advancing waves of neural crest cells meet and potentially pinch off ectoderm. As a general rule, pediatric dermoid cysts occur more anteriorly within the orbit (and are therefore evident in patients at a young age), while dermoids discovered in adults lie deeper and hide from clinical view for decades.
Schwannoma is also a benign, well-circumscribed orbital lesion of adults, arising from the Schwann cells insulating sensory nerves. A superior location within the orbit is the most frequent.
Capillary hemangioma (also known as hemangioma of infancy) is a rapidly proliferating, benign lesion seen exclusively in young children. Capillary hemangioma never occurs in adults.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Severe pain and decreased vision immediately after an orbitotomy are concerning for what finding?
pool.rationale:
This scenario is concerning for orbital hemorrhage. Visual acuity should be checked at frequent intervals postoperatively, and patching of the operative site should be discouraged because it can delay diagnosis of a postoperative hemorrhage.
Postoperative inflammation can cause pain but should not decrease the visual acuity. Measures used to reduce postoperative edema and inflammation are elevation of the head, iced compresses on the eyelids, administration of systemic steroids, and placement of a drain. Ice packs minimize swelling and still allow frequent observation of the operative site and vision monitoring.
Entrapped orbital contents can cause a restrictive strabismus, but visual acuity should remain stable. A retained orbital foreign body may cause various symptoms, depending on the type of foreign body and the location within the orbit.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with tearing that has lasted for several weeks. Upon examination, the ophthalmologist finds a pouting lower punctum and mucopurulent discharge with palpation of the punctum. Irrigation through the superior canalicular system is normal. Warm compresses are applied and antibiotics are given, with minimal improvement. What is the next step in management?
pool.rationale: The scenario describes a patient with acute canaliculitis, which is an infectious process most commonly caused by Actinomyces israelii. This organism produces concretions that mechanically obstruct tear flow; therefore, treatment is required. Medical treatment with topical or oral antibiotics may be an option if the patient presents early; however, some patients will require canaliculotomy to debride the stones. Topical steroids are not effective to treat canaliculitis. Dacryocystorhinostomy and conjunctival dacryocystorhinostomy are surgical procedures that in rare cases may be required, but not as first-line treatment.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Which orbital wall should not be removed to achieve orbital decompression?
pool.rationale: The goal of orbital decompression is to create space within the orbit to allow enlarged muscles and orbital fat to expand into additional space to relieve pressure on the optic nerve and its blood supply, as well as to reduce proptosis. It is usually performed in patients with thyroid eye disease. Disruption of the roof of the orbit could lead to complications involving the anterior cranial fossa.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What does the sum of MRD1 and MRD2 represent?

options.d: ratio of lid position to function

pool.rationale: MRD stands for margin reflex distance. The MRD1 is the distance between the upper eyelid margin and the corneal light reflex. The MRD2 is the distance between the corneal light reflex and the lower eyelid margin. The sum of MRD1 and MRD2 equals the vertical interpalpebral fissure height. Levator function is estimated by measuring the upper eyelid excursion from downgaze to upgaze with frontalis muscle function negated. Orbicularis tone can be assessed with eyelid closure against resistance. The combination of lid position (degree of ptosis) and function (lid excursion) can help determine whether a frontalis sling is required.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What pattern or type of nonspecific orbital inflammation (NSOI) responds poorly to systemic steroids?
pool.rationale: Sclerosing NSOI is a fibrotic variant of NSOI that responds poorly to steroids and to low-dose fractionated radiotherapy. It typically requires more aggressive immunosuppression with agents such as cyclosporine, methotrexate, or cyclophosphamide. NSOI can occur in several locations or patterns including myositis, dacryoadenitis, scleritis, orbital apex, or diffuse inflammation throughout the orbit. These other types typically respond well to systemic steroids.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For an infant with congenital anophthalmos, what additional clinical feature might an ophthalmologist expect to find?

options.a: increased horizontal and vertical palpebral fissure distances

pool.rationale:
Congenital anophthalmia often results in poor orbital growth. It appears that a normal globe is necessary to stimulate growth of the surrounding orbital bones, and lack of a globe in infants or very young children results in significant facial asymmetry. Maxillary hypoplasia may also occur. Patients with anophthalmia typically have horizontal and vertical shortening of their palpebral fissures. Microphthalmia with or without cyst is a separate entity and not true anophthalmia, but can also result in a hypoplastic orbit. 
A variety of maneuvers may help to stimulate orbital growth in cases of congenital anophthalmia, including progressively larger conformers, tissue expanders placed in the orbit, and dermis fat grafts, which have been shown to grow with the child.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In a patient with an orbital fracture, what can rhinorrhea be an indication of?
pool.rationale:
Most orbital fractures involve the orbital floor, leading to hypoesthesia and an elevation deficit if the inferior rectus is entrapped. However, orbital roof fractures can occur in children with relatively low-energy blunt trauma. This is because the frontal sinuses have not developed, and there is nothing to absorb energy as it extends along the orbital roof. The cribriform plate can become involved with the development of a cerebrospinal fluid leak, which can present as clear rhinorrhea.
Nasolacrimal sac injury, tripod fracture, and nasal fracture are not the most likely associated findings in this case.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What lid structure should be purposefully left open in a lid repair following penetrating trauma?
pool.rationale: When perforated, the orbital septum should not be repaired, because this would inevitably cause horizontal scarring and shortening. Prolapsed fat can be repositioned, but the septum will close on its own during the healing process, and skin closure will usually hold prolapsed fat back. All of the other structures mentioned (the medial canthal tendon, levator aponeurosis, and lateral canthal tendon) must be assessed after orbital trauma. If injured, they must be reattached in order to restore support and functionality of the lids.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Middle lamellar deficiency most commonly results from surgical or traumatic shortening of what structure?
pool.rationale: Middle lamellar deficiency results from shortening of the orbital septum and surrounding tissues and is generally caused by trauma or surgery. The tarsal plate, conjunctiva, and lower eyelid retractors are part of the posterior lamella. The anterior lamella includes the skin and orbicularis muscle. The clinical findings associated with middle lamella injury include eyelid retraction in the presence of normal amounts of skin and conjunctiva, inferior keratoconjunctivitis, and an eyelid that is usually stiff or tethered to the rim. Middle lamellar deficiency can also be associated with anterior and posterior lamellar eyelid scarring. Surgical correction usually requires lysis of cicatrix (including septal scarring) and possible placement of a spacer graft.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What surgical step during naso-orbital ethmoid fracture repair is critical to prevent poor apposition of medial eyelid to globe postoperatively?

options.c: posterior attachment of medial canthal tendon to region of posterior lacrimal crest
options.d: bone grafts to restore normal contour and projection of nose

pool.rationale:
Nasoethmoidal complex (NEC) fractures often result in rounding of the medial canthal angle and lacrimal drainage injury. In most cases, the medial canthal tendon (MCT) attachments to bone remain intact, but the MCT is incorrectly positioned because of the displaced bone fragment.
The main difficulty in MCT repositioning in NEC fractures is obtaining the correct posterior vector. Anatomically, the MCT consists of 2 limbs (anterior and posterior), which splay around the lacrimal sac and attach to their respective lacrimal crests. The key to MCT reconstruction is the posterior lacrimal crest attachment; more anterior attachment of the MCT will result in medial ectropion. Not infrequently, the posterior lacrimal crest is involved in the NEC fracture and is unstable. The posterior lacrimal crest positioning of the MCT must therefore be achieved through other means.
If the underlying bone of the NEC fracture is not stable, transnasal wiring will not work: The wire will simply migrate anteriorly because of inadequate bony support. One effective method for MCT reconstruction in NEC fracture is to cantilever a miniplate posteriorly into the medial orbit from stable anterior nasal bone. One of the holes of the miniplate serves as an anchor for the MCT repair.
Lacrimal drainage injury is also common in NEC fractures, but routine intubation is usually not recommended. Intubation may be unnecessary and is often difficult because of soft tissue swelling and underlying fracture; attempted intubation may result in a false passage of the tubes and further injury to the lacrimal sac or nasolacrimal duct. If lacrimal obstruction occurs from the NEC fracture, it can be repaired at a later date with dacryocystorhinostomy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department after suffering a dog bite to the face. What is the most likely ocular or periocular injury in this case?

options.c: laceration of the lacrimal drainage system

pool.rationale:
Periocular dog bite injuries are especially common in children younger than 10 years. However, except in severe dog bites from aggressive breeds, orbital fracture and globe rupture are distinctly uncommon, occurring in 2% to 3% of cases. Intraocular injuries as a whole are uncommon and are usually due to globe contusion (eg, commotio retinae, traumatic iritis).
Lacerations of the canaliculi and/or the lacrimal sac occur frequently with periocular dog bites, presumably because of the animal's natural tendency to bite the victim at the snout (or nose). Any medial lid laceration from a dog bite almost invariably involves the lacrimal drainage system, and if the child cannot be probed and irrigated during initial evaluation, they should be examined under anesthesia with the assumption that canalicular/lacrimal sac repair will be needed.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In what demographic are orbital roof fractures most common?
pool.rationale: Orbital roof fractures are usually caused by blunt trauma or projectile injuries. They are more common in younger children whose frontal sinuses have not yet pneumatized. The frontal sinus is the last to pneumatize, usually starting at around age 7 and completing development by mid-teenage years. In addition, the cranial vault is relatively larger in comparison to the mid-face in young children, making frontal impact more likely. Older patients' frontal sinuses act as a crumple zone, preventing extension to the orbital roof. Given that complications such as intracranial injuries, cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea, and pneumocephalus can occur, consultation with the neurosurgery department is recommended.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 17-year-old boy has a pigmented eyelid lesion. Complete excision of the lesion shows it to be an ephelis (freckle). How should the patient's follow-up be managed?

options.a: Return for regular postoperative wound care only.
options.b: Return every 3 months for evaluation of new lesions.
options.c: Return every 12 months for evaluation for new lesions.
options.d: Return every 6 months for evaluation of recurrence.

pool.rationale: An ephelis, or a freckle, is a small, flat, brown spot on the skin. Ephelides are on the basal layer of the epidermis, and the number of epidermal melanocytes is not increased, but they extrude more than the usual amount of pigment onto the epidermal basal cell layer. Once completely excised they do not return. No treatment is necessary other than sun protection. Therefore, follow-up should be for wound care only.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The patient shown in the photo presents with a history of dry eye and chalazion incision and drainage. He wants the ophthalmologist to excise the "rotten annoyance" again. He admits that he is not consistent with warm compresses and lid scrubs. What would be the most appropriate procedure or treatment recommendation at this time?
pool.rationale:
Carcinoma of the sebaceous glands is highly malignant. It can be missed, since it may simulate the more common chalazia and chronic blepharitis. (It can also be confused with basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma, mucous membrane pemphigoid, superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis, or pannus associated with adult inclusion conjunctivitis.) 
Sebaceous adenocarcinoma can arise from meibomian glands in the tarsal plate, glands of Zeis (associated with eyelashes) (see Figure 1 for eyelid anatomy review) or sebaceous glands of the caruncle, eyebrow or facial skin. In the photograph, there is a yellow lesion in the upper eyelid on the margin and tarsal conjunctiva. It is yellow due to lipid material, which may prompt the examiner to think of sebaceous gland carcinoma (the neoplastic cells have lipid material within them); however, the sign, along with the history of the recurrent chalazion, that must lead the examiner to suspect malignancy is the associated loss of eyelashes (madarosis) in the area of the lesion. The tumor typically destroys the follicles of the cilia and thus eyelashes can no longer be supported. Effacement of the meibomian gland orifices also occurs, as can be seen in the photograph. (Of note, per the BCSC, staphylococcal blepharitis can also cause madarosis; thus, it is worth pointing out that having the history of a nodule that then causes madarosis is more characteristic of sebaceous adenocarcinoma.)
It is also good to be aware that marked conjunctival inflammation and hyperemia may be present with sebaceous carcinoma, especially with pagetoid spread of tumor cells. Pagetoid spread may be seen on examination as a fine papillary elevation of the tarsal conjunctiva. Intraepidermal growth may lead to extension from the tarsal plate across the palpebral and bulbar conjunctiva and even onto cornea with replacement of corneal epithelium with tumor cells.
To evaluate for sebaceous adenocarcinoma, a full-thickness eyelid biopsy or full-thickness tarsal punch biopsy is recommended, as the lesion may originate in the tarsal plate or in the eyelid margin. Because the rate of misdiagnosis is high among general pathologists, the clinician should ask for special stains or ask for outside consultation if clinical suspicion is high.
The history of recurrent nodule with now-associated madarosis suggests malignancy and not an inflammatory nodule, such as a chalazion or pyogenic granuloma, which could be treated with intralesional steroid.
The history of recurrent nodule, now with the presence of madarosis, suggests malignancy and not a chalazion or benign process such as rosacea. Tetracyclines are used in chronic blepharitis for their anti-inflammatory properties, especially if there is ocular rosacea.
Sebaceous adenocarcinomas start in the tarsus. Shaving the superficial portion of the nodule would not reach the tarsus and pathology may only reveal chronic inflammation and miss the underlying tumor.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common bacterial pathogen in acute dacryocystitis?
pool.rationale:
Streptococcus pneumoniae

Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause of acute dacryocystitis. Other gram-positive bacteria, such as Staphylococcus epidermidis, occur less commonly. Gram-negative organisms may cause disease in patients who are diabetic or immunocompromised, or in nursing home environments with atypical pathogens present.
Actinomyces israelii is the most common cause of acute canaliculitis. The most common cause of acute dacryocystitis is a complete nasolacrimal duct obstruction that leads to tear stasis and infection. Complications of dacryocystitis include dacryocystocele, chronic conjunctivitis, and cellulitis. Probing and irrigation of the nasolacrimal duct should be avoided until the infection resolves, as it can be extremely painful. Empiric treatment is with oral antibiotics, most commonly with amoxicillin (Augmentin) or cephalexin (Keflex). Any abscess formation should be incised and drained and left open to heal by second intention. If the infection does not clear with oral antibiotics, a dacryocystorhinostomy is often required to relieve the obstruction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A child is born with craniofacial abnormalities and fingers that are fused together. What syndrome is the child most likely to have?
pool.rationale:
Craniosynostosis is the premature closure of one or more of the sutures of the skull bones, which results in various cranial abnormalities. Hypertelorism and proptosis are features commonly seen in these syndromes. Apert syndrome is a craniosynostosis characterized by syndactyly.
Crouzon syndrome is the most common craniosynostosis and syndactyly is absent. Treacher Collins and Goldenhar syndromes are a result of craniofacial clefting abnormalities. Treacher Collins-Franceschetti syndrome is also known as mandibulofacial dysostosis and commonly exhibits an underdeveloped lower jaw. Goldenhar syndrome is also known as oculoauriculovertebral syndrome and is marked by incomplete development of the first and second branchial arches, resulting in unilateral ear, nose, soft palate, lip, and mandible deformities. It is associated with limbal dermoids and strabismus.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the cell most likely to act as both target and effector in Graves ophthalmopathy?
pool.rationale: Orbital fibroblasts are embryologically derived from the neural crest and possess developmental plasticity. They express CD40 receptors, generally found on B cells. When engaged by T-cell-bound CD154, fibroblast proinflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), IL-8, and prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), are upregulated, which in turn increases the synthesis of hyaluronan and glycosaminoglycan (GAG). Circulating immunoglobulin (IgG) may also stimulate orbital fibroblasts to secrete GAG and other cytokines that trigger orbital inflammation. Furthermore, signaling through thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor (TSH-R) on orbital fibroblasts may promote adipogenesis, thereby stimulating the expansion of the orbital fat compartments seen in patients with Graves ophthalmopathy.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What clinical feature results from downward displacement of the suborbicularis oculi fat pads?

options.a: decrease in the depth of the nasolabial folds

pool.rationale: Descent of the suborbicularis oculi fat accounts for the midface ptosis seen in the aging face. It causes an increase in the prominence of the nasolabial fold, not a decrease. Being below the eye, it does not contribute to brow ptosis or redundant upper lid skin.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Pulsatile exophthalmos is most closely associated with what neuro-oculocutaneous disorder?
pool.rationale:
Orbital pulsations can occur in various situations and can often be divided, depending on the presence or absence of a bruit. With bruits, pulsations can be seen in carotid cavernous fistulas, orbital arteriovenous fistulas, and dural arteriovenous fistulas. Without bruits, they can be found in meningoencephaloceles, neurofibromatosis 1 (NF1), and in cases involving orbital roof defects, such as removal of the orbital roof. Sphenoid wing dysplasia or aplasia in NF1 is associated with this orbital finding. Patients with NF1 with pulsatile proptosis have sphenoid wing dysplasia or aplasia.
Tuberous sclerosis, von Hippel-Lindau disease, and neurofibromatosis type 2 are other neuro-oculocutaneous disorders (phakomatoses) but are not associated with pulsatile exophthalmos.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 30-year-old man was using an electric power saw on a piece of wood and hit a nail. He noticed a sharp pain in the left eye, with worsening vision over the next 2 days. He was not wearing goggles. He presents with visual acuity of 20/20 and redness and chemosis inferotemporally in his left eye 4 mm from the limbus. The pupil is round and reactive. Dilated examination is remarkable for a localized hemorrhage in the inferior vitreous, but no foreign body is visualized. What is the next appropriate step in management?

options.c: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the orbits

pool.rationale:
The history and appearance in this scenario are highly suggestive of an occult ocular or orbital foreign body (high-velocity projectile). Prior to a surgical intervention, urgent imaging is necessary to determine the extent of the injury and the presence or absence of a foreign body that may require removal. CT scanning is the study of choice, although plain films may be used in select cases.
Operative exploration without imaging is inappropriate in the event that an occult foreign body is present. Close observation would be inappropriate in this scenario, based on the high suspicion for a penetrating ocular injury and possible foreign body.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 59-year-old patient with diabetes mellitus presents with a severe, necrotizing, soft-tissue infection involving the right eyelids, temple, and scalp. What initial intervention should be considered when treating this patient?

options.b: admittance for observation and blood cultures

pool.rationale: Necrotizing fasciitis is a severe, vision-threatening or life-threatening bacterial infection of the subcutaneous soft tissues (superficial and deep fasciae) that requires early surgical debridement, along with broad spectrum intravenous (IV) antibiotics. The most common organism responsible is group A beta-hemolytic streptococcus, but a variety of organisms including aerobic and anaerobic, gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria may cause this disorder.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the condition in which eyelashes originating from the normal anatomic position are misdirected and curve in toward the cornea?
pool.rationale: Trichiasis is misdirection of the lashes with a normal origin from the anterior aspect of the lid. Distichiasis is the abnormal growth of lashes from the meibomian gland orifices. Hypertrichosis is the excess growth of hair. Trichomegaly is a congenital condition in which the eyelashes are abnormally long, greater than 12 mm in the central area and 8 mm in the peripheral.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What finding on orbital imaging is suggestive of a carotid-cavernous fistula?
pool.rationale:
Carotid-cavernous fistula (CCF) is an abnormal communication between the venous plexus of the cavernous sinus and the internal carotid artery (ICA), the external carotid artery (ECA), or both. A variety of classification schema exist, but for the ophthalmologist a designation of direct (ICA directly feeding the cavernous sinus) or indirect (a branch of the ICA/ECA feeding the cavernous sinus) CCF suffices.
The major venous drainage for the orbit is via the superior ophthalmic vein (SOV) into the cavernous sinus. If the cavernous sinus is backed up with arterial blood, orbital outflow is blocked, with resultant congestive orbitopathy, arterialization of the conjunctival vessels, and increased intraocular pressure from increased episcleral venous pressure.
Typical findings of CCF on computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are enlargement of the SOV and mild to moderate enlargement of the extraocular muscles from venous engorgement (sometimes confused with thyroid eye disease). The angular vein may be enlarged on cerebral arteriography, but typically does not manifest on CT or MRI. Neither the optic nerve sheath nor the ophthalmic artery shows abnormality on imaging. On occasion, MRI may also show thrombus within the SOV if spontaneous closure is occurring.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What location of periocular lymphoma has the highest association with systemic lymphoma?
pool.rationale: The risk of having or developing systemic non-Hodgkin lymphoma is lowest for conjunctival lesions, greater for orbital lesions, and highest for lesions arising in the eyelid. Lymphoid lesions developing in the fossa of the lacrimal gland may carry a greater risk of systemic disease than those occurring elsewhere in the orbit. Bilateral periocular involvement markedly increases the risk of systemic disease, but such involvement is not definitive evidence of systemic disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 30-year-old woman with blepharoptosis, telecanthus, and epicanthus inversus is concerned about having children with droopy lids. What is the probability of this happening with her first child?
pool.rationale: Blepharophimosis–ptosis–epicanthus inversus syndrome (BPES), also called blepharophimosis syndrome, is an autosomal dominantly inherited blepharophimosis, usually presenting with telecanthus, epicanthus inversus (fold of skin extending from the lower to upper eyelid), and severe ptosis. The syndrome is caused by mutations in the FOXL2 gene, located on chromosome 3.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 45-year-old woman has bilateral lower lid retraction and ectropion 1 year after cosmetic blepharoplasty. There is a vertical deficiency of anterior lamella of the lower lids. What  procedure is preferred to treat the ectropion?
pool.rationale:
Reconstruction of the eyelid, whether necessitated by trauma or a surgical intervention, requires reestablishment of the lamellar planes. The eyelid has an anterior and posterior lamella, with the posterior lamella consisting of the conjunctiva, tarsus, and lower lid retractors. The anterior lamella consists of skin and muscle. 
With an anterior lamellar deficiency, the skin and muscle needs to be augmented. The most appropriate option is a full-thickness skin graft.
A free tarsal graft augments the posterior lamella, and a Hughes flap is a tarsoconjunctival flap from the upper lid used to reconstruct the posterior lamella, often after surgery for skin cancer.

pool.q: During conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR), where is a Jones tube best positioned?
pool.rationale:
Positioning and angulation of a Jones tube are critical for its success. A CDCR bypasses the lacrimal anatomy and allows tears to drain directly from the lids and eye into the nasal cavity via capillary action of the glass Jones tube. The lacrimal sac is normally found along the anterior aspect of the middle meatus and extends superiorly to the root of the middle turbinate. The Jones tube passes through the lacrimal sac and, similarly to a dacryocystorhinostomy, passes through a surgical osteotomy in the medial wall of the sac and lateral wall of the nasal cavity. Positioning the Jones tube just anterior to the middle turbinate provides the correct angulation for tear drainage.
The valve of Hasner is located in the inferior meatus, beneath the inferior turbinate. It would be extremely difficult to position the tip of the Jones tube in this location because of the length, amount of bone, and acute angulation.
Positioning the tip of the Jones tube against the nasal septum would defeat the tube's purpose: The tip of the tube must be free of obstruction to work. It is not uncommon for Jones tubes to migrate against the nasal septum, requiring either repositioning or exchange.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An otherwise healthy 12-year-old boy with no prior ocular history presents to the office for an eye examination. He has a pattern of incomplete hair loss on the scalp. The remaining hairs on his scalp have variable length. He is also missing hair from part of his left eyebrow. According to his parents, the patient has been acting distant ever since their divorce 3 months ago. What is the next appropriate action?
pool.rationale:
The patient presents with trichotillomania. This disorder is seen most commonly in patients aged 9 to 13 years old. It is characterized by the compulsive urge to pull out one’s own hair. Typically the patient presents with hair loss on the scalp or eyebrows or eyelashes. The remaining hair on the scalp may have variable lengthens due to repeated hair removal. Stress is thought to be a precipitating factor. Consultation with a psychologist or psychiatrist to evaluate the causes of this behavior is the recommended treatment.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have risks that are beyond the scope of an ophthalmology visit, but may be effective treatment. Atomoxetine (Strattera) is a selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor used to treat attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. With the classic appearance of hair in several stages of growth, skin biopsy is not recommended at this time.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What imaging modality is most appropriate in the evaluation of blunt orbital trauma?
pool.rationale: Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are both important imaging modalities in the detection and characterization of orbital and ocular diseases. For evaluating a trauma, however, CT is currently the primary and single most–useful orbital imaging technique. It is often readily available and rapidly provides the information necessary for decision making. Although contrast agents can be used, they are not necessary for orbital evaluation following trauma. MRI generally provides better tissue contrast than CT; however, in most orbital conditions, the orbital fat provides sufficient natural tissue contrast to allow ready visualization of orbital tumors on CT.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Measuring eyelid excursion from extreme downgaze to extreme upgaze evaluates what aspect of eyelid function?
pool.rationale: Measuring eyelid excursion from extreme downgaze to extreme upgaze is a method to evaluate levator function and is helpful in determining which surgical procedure may be most effective for treatment of ptosis. Levator advancement is less effective in patients with poor levator function. Lid lag refers to immobility or lagging of the upper eyelid in downgaze and may be associated with Graves orbitopathy. Lagophthalmos is the inability to close the eye completely. The degree of ptosis is judged from the interpalpebral measurement, not by measuring eyelid excursion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient has sustained a full-thickness laceration to the central lower eyelid that involves the margin. What is the most appropriate management?

options.a: realignment of the tarsus with partial-thickness sutures and flush realignment of the eyelid margin with vertical mattress sutures
options.b: realignment of the tarsus with full-thickness sutures and flush realignment of the eyelid margin with vertical mattress sutures
options.c: realignment of the tarsus with full-thickness sutures and eversion of the eyelid margin with vertical mattress sutures
options.d: realignment of the tarsus with partial-thickness sutures and eversion of the eyelid margin with vertical mattress sutures

pool.rationale:
Full-thickness lacerations involving the eyelid margin require repair of the tarsal plate, with attention to the lid margin to prevent formation of a notch.
The tarsus is reapproximated with partial-thickness sutures, because full-thickness tarsal sutures would typically cause a corneal abrasion. The tails of the partial-thickness sutures should also be directed anteriorly.
The lid margin is best approximated with a vertical mattress suture. To prevent late notch formation, the margin is best reapproximated with an eversion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Acquired nasolacrimal duct obstruction in adults is effectively treated using what procedure?
pool.rationale:
Dacryocystorhinostomy is the treatment of choice for most adults with acquired nasolacrimal duct obstruction. This procedure involves the creation of an anastomosis between the lacrimal sac and the nasal cavity through a bony ostium.
Infracture of inferior turbinate can be performed during probing of the nasolacrimal system for congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, if the inferior turbinate is lateralized against the nasolacrimal duct.
Conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy is performed when the canalicular system has failed (ie, when one or both canaliculi are obstructed) and consists of bypassing the lacrimal drainage system entirely and inserting a Jones tube.
Probing of the nasolacrimal duct may be used to treat congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction in children.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common site for metastasis to the orbit?
pool.rationale: In adults, the most common metastatic tumors to the orbit are from the breast and lung. Signs of metastasis to the orbit include pain, proptosis, inflammation, bone destruction, and early ophthalmoplegia. The most common site for metastasis is the extraocular muscles because of their abundant vascular supply. The bone marrow space of the sphenoid bone is the second most common site of metastasis because of the high volume of low-flow blood in this area.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Sebaceous carcinoma is most likely to arise from what ocular adnexal gland?
pool.rationale:
Sebaceous carcinoma (also termed sebaceous gland carcinoma, sebaceous cell carcinoma, sebaceous adenocarcinoma, meibomian gland carcinoma) arises from sebaceous glands. The 2 sebaceous glands present in the periocular region are the meibomian glands of the tarsal plate and the glands of Zeis that lie along the cilia of the lid; both are examples of holocrine glands.
The glands of Moll are apocrine sweat glands. The accessory glands of Krause (located deep within the superior fornix) and Wolfring (located just above the superior border of the tarsus) are exocrine glands.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What orbital fracture is closely associated with trismus as a symptom?
pool.rationale:
Zygomatic fractures (tripod fractures, malar complex fractures) typically involve one of the maxillary buttresses of the midface, the inferior orbital rim, the lateral orbital wall, and the zygomatic arch. The muscles of mastication pass beneath the zygomatic arch on their way to the mandible. Any impingement on these muscles by a depressed zygomatic arch may result in trismus.
Nasoethmoidal fractures are associated with injury to the lacrimal drainage system, telecanthus, and cerebrospinal fluid leakage. Orbital floor fracture may present with infraorbital hypesthesia. A Le Fort I fracture is a pyramidal break that involves the lower portion of the maxillary bone, resulting in a "floating palate." A Le Fort I fracture is of little significance to the ophthalmologist, since it causes no ophthalmologic problems.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An otherwise healthy patient undergoes an uncomplicated repair of an orbital floor fracture. What is the appropriate postoperative management for this patient?

options.a: The patient's visual and pupillary function should be closely monitored postoperatively.
options.b: The affected side should be pressure-patched before extubation and maintained for 24 hours to minimize the risk of orbital hemorrhage.
options.c: Intravenous antibiotics should be infused postoperatively and oral antibiotics maintained for another 7 days to prevent postoperative infection.
options.d: Intravenous corticosteroids should be infused for 24 hours to decrease orbital inflammation; ice packs should be used to reduce swelling.

pool.rationale:
One of the most feared complications of orbital surgery is visual loss, which can occur either intraoperatively or within the immediate postoperative period. The intraoperative etiologies include excessive compression of the globe or optic nerve, excessive traction on the optic nerve, vasospasm of the arterial supply to the optic nerve and/or globe, and direct contusion or lacerating injury to these structures. Postoperative orbital hemorrhage or inflammation may result in an orbital compartment syndrome (OCS), which can also damage vision.
Pressure-patching the affected orbit for extubation is not unreasonable, since it may help to tamponade the orbit against any bleeding caused by Valsalva during extubation ("bucking the tube"). However, the patient's visual and pupillary function must be checked once the patient is awake enough to cooperate, and should be monitored over a few hours postoperatively. In an unresponsive patient (comatose, etc.), at the very least the orbit should be checked to rule out OCS and a pupillary exam should be attempted.
The use of postoperative corticosteroids or antibiotics postoperatively is a common practice postoperatively, but neither modality has any proven efficacy and is much less important than checking visual function.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Why is a Hughes tarsoconjunctival flap contraindicated in young children?
pool.rationale: A standard Hughes flap requires 2 to 4 weeks of occlusion and therefore creates a risk of amblyopia. The marginal arcades are adequately developed in children. The tarsal plate has adequate rigidity in children and there is no shortage of conjunctiva.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What inheritance pattern is associated with fibrous dysplasia?
pool.rationale: Fibrous dysplasia is a benign developmental disorder of bone that may involve a single region or be polyostotic. It is a sporadic condition without a known inheritance pattern. Computed tomography (CT) scan shows hyperostotic bone and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows a lack of dural enhancement, which helps differentiate it from meningioma. When it is associated with cutaneous pigmentation or endocrine abnormalities it is referred to as Albright syndrome. Surgical resection or debulking is performed when the lesion becomes disfiguring or vision loss is present from stricture of the optic canal.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with benign essential blepharospasm has had no improvement in their incapacitating facial spasms despite multiple periodic injections of botulinum toxin. What is the best next step in management?

options.d: surgical ablation of the facial nerve

pool.rationale:
Treatment with surgical myectomy is reserved for patients who are poorly responsive to botulinum therapy and incapacitated by the spasms. Meticulous removal of the orbital and palpebral orbicular muscle in the upper (and sometimes lower) eyelids is an effective and permanent treatment for blepharospasm.
Muscle relaxants and sedatives are rarely effective in the primary treatment of benign essential blepharospasm (BEB). Psychotherapy has little or no value for the patient with blepharospasm. Surgical ablation of the facial nerve has been largely abandoned. Though selective facial neurectomy can be effective, high recurrence rates and frequent hemifacial paralysis limit this treatment’s appeal.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 50-year-old patient presents with a slow-growing, firm mass of the lateral orbital rim. The ophthalmologist suspects a bony tumor. What imaging modality should be used?
pool.rationale: CT is the imaging modality of choice for most orbital issues. It is particularly good at examining osseous structures. MRI does not image bone well. PET and bone scans are most useful for metastatic surveillance, not for examining a bony orbital mass.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What subtype of cutaneous melanoma is most common in the eyelids?
pool.rationale:
Cutaneous malignant melanomas of the eyelids are rare. They may develop de novo or from a pre-existing nevus. Clinically, invasive melanoma is often preceded by a vertical growth phase, resulting in an elevated, indurated mass. Histologic features suggesting malignancy include nuclear enlargement, hyperchromasia, prominent nucleoli, or atypical mitotic figures. Melanoma invades the epidermis and lacks the polarity found in melanocytic nevi.
There are 4 main histologic subtypes of dermal melanoma. The superficial spreading variant is the most common type of cutaneous melanoma. It demonstrates a spreading intraepidermal growth pattern. The lentigo maligna subtype is the most common cutaneous melanoma affecting the eyelids. It has a long pre-invasive phase, and carries the best prognosis. It appears histologically as a nest or line of atypical melanocytes, predominantly in the basal layers of the epidermis. Acral lentiginous melanoma involves the extremities and is not found on the eyelids. Nodular melanoma is histologically characterized by a minimal intraepidermal component and more pronounced vertical growth, making it more deeply invasive. It carries the worst prognosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 10-year-old boy is struck in the left eye with a baseball. He complains of immediate diplopia, pain with eye movement, and severe nausea. There is no globe rupture or optic nerve injury on examination. Figure 1 shows his external examination and computed tomography (CT) scan. What is the best course of action?

options.a: oral corticosteroids with planned fracture repair in 1 week
options.b: referral to a neurologist for management of concussion
options.c: urgent orbital exploration for fracture repair
options.d: lateral rectus muscle recession on the left

pool.rationale:
The clinical presentation is consistent with the so-called "white-eyed" blowout fracture (WEBOF) that occurs primarily in children and teenagers. Children have incompletely calcified bones and are at risk for greenstick fractures of the orbital walls. This "trapdoor fracture" allows for herniation of an extraocular muscle into the adjacent paranasal sinus, followed by incarceration of the muscle within the narrow fracture as the bony trapdoor snaps shut. This results in severe muscle restriction on examination with only minimal external signs of injury, along with nausea and vomiting from the oculocardiac reflex. Of note, the nausea and vomiting is often misdiagnosed initially as concussion.
Because of the muscle ischemia that occurs with WEBOF, urgent exploration  with release of the entrapped muscle and fracture repair is indicated. Oral corticosteroids with delay of repair for 1-2 weeks is a good option for more classic orbital fractures that occur in adults to allow orbital soft tissue edema to settle before orbital surgery. Strabismus surgery is indicated in any patient with residual significant diplopia after fracture repair who has not improved after 6 months of observation, but is not a reasonable option for immediate management of orbital fracture.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient arrives in the trauma bay after a motor vehicle crash in which his forehead hit the dashboard. He has bruising to his forehead, but minimal edema of his periorbital region. He states that he cannot see out of his right eye. The pupil exam demonstrates a right rAPD. No intraocular pathology is noted, IOP is normal, and his vision is 20/20 in the left eye and count fingers in the right. Where is the injury?

options.a: greater wing of the sphenoid bone
options.b: lesser wing of the sphenoid bone

pool.rationale: Traumatic optic neuropathy can cause vision loss in the setting of a relatively normal intraocular examination. However, there will be an afferent pupillary defect due to optic nerve dysfunction. Frequently, thin-section computed tomography (CT) of the orbital apex and anterior clinoid process will show fractures through or adjacent to the optic canal, which runs through the lesser wing of sphenoid. While high-dose steroids and decompression of the nerve have been studied, treatment for traumatic optic neuropathy is controversial, and no definitive therapy beyond observation is recommended.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A breast cancer patient is being treated with docetaxel. For 2 months, she has had tearing with epiphora. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
pool.rationale: Docetaxel, among other chemotherapy agents (5FU, idoxuridine) and, less commonly, other medications (eserine, phospholine iodide), can cause canalicular stenosis by local inflammation and scarring of the canaliculi. Use of topical steroids and artificial tears during chemotherapy may prevent scarring.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In an external dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR), what sinus may be encountered during formation of the ostium?
pool.rationale: During dacryocystorhinostomy, an anterior ethmoid air cell may occasionally be encountered. It is important to recognize this so that the creation of the ostium is continued into the nasal passageway. The frontal sinus is above the ostium, and the maxillary sinus is below the ostium. There is no "lacrimal" sinus.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Aside from infection, what disease should be considered when orbital inflammation is present in conjunction with sinus disease?
pool.rationale: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly known as Wegener granulomatosis) classically causes inflammation of the orbit, sinuses, and lungs, and should always be considered in patients with simultaneous orbit and sinus disease. Thyroid eye disease, amyloidosis, and Sjögren syndrome are not associated with sinus disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Into what anatomical location does the nasolacrimal duct empty?
pool.rationale: The nasolacrimal duct empties into the inferior meatus, which is located under the inferior turbinate. The maxillary sinus, anterior and middle ethmoid sinuses, and frontal sinus empty into the middle meatus. The posterior ethmoid sinus empties into the superior meatus. The sphenoid sinus empties into the sphenoethmoidal recess of each nasal fossa.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents following Mohs surgery with a lower eyelid defect greater than 60%. What is the best technique to repair this large lower eyelid defect?

options.a: tarsoconjunctival flap from upper eyelid with full-thickness skin graft
options.b: free tarsal graft from upper eyelid and full-thickness skin graft
options.c: direct primary closure of the lower eyelid

pool.rationale: The most appropriate technique to perform in the situation described is a tarsoconjunctival flap from upper eyelid with full-thickness skin graft. This procedure allows for the reconstruction of the posterior and anterior lamella without violating the principle of placing 2 grafts (eg, free tarsal graft from upper eyelid and full-thickness skin graft) adjacent to one another. Rotational or primary direct closure is not amenable in defects greater than 50%.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common cause for preseptal cellulitis in children?
pool.rationale: Preseptal cellulitis in children is almost always due to underlying sinusitis. Bacteremia in preseptal cellulitis is rare. Trauma and foreign bodies are common causes of preseptal cellulitis in adults but are less common than underlying sinus disease in children.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents to the emergency department with sinus pain, proptosis, no light perception (NLP) vision, and ophthalmoplegia of the left eye. There is a blackened area of skin along the medial aspect of the lower lid. Nasal endoscopy demonstrates eschars. She is started on broad-spectrum antibiotics and antifungals; however, she continues to worsen. What intervention would be most appropriate for this patient?
pool.rationale: Exenteration should be considered in: (1) intraocular melanoma or retinoblastoma that has extended outside the globe in the absence of distant metastases, (2) destructive tumors extending into the orbit from the sinuses, face, eyelids, conjunctiva, or intracranial space, (3) malignant epithelial tumors of the lacrimal gland, (4) fungal infections, (5) sarcomas and, (6) other primary orbital malignancies that do not respond to nonsurgical therapy. Exenteration can be subtotal, total, or extended, with the goal to remove all lesions along with appropriate margins of adjacent tissue.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What type of organism most often causes adult orbital cellulitis?
pool.rationale: Infectious orbital cellulitis is an infection posterior to the orbital septum. The vast majority of cases are caused by bacterial sinusitis. In a young child, the maxillary and frontal sinuses are underdeveloped. Therefore, orbital cellulitis is most likely to arise from the ethmoidal sinus. In addition, the lamina papyracea is thin, and veins connect the ethmoid sinus to the orbit. In adults, infections are usually polymicrobial, including gram-positive cocci, Moraxella, and H. influenzae. However in children, the causative agent is usually a single organism that is typically a gram-positive organism. Adults often require early surgical intervention, whereas children typically improve with intravenous antibiotics alone.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For 1 week, a 4-year-old patient has had inflammation of the right lower lid margin that has not been improving, is tender to touch, and is associated with localized erythema. What is the most likely cause?

options.a: inspissation and inflammation of the glands of Moll
options.b: inspissation and inflammation of the sebaceous glands
options.c: inspissation and inflammation of the eccrine glands
options.d: inspissation and inflammation of the apocrine glands

pool.rationale: The clinical description is of a chalazion, which is inflammation of the meibomian (sebaceous) glands of the eyelid. The other choices (apocrine and eccrine glands, glands of Moll) are sweat glands that are not a cause of chalazion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient in his mid-40s has painless, progressive proptosis OD, blurred vision, and a trace right relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD). He also has normal acuity (needs new hyperopic correction OD) and normal motility. What finding would most likely be found on orbital magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast?

options.a: well-circumscribed intraconal lesion with early stippled enhancement
options.c: diffuse extraocular muscle enlargement with avid enhancement
options.d: irregular, poorly defined cystic spaces with minimal enhancement

pool.rationale:
Contrast-enhanced orbital imaging of cavernous venous malformations shows a stippled pattern in the early phase of contrast that develops into homogeneous staining in the late phase (Figs. 1, 2). It is the most likely diagnosis, given the age of the patient; the examination finding of painless, progressive proptosis without significant motility dysfunction; and otherwise normal eye examination. Orbital cavernous hemangioma is the most common orbital tumor in this age group. Its intraconal location causes posterior globe compression, leading to hyperopic shift. Indication for surgical excision in this patient would be proptosis, progressive refractive change, and compressive optic neuropathy.
Diffuse extraocular muscle enlargement with avid enhancement describes MRI findings in orbital inflammatory syndrome or myositis, which usually causes motility dysfunction and eye pain.
Fusiform optic nerve thickening describes optic nerve glioma, primarily a disease of childhood. In adults, it is very rare and more likely to be malignant. Both are unlikely in this case, as they would usually cause visible optic nerve pallor and more prominent optic neuropathy.
Irregular, poorly defined cystic spaces with minimal enhancement describes lymphatic malformation, or lymphangioma. In the orbit, they usually manifest in the first decade of life and are unlikely to present in this patient's age group.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: There can be a 50% recurrence rate for lacrimal sac carcinomas, with a significant mortality. What course of treatment is most appropriate?

options.b: aggressive surgical resection, including exenteration if necessary.

pool.rationale: Though rare, primary lacrimal sac tumors should be suspected in patients with a mass located above the medial canthal tendon. These patients present with symptoms similar to dacryocystitis and nasolacrimal duct obstruction, but they may endorse a history of bleeding. On examination, these patients may exhibit reflux bleeding from the punctum on irrigation. Forty-five percent (45%) of lacrimal sac tumors are benign, while 55% are malignant. There is a 50% recurrence rate of malignant invasive squamous and transitional cell carcinoma of the lacrimal sac. This can be fatal in 50% of the cases; therefore, it must be treated aggressively. While benign lacrimal sac tumors can be treated via dacryocystectomy, malignant tumors require a more aggressive treatment measure. These patients require dacryocystectomy with lateral rhinotomy, and may further require exenteration, with bone removal in the medial canthal area. Radiation is used to treat lymphomatous lesions or as a palliative treatment in extensive epithelial lesions.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the goal of treatment in a patient with severe microphthalmia?

options.b: functional vision in the microphthalmic eye
options.c: identification of mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor genes

pool.rationale: Microphthalmia with orbital cyst results from failure of the choroidal fissure to close in the embryo. Because most microphthalmic eyes have no potential for vision, treatment focuses on achieving a cosmetically acceptable appearance that is reasonably symmetrical. Enucleation is usually not necessary for the fitting of a conformer or prosthesis and is generally avoided. These cysts do not undergo malignant transformation. Mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor genes typically occur in syndromic craniosynostosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: During a direct brow lift, trauma to what nerve would likely cause tingling pain on the scalp?
pool.rationale:
The supraorbital nerve is frequently traumatized during brow-lifting procedures, which can result in paresthesias of the forehead and scalp.
The zygomaticotemporal and zygomaticofacial nerves are located much lower on the face, providing sensation to the cheek areas, and are typically traumatized during lateral orbitotomy procedures.
The supratrochlear nerve, like the supraorbital nerve, is a branch of the frontal nerve but provides sensation to the medial canthal area, not the scalp.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common presentation of rhabdomyosarcoma?
pool.rationale:
Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common primary orbital malignancy of childhood. The average age of onset is 5–7 years. The classic clinical picture is that of a child with sudden onset and rapid progression of unilateral proptosis. However, patients in their early teens may experience a less dramatic course, with gradually progressive proptosis developing over weeks to more than a month. There is often a marked adnexal response with edema and discoloration of the eyelids. Ptosis and strabismus may also be present. A mass may be palpable, particularly in the superonasal quadrant of the eyelid, and it may cause proptosis if sufficiently large. However, the tumor may be retrobulbar, may involve any quadrant of the orbit, and may in rare cases arise from the conjunctiva.
Although pain is an occasional complaint, it is seen in only a minority of rhabdomyosarcoma cases. Optic neuropathy is uncommon in rhabdomyosarcoma unless the tumor is allowed to progress without timely diagnosis and treatment.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What type of ocular adnexal lymphoma has the worst prognosis?
pool.rationale: Ocular adnexal lymphoma comprises approximately 6%-8% of orbital tumors. The vast majority are non-Hodgkin B-cell type with less than 3% T-cell types. Bilaterality is reported in 10%-20% of cases. The most common type is extranodal marginal zone lymphomas (EZML), which is 50%-90% of all cases of ocular adnexal lymphoma. Of the tumor types, EZML, follicular, and lymphoplasmacytic are considered low-grade or indolent tumors, whereas diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and mantle cell lymphoma are considered high-grade tumors. Treatment typically involves surgery and radiation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with intermittent episodes of lacrimal drainage obstruction, including pain and distention of the lacrimal sac. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: A dacryolith is a concretion formed within the lacrimal sac. This can cause an obstruction within the nasolacrimal duct. Dacryoliths are composed of shed epithelial cells, lipids, amorphous debris with or without calcium. There is usually no inciting event or other abnormality identified. There may be an association with an infection with Actinomyces israelii or Candida species or long-term administration of topical drops, such as epinephrine. Intermittent tearing is dependent upon the position of the dacryolith, which can shift position. Impaction of the dacryolith in the nasolacrimal duct can produce lacrimal sac distension and pain. Removal is performed during DCR surgery.
