pool.q: What is a contraindication for conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR)?
pool.rationale: A conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) creates a complete bypass of the lacrimal drainage system. It is performed by creating a tract to place a Jones tube through the inferior half of the caruncle and then through an ostomy site into the middle nasal meatus. A CDCR is indicated when the canalicular abnormality is so severe that the canalicular system cannot be used or reconstructed. This leads to canalicular obstruction, which can happen with docetaxel chemotherapy. It is also possible to have an open and patent punctum but an occluded canaliculus, resulting in epiphora, which would be an indication for a CDCR. However, if there is a malignant skin cancer in the medial canthal area, a CDCR should be avoided in order to minimize the risk of spread to the nasal cavity. CDCR should be delayed until the lesion has clear margins and the patient is free from recurrence.

pool.q: What is the preferred initial treatment for acute dacryocystitis with abscess formation?
pool.rationale: Acute dacryocystitis with abscess formation causes painful distention of the lacrimal sac, and incision and drainage of the abscess are required in severe cases. However, this treatment should be reserved for severe cases that do not respond to more conservative measures. Warm compresses would not be expected to be effective if the situation has progressed to the level of an abscess. Topical antibiotics would not be expected to adequately penetrate the abscess to have an effect. Nasolacrimal probing and balloon dacryoplasty are contraindicated in the acute setting. Oral antibiotics are often effective in this situation. Parenteral antibiotics may be needed in severe cases, such as when cellulitis or orbital extension is present.

pool.q: A patient presents after orbital trauma that resulted in an orbital roof fracture. What is a common clinical presentation of this type of fracture?

options.a: optic neuropathy in a young patient
options.b: delayed ecchymosis of the upper eyelid in a young patient
options.d: horizontal diplopia in an older adult

pool.rationale: Orbital roof fractures are typically due to blunt forehead trauma. They are more prevalent in children whose frontal sinuses have not yet pneumatized (the mature frontal sinuses serve as an impact crumple zone in adults). Early diplopia is usually from a hematoma or orbital swelling. Muscle entrapment is very rare with orbital roof fractures. Optic neuropathy is uncommon. Delayed ecchymosis of the upper eyelid may be the presenting subtle sign of an orbital roof fracture in a young patient. Most orbital roof fractures do not require surgical intervention, unless the fracture is large enough to threaten brain function.

pool.q: The optic canal traverses which orbital bone?
pool.rationale: The optic canal is 8-10 mm long and is located within the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone. The ethmoid, maxillary, and palatine bones are also components of the orbit, but they are not part of the optic canal.

pool.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with 3 days of pain and redness in her right eye. She also notes 1 week of nasal swelling and redness, as shown. The slit-lamp photograph shows her right eye following instillation of topical phenylephrine. What diagnostic test would be useful to evaluate the most likely diagnosis in this setting?
pool.rationale: The photographs depict a patient with scleritis (does not blanch with topical phenylephrine) and nasal inflammation. It is important for the ophthalmologist to recognize that scleritis may be the ocular manifestation of a systemic disease, and therefore a thorough review of systems is mandatory. In the case of scleritis and nasal inflammation, the differential diagnosis includes conditions such as a cANCA-associated vasculitis, relapsing polychondritis, and syphilis. Early mortality can occur in patients with untreated systemic illnesses. Sarcoidosis may present with scleritis but does not commonly present with nasal inflammation. Multiple sclerosis and HLA-B27 positivity are more often associated with intraocular inflammation and again, nasal inflammation is not a manifestation of these conditions.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In the emergency department following a motor vehicle accident, a patient has a normal globe examination and some periorbital ecchymosis, but no displacement of lateral canthus or malar flattening. He denies any trismus.  A computed tomography (CT) scan shows a nondisplaced zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture. What management is recommended?
pool.rationale:
A zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture (ie, malar complex fracture) is a relatively frequent midfacial fracture pattern that typically involves 3 facial buttresses: the zygoma (typically along the lateral orbital wall at the level of the frontozygomatic suture), the zygomatic arch, and either the medial or lateral malar buttress extending to involve the inferior orbital rim. Not infrequently, the orbital floor is also fractured.
Clinical problems occur for patients if the fractured complex rotates. This typically results in inferior lateral canthal dystopia, a step-off deformity along the inferior orbital rim, malar flattening, and trismus (limitation of mandibular opening from impingement on the muscles of mastication by the displaced zygomatic arch). Once enough rotation occurs, repair is indicated. However, observation is all that is needed in cases of nondisplaced or minimally displaced tripod fractures. High-dose corticosteroids are not indicated in facial fractures, especially if concomitant intracranial injury exists. In this case, there is minimal soft tissue edema, and even normal doses of steroids would provide little, if any, benefit.
It is also important to remember that displaced (rotated) ZMC fractures are notorious for "hiding" or minimizing the extent of the orbital floor defect, so the orbital floor fracture tends to look much smaller than it actually is. However, once the ZMC is rotated and plated back into its native position, the floor defect will open more widely, expanding the orbital volume and potentially causing posttraumatic enophthalmos or hypoglobus. It is therefore prudent to explore the orbital floor defect once the ZMC has been rotated back into normal position, and, as necessary, to repair the floor appropriately.

pool.q: A 45-year-old male complains of pain around the right orbit that began 9 months ago. His computed tomography (CT) scan is shown in Figure 1. What is the best next step in management of this patient's condition?

options.b: positron emission tomography (PET) scan for lymphoma staging
options.c: incisional biopsy of the lacrimal gland
options.d: excisional biopsy of the lacrimal gland

pool.rationale:
The CT scan shows a lacrimal gland mass with calcification and adjacent bony thinning/erosion (best seen on the coronal bone window). These findings, coupled with the history of pain, are highly suspicious for a primary lacrimal gland malignancy, most likely adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC). 
Dacryoadenitis, a form of idiopathic orbital inflammatory syndrome (IOIS), does not typically present with chronic pain and does not cause bone erosion. Orbital lymphoma is also unlikely for the same reasons, although it should be noted that inflammatory signs or pain can be present in up to 25% of orbital lymphomas, and aggressive subtypes can show bony erosion on CT. Pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumor) may cause expansion of the lacrimal gland fossa (“fossa formation”), but not frank erosion, and is usually an indolent, painless process.
The key issue here is whether or not to excise the lesion completely or to simply perform an incisional biopsy for diagnosis. If pleomorphic adenoma is suspected, the ENTIRE lesion must be excised. Incompletely excised pleomorphic adenomas have a higher recurrence rate, will be more difficult to excise if they recur, and can undergo malignant transformation. Complete excision of an ACC can require exenteration and radical orbitectomy with removal of the roof, lateral wall, and floor along with the overlying soft tissues. There is no evidence that this disfiguring approach or other aggressive treatment such as radiation, chemotherapy, or a combination of these modalities improves prognosis. The data on intra-arterial chemotherapy infusion for these lesions is limited. The basaloid variant of ACC carries the worst prognosis.

pool.q: What is the preferred initial treatment of punctal stenosis?

options.b: vertical cut down through lid margin
options.d: retrograde probe through via the common canaliculus

pool.rationale: Punctal stenosis is a common condition that can often be addressed by simply probing and dilating the punctum. If this fails, more aggressive maneuvers such as surgical punctoplasty or temporary silicone intubation can be considered. Vertical cut down through the lid margin or retrograde probe through the common canaliculus can be helpful if these simpler measures fail. Conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) with Jones tube is the most definitive treatment for upper lacrimal obstruction with epiphora, but is saved as a last resort, if the above measures fail.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist is called to the emergency room to repair an eyelid laceration in a 25-year-old man who was assaulted by 2 men. There is a horizontal laceration 16 mm above the margin, with yellow tissues protruding through the wound. What is the best next step in management?

options.a: Reposition the orbital fat posterior to the septum, suture the septum, then suture the overlying skin and orbicularis.
options.b: Reposition the orbital fat posterior to the septum then suture the overlying skin and orbicularis without incorporating the septum into the closure.
options.c: Cut the protruding fat, then suture the overlying skin and orbicularis while incorporating the septum into 1 or 2 throws to reapproximate the lid crease.
options.d: Take the patient to the operating room for exploration of the levator and aponeurosis.

pool.rationale: When orbital fat is present in an upper lid laceration, it is imperative to ensure that the levator muscle is not damaged. A laceration involving the levator muscle or aponeurosis must be carefully repaired to ensure proper function of the eyelid. When repairing upper eyelid lacerations involving the orbital septum, sutures should not be used to close it. If the septum is incorporated into the closure, lagophthalmos and tethering to the superior orbital rim can occur.

pool.q: Six weeks after probing of the lacrimal system, the family of a 13-month-old child reports that she continues to tear. A review of the operative notes indicates that the ophthalmologist had difficulty passing the probe past the canaliculus and into the lacrimal sac. What might have occurred during the procedure?

options.d: reactive stenosis at the canalicular-sac junction

pool.rationale: Pushing through a "soft stop" can create a false passage.  In this case, the site of resistance is located along the canaliculus, which would suggest canalicular stenosis or obstruction.  A "soft stop" is usually accompanied by a wrinkling of the overlying skin. If this is encountered, the probe should be removed, and passage should be attempted again with proper horizontal tension along the lid to prevent bunching of soft tissue in front of the probe tip. Successful probing through the canalicular system will lead to a "hard stop" as the tip encounters the medial wall of the lacrimal sac and lacrimal bone.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most superior structure traveling through the annulus of Zinn?
pool.rationale: The annulus of Zinn is a fibrous ring formed by the origin of the 4 rectus muscles. The annulus of Zinn divides the superior orbital fissure and encircles the optic foramen. The optic foramen transmits the optic nerve and ophthalmic artery (inferior to the optic nerve), which are the most superior structures traveling through the annulus of Zinn. The inferior portion of the superior orbital fissure within the annulus of Zinn transmits CN III (upper and lower divisions), CN VI, and the nasociliary nerve (branch of CN V). The presence of many nerves along the lateral wall of the orbit is the reason a superonasal surgical approach is used to access the optic nerve in the orbital apex.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist orders a biopsy of a pigmented lesion of an older white patient. The pathology reveals lentigo maligna. What is the next step in management?

options.a: close observation, with serial measurements and photography
options.b: surgical resection of the pigmented lesion, with wide margins
options.c: incisional biopsy, since these lesions exhibit a vertical growth pattern

pool.rationale: Lentigo maligna is a premalignant melanocytic lesion. These lesions are more common in older white people and typically occur in the malar region. The intraepidermal growth of these lesions is described as exhibiting a radial pattern of uncontrolled melanocyte proliferation. These lesions will progress to an invasive melanoma in up to 50% of patients. As opposed to more benign entities such as senile or solar lentigo, lentigo maligna lesions exhibit pigmentary variation, have irregular borders, and enlarge over time. Importantly, the pathologic areas of these lesions may extend beyond the pigmented borders of the lesion; thus, complete excision with generous borders is recommended. Pathology with close attention to surgical margins is required, and long-time monitoring is needed to look for recurrence.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Plexiform neurofibromas are most commonly associated with what ocular disorder?
pool.rationale:
Plexiform neurofibroma can lead to secondary glaucoma. Plexiform neurofibroma stems from a proliferation of Schwann cells and can present with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1, also known as von Recklinghausen disease). The upper eyelid and orbit are usually affected, and neurofibromas can directly infiltrate the angle.
A subretinal osteoma is generally a benign, ossifying tumor in which the choroid is replaced by bone. It is not associated with NF-1 but is rather a sporadic disease with no known risk factors. A choroidal melanoma is a malignant neoplasm of the choroid and is usually sporadic without association with NF-1. Iris nevi or iris melanoma are also not related to NF-1.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 25-year-old man who admits to intravenous (IV) drug use has a lesion on the left upper and lower lid (Figure 1). What additional diagnostic testing is most important for this patient?
pool.rationale: The mass depicted is a Kaposi sarcoma. It presents as a reddish dermal mass and is a frequent manifestation of AIDS. These lesions are associated with human herpesvirus 8. In addition to the eyelid manifestations, conjunctival lesions can also present and appear similar to foreign body granulomas or cavernous hemangiomas. Histologically, they are composed of spindle cells. Treatment can include cryotherapy, excision, radiation, or intralesional chemotherapeutic agents. Often, these lesions can regress following immune reconstitution with adequate antiviral treatment of the HIV infection.

pool.q: A patient who has had forniceal reconstruction following Mohs surgery for a medial canthal squamous cell carcinoma develops numbness of the forehead. The ophthalmologist suspects perineural spread of recurrent carcinoma. What nerve is likely to be compromised?

options.a: supraorbital branch of the frontal nerve
options.b: zygomatic branch of the facial nerve
options.c: temporal branch of the facial nerve
options.d: lacrimal branch of the trigeminal nerve

pool.rationale:
The oculomotor and facial nerves are motor nerves that are not involved in sensation. The optic nerve is sensory but carries visual data to the brain.
The trigeminal nerve supplies sensation to the entire face. Perineural spread of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) often presents in a subtle fashion, with complaints of tingling, numbness, and itching before progressing to pain. These ominous symptoms are sometimes ignored by the clinician. Often, the patient either has a distant history of facial SCC, has never had a definitive diagnosis because of cryotherapy or chemical peeling of suspicious lesions, or has never had an obvious lesion. In many patients, only actinic changes are present.
Perineural spread of SCC can progress rapidly into the skull base, usually along the supraorbital nerve into the cavernous sinus, at which point motor neuropathies manifest. The supraorbital nerve supplies sensation to the forehead, while the lacrimal nerve supplies sensation to the upper eyelid.
The facial nerve may also be involved as an initial site of perineural spread, but typically presents with slowly progressive facial nerve weakness without sensory changes.
The clinician should always be wary of sensory changes or facial weakness in any patient with a known history of cutaneous SCC or actinic changes of the face. Prompt magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the skull base with attention to the trigeminal and facial nerves, as well as the cavernous sinus, is recommended.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the recommended approach to treat a hemangiopericytoma?

options.a: systemic chemotherapy, because of the high rate of metastasis by the time of diagnosis
options.b: radiotherapy, because the tumor is localized and sensitive to external beam radiation
options.c: total resection, because the tumor can metastasize
options.d: observation, because there is frequent spontaneous resolution of small tumors

pool.rationale: Hemangiopericytomas are uncommon encapsulated, hypervascular, and hypercellular lesions, now referred to as a solitary fibrous tumor. The tumor can occur anywhere in the orbit and typically affects adults in midlife. It can resemble a cavernous hemangioma on computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). If incompletely excised it can recur, undergo malignant transformation, and metastasize. Because of this, treatment is complete excision. Observation is not appropriate for an unknown mass in the orbit, and radiation therapy is not a primary treatment option, since total excision of the encapsulated lesion can be performed. Systemic chemotherapy is not required as an initial treatment option with a solitary fibrous tumor.

pool.q: Six months after enucleation, a patient returns to the office reporting mucoid discharge from the anophthalmic side. There is no pain. She states that the prosthesis fits well. What is the most likely cause of the mucus discharge?
pool.rationale:
Chronic mucus discharge from an anophthalmic socket is usually due to a papillary conjunctivitis. This is due to mechanical friction between the palpebral conjunctival surface and the prosthesis. Everting the upper eyelid will demonstrate the papillary reaction. Treatment consists of topical corticosteroids and occasionally prosthetic modification.

Implant extrusion can present in a similar fashion, but it is less common than papillary conjunctivitis. The formation of a pyogenic granuloma is suggestive of an implant exposure. Implant infection is usually painful, and examination reveals purulent discharge. The weight of the prosthesis can stretch the lower eyelid over time, but this typically manifests as lower eyelid laxity with or without ectropion rather than entropion.

pool.q: What is the pathophysiologic etiology of epiblepharon?

options.a: shortening of the horizontal palpebral fissure and narrowing of the vertical palpebral fissure
options.b: vertical shortening and horizontal lengthening of the lower eyelid
options.c: override of the pretarsal skin and muscle over the lid margin

pool.rationale: Epiblepharon refers to override of the pretarsal skin and orbicularis over the lid margin, causing the lashes to rub on the eye. It is typically a congenital feature in Asians, and not related to weakness of the orbicularis or laxity of the lid. Horizontal lid laxity can lead to ectropion or entropion. Vertical shortening and horizontal lengthening of the lower eyelid is a feature of euryblepharon. Shortening of the horizontal palpebral fissure and narrowing of the vertical palpebral fissure is a feature of blepharophimosis.

pool.q: For 1 month, an 81-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer has had diplopia on left gaze. Ductions for the left eye are mildly limited in all directions. After the extraocular muscles, the most common site of orbital metastasis is what location?
pool.rationale:
Pain, bony destruction, ophthalmoplegia, and proptosis are all signs suggestive of orbital carcinoma metastasis. Due to their ample blood supply, the extraocular muscles represent the most common site of orbital metastasis. The bone marrow of the sphenoid bone, another highly vascular space, is the second most common site of orbital metastasis. Lytic bone destruction of the lateral orbital wall is considered to be radiographic evidence of sphenoid bone metastasis.
The orbital fat, cavernous sinus, and lacrimal gland are less frequently involved areas of orbital metastasis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A computed tomography (CT) scan of the orbit demonstrates a lesion in the lacrima fossa with surrounding bony destruction. What is the most likely cause of these findings?
pool.rationale:
In general, CT evidence of orbital bone destruction from an adjacent lesion is an ominous sign and usually (though not always) suggests malignancy. In the area of the lacrimal gland, the 2 most common malignant processes that cause bone destruction are adenoid cystic carcinoma (the most common primary epithelial lacrimal gland malignancy) and metastatic disease (especially prostate cancer).
The most common nonepithelial malignancy of the lacrimal gland is non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma, and the majority of such lesions are indolent extranodal marginal zone lymphomas (EMZL, also termed mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, or MALT lymphomas); bone erosion from lymphoma occurs only in aggressive subtypes, such as diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, which are much less common than MALT lymphomas. Of note, 2 benign conditions may cause bone erosion in the lacrimal gland fossa: dermoid cyst and eosinophilic granuloma.
Pleomorphic adenoma (benign mixed tumor) causes chronic remodeling of the bone known as "fossa formation," but true bone erosion typically occurs only with malignant transformation.
Plexiform neurofibromas often are found near the superotemporal orbit, but are not expected to cause bony erosion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 62-year-old woman presents with a focal nodule of the upper eyelid that has persisted despite treatment with warm compresses and topical antibiotics. The lesion is yellow, with loss of surrounding eyelashes and meibomian gland orifices. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: Sebaceous adenocarcinoma is a highly malignant and potentially lethal tumor. The tumor often exhibits a yellow coloration as a result of lipid material within the neoplastic cells. Sebaceous carcinoma often masquerades as benign eyelid disease such a chalazia or chronic blepharitis, but it may also simulate basal cell or squamous cell carcinoma, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, or superior limbic keratoconjunctivitis. A nodule that initially simulated a chalazion but later causes loss of eyelashes and destruction of the meibomian gland orifices warrants a biopsy, as this presentation is characteristic of sebaceous cell carcinoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What arteries supply blood to the bulbar conjunctiva?
pool.rationale: The bulbar conjunctiva is supplied by the anterior ciliary arteries, which arise from muscular branches of the ophthalmic artery. The blood flow to the upper eyelid is provided by the marginal arterial arcade, which is located 2 mm superior the margin anterior to the tarsal plate, and the peripheral arcade, which lies superior to the tarsus between the levator aponeurosis and the Müller muscle. The temporal artery supplies the temporal aspect of the scalp and is commonly biopsied when giant cell arteritis is suspected.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Why are adolescents and adults more likely to require surgical drainage for a subperiosteal abscess than children less than 9 years old?

options.a: Adults and adolescents over 9 are more likely to have infection caused by anaerobes.
options.b: The sinuses in children less than 9 years old are not fully aerated.
options.c: Children under the age of 9 are more likely to have an abscess containing a single gram-negative organism.
options.d: Adults and adolescents over 9 are more likely to have infection caused by aerobes.

pool.rationale: Infectious orbital cellulitis is an infection posterior to the orbital septum. The vast majority of cases are caused by bacterial sinusitis. In a 2-year-old patient, the maxillary and frontal sinus are underdeveloped. Therefore, orbital cellulitis is most likely to arise from the ethmoidal sinus. In adults, infections are usually polymicrobial, including gram-positive cocci, Moraxella, and H. influenzae. However, in children the causative agent is usually a single organism that is typically a gram-positive organism. Adults often require early surgical intervention, whereas children typically improve with intravenous antibiotics alone. Orbital cellulitis may progress to a subperiosteal abscess. In children less than 9 years old, expectant management with medical therapy is indicated if the diagnosis is an isolated medial or inferior subperiosteal abscess, with intact vision, absence of frontal sinusitis, small-sized abscess, no evidence of chronic sinusitis (eg, nasal polyps), and a non-dental cause (anaerobes). Adults often have multidrug-resistant organisms or anaerobes in the abscess and require early surgical intervention. Gas within the abscess on computed tomography (CT) imaging may suggest an anaerobe.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Clinical evaluation of a 67-year-old woman reveals a slowly progressive left-sided proptosis of approximately 4 mm. She has full motility bilaterally. What imaging modality is the most appropriate next step?
pool.rationale:
CT is the most valuable technique overall for delineating the shape, location, extent, and character of lesions in the orbit. In addition to adequate soft tissue delineation, CT provides the most advanced assessment of bony anatomy of the available imaging modalities. CT helps refine the differential diagnosis, and when orbitotomy is indicated, CT helps guide the selection of the surgical approach by showing the relationship of the lesion to the surgical space or spaces of the orbit.
MRI provides better tissue contrast of structures in the orbital apex, intracanalicular portion of the optic nerve, structures in periorbital spaces, and orbitocranial tumors, as there is no artifact from the skull base bones. Further detail may be achieved with use of contrast, and it is not uncommon for both MRI and CT scans to be utilized in complete evaluation of an orbital disease process. However, as a first step, CT yields greater value.
Ultrasonography has high resolution in the area of the sclera and optic nerve insertion and is useful for evaluating scleritis and other anterior inflammation that produces fluid in the sub-Tenon space. However, ultrasonography is of limited value in assessing lesions of the posterior orbit (because of sound attenuation) and is therefore not the first step in evaluating an orbital process. Doppler ultrasonography is particularly useful for assessing orbital blood flow, as might be desired in cases of carotid cavernous fistulae or arteriovenous malformations.
CT angiography or MR angiography can be used as a secondary diagnostic study in detection of arteriovenous malformations or fistulas and aneurysms, but neither of them would be the most appropriate first choice study.

pool.q: A 25-year-old white woman is concerned about a 1.5-mm diameter, tan, flat lesion on her lower eyelid. The lesion has been unchanged since birth and darkens with sun exposure. What is the recommended management of the lesion?

options.a: continued observation, and biopsy if there are any changes

pool.rationale: The clinical description is consistent with benign ephelis (freckle). Ephelides arise from hyperpigmentation of the basal layer of the epidermis. The number of epidermal melanocytes is not increased, but they extrude more than the usual amount of pigment into the epidermal basal cell layer. These lesions are common in fair-skinned individuals and darken with sun exposure. No treatment is necessary other than sun protection. The patient should be reassured, although it is always prudent to consider biopsy if the lesion changes. Given the description of stable behavior of the ephelis, excision and/or biopsy is not appropriate at this time.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 7-year-old boy has had relapsing episodes of unilateral proptosis and swelling of the right superotemporal orbit unresponsive to oral antibiotics. Computed tomography (CT) scan reveals a lytic defect in the frontal bone. What is the next step in management?
pool.rationale:
Any orbital mass causing bony destruction raises concern for malignancy. The most common malignancies to consider in children are primary rhabdomyosarcoma, metastatic neuroblastoma, and granulocytic sarcoma. These 3 processes typically progress rapidly rather than having relapsing episodes as described in the stem.
In addition to malignancy, a variety of histiocytic disorders that preferentially affect children must be considered. Previously known as histiocytosis X, this group of disorders is now called Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH). The most frequent presentation in the orbit is a lytic defect, usually affecting the superotemporal orbit or sphenoid wing and causing relapsing episodes of orbital inflammation, often initially misinterpreted as infectious orbital cellulitis.
Treatment of localized orbital disease consists of confirmatory biopsy with debulking, which may be followed by intralesional steroid injection or low-dose radiation therapy. Children with systemic disease are treated aggressively with chemotherapy.
No infection is present, so converting to intravenous antibiotics or performing incision and drainage is inappropriate. An empiric trial of corticosteroids is contraindicated because of the bone involvement—idiopathic orbital inflammatory syndrome does not cause bone destruction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: After cosmetic blepharoplasty, a 45-year-old woman presents with bumps on one of the incisions. The bumps are smooth, round, and freely mobile. There is no erythema, edema, or tenderness. What is the likely mechanism of these lesions?
pool.rationale:
The answer is a common postoperative finding in patients undergoing upper eyelid blepharoplasty: iatrogenic inclusion cysts along the incision/suture line, known as epidermal inclusion cysts. When multiple tiny epidermal inclusion cysts are found, they are sometimes referred to as milia. In most cases, the lesions are small, resolve over time, and are "felt more than seen." Occasionally, larger milia may require excision. Whether or not specific suture material and technique increase the risk of milia formation is debatable.
One additional entity for the surgeon to consider in a patient presenting with postoperative "bumps" along the incision line is infection. Typical bacterial infection usually presents with diffuse erythema and tenderness across the surgical site, and responds rapidly to oral antibiotics. However, on occasion a smoldering, minimally erythematous, minimally tender nodular process may manifest several weeks postoperatively. Fungal and atypical mycobacterial infection must be considered in such cases. A biopsy for histopathologic and microbacterial studies is usually required for the diagnosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A fracture of what structure defines a Le Fort fracture?
pool.rationale: By definition, Le Fort fractures must extend posteriorly through the pterygoid plates. They can have orbital and nasal involvement. The pterygoid plates are part of the sphenoid bone. Although every LeFort fracture involves the maxilla, not all maxillary fractures are LeFort fractures.

pool.q: The patient in the figure is unhappy with his facial appearance. What surgical approach could be used to improve his appearance around his eyes?
pool.rationale:
Along with dermatochalasis and prominent lower lid fat pads, the figure shows involutional skin changes and descent and deflation of the midface. When approaching the lower lid, the continuum between the lower lid and the cheek must be addressed together. SOOF is suborbicularis oculi fat found posterior to the orbicularis muscle and attached superiorly at the arcus marginalis. Midface rejuvenation involves SOOF and midface elevation, combined with midface inflation and lower lid fat sculpting. A preperiosteal SOOF lift can create midface rejuvenation as well as correct mild to moderate lower eyelid ectropion/retraction when there is anterior lamellar skin shortage. The midface is accessed either transconjunctivally, subciliary, or from the temporal scalp. The SOOF is observed as dark-yellow fat on the anterior surface of the maxilla beneath the orbicularis oculi. The SOOF is then dissected from the underlying periosteum, then lifted and sutured to the arcus marginalis.
In addition to preperiosteal midface lifting, a subperiosteal approach can also be used to elevate the midface. Finally, fat transfer or injectable fillers can be utilized to sculpt the midface as a means to reinflate the soft tissue.
A subperiosteal midface lift can also be used for facial rejuvenation as well as for cases of severe lower eyelid retraction, which is not seen in the figure. The subperiosteal midface can be accessed through the lateral canthus, superior gingival sulcus, or temporal scalp incision. The periosteum is incised 3 mm inferior to the orbital rim, and a periosteal elevator is used to undermine the midface/maxilla/zygoma periosteum.
The mobilized midface is then sutured to the arcus marginalis medially and temporalis fascia laterally. Lower facelift will improve the nasolabial folds, jowls, and neck but will not help with the area around his eyes. Platysmaplasty can correct troublesome platysmal bands within the neck. The neck is not visualized in the figure and again, will not change the periocular appearance. A frontalis sling is used often to manage severe congenital ptosis or ptosis with poor levator function.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 72-year-old man has several months of chronic epiphora and blurred vision. He feels better only when he pulls his eyelid down and away from his eye. Given his external appearance as shown in Figure 1, what anatomical structure is most likely abnormal, leading to his symptoms?
pool.rationale:
The photograph shows trichiasis and distichiasis, and possibly a cicatricial entropion. The most likely cause of this abnormality is pathology in the posterior lamella.
Along the eyelid margin, the eyelid can be divided into 2 major lamellae: the anterior (made up of skin and orbicularis muscle) and the posterior (tarsus and conjunctiva). A cicatrizing process in each individual lamella tends to rotate the eyelid toward the pathology. Thus, ocular cicatricial pemphigoid or Stevens-Johnson syndrome would rotate the eyelid margin inward (cicatricial entropion), while a skin burn or eyelid eczema would rotate the lid outward (cicatricial ectropion).
Medial and lateral canthal laxity can certainly result in eyelid margin malposition, but this is typically involutional in nature.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the primary cell type involved in lentigo maligna?
pool.rationale: Lentigo maligna, also known as Hutchinson melanotic freckle or precancerous melanosis, is a flat, irregularly shaped, unevenly pigmented, slowly enlarging lesion that typically occurs in the malar regions in older white persons. It is characterized by the radial, intraepidermal, uncontrolled growth phase of melanocytes. The absolute risk of lentigo maligna melanoma is approximately 2.0%-2.6%.

pool.q: The orbital septum fuses with what structure 2 mm to 5 mm above the superior border of the tarsal plate in the non-Asian upper eyelid?
pool.rationale: The orbital septum, a thin, multilayered sheet of fibrous tissue, arises from the periosteum over the superior and inferior orbital rims at the arcus marginalis. In the upper eyelid, the orbital septum fuses with the levator aponeurosis 2 mm to 5 mm above the superior tarsal border in non-Asians. In the lower eyelid, the orbital septum fuses with the capsulopalpebral fascia at or just below the inferior tarsal border.

pool.q: A patient comes to the emergency department after being hit on the left side of the head with a baseball. He reports a progressive decrease in vision in the left eye. On examination, the globe is intact, the eyelids are tense, the intraocular pressure is elevated, there are pulsations of the central retinal artery, and a left afferent pupillary defect is present. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
pool.rationale: The situation described is concerning for an orbital compartment syndrome (OCS) from retrobulbar hemorrhage. The presence of an optic neuropathy and retinal arterial pulsations point to decreased perfusion to the globe and optic nerve and require emergency intervention. The most expeditious method to decompress the orbital soft tissue compartment is to perform lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis. It is critical to remember that OCS is a clinical diagnosis. A CT of the orbits often delays definitive treatment and should only be obtained once the cantholysis has been performed and the OCS reversed. Intravenous corticosteroids can be helpful for orbital edema but take time to work. Topical administration of glaucoma medications is not an inadequate emergent treatment for OCS.

pool.q: Biopsy of a lacrimal gland mass via the palpebral lobe of the lacrimal gland risks damage to what structure?
pool.rationale:
The lacrimal gland is divided into orbital and palpebral lobes by indentation from the lateral horn of the levator aponeurosis. Lacrimal excretory ducts pass through the palpebral portion of the gland, so removal of, or damage to (by biopsy), the palpebral portion of the gland can severely reduce secretion from the lacrimal gland. The accessory lacrimal glands are located in the superior fornix (Krauss) and superior border of the tarsus (Wolfring).
The origin of the lacrimal artery is the ophthalmic artery, which is not near the palpebral lobe. The efferent nerve supply to the lacrimal gland is by way of parasympathetic fibers from cranial nerve VII in the greater superficial petrosal nerve, which sends fibers to the sphenopalatine ganglion, and then by way of the zygomatic nerve.
Biopsy of the palpebral lobe of the lacrimal gland should be avoided because of potential ductal damage and not due to concern for the accessory glands or the arterial or nerve supply.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common cause of orbital cellulitis among adults?
pool.rationale:
Orbital cellulitis involves structures posterior to the orbital septum. It is most often due to secondary extension of acute or chronic bacterial sinusitis. Orbital cellulitis in adults usually involves multiple organisms, which can include gram-positive cocci as well as gram-negative bacteria such as H. influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis, and anaerobes; therefore, broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy is recommended in these cases.
Fungal infections occur in patients with predisposing factors, such as systemic disease with associated metabolic acidosis, diabetes mellitus, malignancies, and treatment with antimetabolites or steroids. Children are more likely to have orbital cellulitis caused by a single gram-positive organism. Trauma also can cause orbital cellulitis, which can be related to a foreign body or to an orbital fracture in a patient with pre-existing sinus disease.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is a contraindication to evisceration?
pool.rationale:
The potential for sympathetic ophthalmia is a common admonition against evisceration and for enucleation. In fact, sympathetic ophthalmia is a rare event, and no definitive correlation with evisceration has been proved (although some anecdotal evidence does exist). The most ominous risk of evisceration is an occult intraocular malignancy; evisceration would allow spillage of tumor out of the eye. Because of this possibility, evisceration should not be performed without a detailed view of the fundus.
If the funduscopic view is poor or incomplete, then either B-scan ultrasonography should be performed or the patient should undergo enucleation. Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are often inadequate in providing a detailed view of intraocular pathology, and should not be relied upon exclusively. On occasion, even B-scan ultrasonography can miss a subtle, relatively flat choroidal melanoma, especially if other intraocular processes have distorted the posterior anatomy of the globe. On the other hand, evisceration is a much simpler and faster procedure to perform, which is an important consideration in frail patients with multiple comorbidities who are poor anesthesia candidates.
Corneal thinning is a moot point, since the cornea is removed with the most widely used evisceration techniques. Restrictive strabismus has no bearing on evisceration. One could argue that this is, in fact, a relative indication for evisceration because the extraocular muscles may be difficult to identify and dissect during enucleation in such cases. A blind, painful eye is the most common indication for both enucleation and evisceration.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What should the physician do during an epiphora evaluation after assessing for pseudoepiphora and as an initial step for evaluation of lacrimal outflow problems?

options.a: Instill topical anesthetic in each eye and wait 30 seconds.
options.b: Observe the eyelid and puncta positions during the blink cycle.
options.c: Evaluate the corneal and conjunctival epithelium.

pool.rationale: Examination of a patient with epiphora starts by distinguishing between an etiology of hypersecretion and an etiology of lacrimal outflow obstruction. Pseudoepiphora evaluation includes assessment of the tear meniscus, tear breakup time, corneal and conjunctival epithelium, basal tear secretion (assessed with the use of topical anesthetic), and corneal irritation. Observation of the patient's eyelid and punctal positions during the blink cycle prior to manipulation of the lids is the first step in evaluation for lacrimal outflow obstruction. Slit-lamp examination during the blink cycle allows for the determination of correct position of the punctum, weakened or incomplete blinks, poor lacrimal pump function, and mechanical blockage of the punctum as causes of epiphora. Performing lacrimal irrigation for evaluation of lacrimal outflow obstruction would be one diagnostic test in the evaluation of epiphora after the assessment of the blink dynamics.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common clinical feature of thyroid eye disease (TED)?
pool.rationale:
Eyelid retraction is the most common ophthalmic feature of TED, being present either unilaterally or bilaterally in more than 90% of patients at some point in their clinical course. Exophthalmos of one or both eyes affects approximately 60% of patients, restrictive extraocular myopathy is apparent in about 40% of patients, and optic nerve dysfunction occurs in one or both eyes in approximately 5% of patients with TED. Only 5% of patients have the complete constellation of classic findings: eyelid retraction, exophthalmos, optic nerve dysfunction, extraocular muscle involvement, and hyperthyroidism. Upper eyelid retraction, either unilateral or bilateral, is documented in approximately 75% of patients at the time of diagnosis of TED.
Lid lag in downgaze also is a frequent early sign, being present either unilaterally or bilaterally in 50% of patients at the initial examination. The most frequent ocular symptom when TED is first confirmed is dull, deep orbital pain or discomfort, which affects 30% of patients. Some degree of diplopia is reported by approximately 17% of patients, lacrimation or photophobia by 15%–20% of patients, and blurred vision by 7% of patients. Decreased vision attributable to optic neuropathy is present in less than 2% of eyes at the time of diagnosis of TED. Pretibial myxedema and acropachy (soft‑tissue swelling and periosteal changes affecting the distal extremities, principally fingers and toes) accompany TED in approximately 4% and 1% of patients, respectively, and are associated with a poor prognosis for the orbitopathy. Myasthenia gravis occurs in less than 1% of patients.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 57-year-old woman with known metastatic uveal melanoma has developed a blind, painful eye. Treatments for the uveal melanoma have been exhausted and the vision is bare light perception. What is the best next step in management of this patient's condition?
pool.rationale:
Although the patient has a known metastasis, evisceration would not be the best option, given the risk of further local dissemination. Enucleation would allow for pain control as well as further histopathologic testing on the uveal melanoma.
The use of retrobulbar lidocaine would provide transient pain control but is of limited long-term value. A Gunderson conjunctival flap is beneficial for ocular surface pain but would not allow for the pain control necessary in patients with uveal melanoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What tissue feature characterizes the valve of Rosenmüller?

options.a: It is located at the distal portion of the nasolacrimal duct.
options.b: It prevents reflux of tears from the lacrimal sac into the canaliculi.

pool.rationale: The valve of Rosenmüller is actually a mucosal fold. Located at the junction of the common canaliculus and the lacrimal sac, it functions as a 1-way valve to prevent the reflux of tears into the common canaliculus during the lacrimal pump cycle. The valve of Hasner is located in the inferior meatus at the distal end of the nasolacrimal duct.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What cranial structure separates the optic nerve within the optic canal from the internal carotid artery?

options.b: optic strut of lesser wing of sphenoid

pool.rationale:
The optic canal follows a superomedial course as it exits the orbit toward the cranial vault. It is separated from the internal carotid artery (ICA) inferiorly by the so-called optic strut, an extension of the lesser sphenoid wing.
Cribra orbitalia describes porosities found along the orbital roof. Although in the past this condition was attributed to an iron-deficient diet, the true cause is unclear and may be multifactorial.
The cavernous sinus is part of the central venous sinus system and contains the carotid artery. It communicates with the orbit via the superior orbital fissure.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Bowen disease is a risk factor for the development of what type of invasive skin cancer?
pool.rationale: Bowen disease refers to squamous cell carcinoma in situ of the skin. In 5% of patients, Bowen disease may progress to vertically invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Bowen disease is not related to the other types of skin cancer listed (basal cell carcinoma, malignant melanoma, Merkel cell carcinoma).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What upper eyelid mass most commonly causes mechanical ptosis?
pool.rationale: Ptosis can be classified by the cause: myogenic, aponeurotic, neurogenic, mechanical, or traumatic. Mechanical ptosis is caused by an eyelid mass or orbital mass that weighs down the upper eyelid. Causes include plexiform neuroma, hemangioma, chalazion, skin carcinoma, orbital mass, and postsurgical or post-traumatic edema. Of these sources, chalazia are the most commonly encountered and therefore are the most common cause of mechanical ptosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common additional disorder that an infant with congenital anophthalmos is at risk to develop?
pool.rationale: Orbital bone growth is normally stimulated by the eye. In cases of microphthalmos or anophthalmos, it is common for the orbit to become hypoplastic compared to the non-affected side over time. Enlarged socket and hyperplastic eyelids would not be expected. Ptosis can be seen in cases of anophthalmia, but not as commonly as the development of a hypoplastic orbit, which is the most common concern in this disorder.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 35-year-old woman complains of drooping of her eyelids. She reports several previous episodes of intermittent painless swelling of her eyelids. Her findings at presentation are shown in the figure. What diagnosis is most likely?
pool.rationale: Blepharochalasis is a rare condition that is a variant of angioneurotic edema. Typically, it occurs in young females and is characterized by intermittent swelling of the eyelid, resulting in thin and wrinkled skin that can give the appearance similar to dermatochalasis. In older patients, dermatochalasis and blepharoptosis are very common complaints that can reduce the upper visual fields. Brow ptosis can also accentuate the appearance of a drooping upper lid. For these entities, it is important to assess the upper eyelid MRD1 to determine if the upper lid is ptotic or if dermatochalasis is the main component of the visual field obstruction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 6-year-old child presents for evaluation of a rapid onset of proptosis with lateral and downward displacement of left eye as shown. Biopsy reveals a pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma. With respect to frequency and prognosis, what characteristics does this type of rhabdomyosarcoma have relative to others?

options.a: It is least common, with the best prognosis.
options.b: It is most common, with the worst prognosis.
options.c: It is least common, with the worst prognosis.
options.d: It is most common, with the best prognosis.

pool.rationale: This child has rhabdomyosarcoma, which is the most common orbital malignancy in childhood. Although onset can occur at any age, the average age at onset is 5 to 7 years, with the typical age at diagnosis being 7 to 8 years. Children with rhabdomyosarcoma have a history of the sudden onset and rapid evolution of proptosis. Periorbital ecchymosis may also be present. A history of trauma is often elicited, but trauma is frequent and misleading. Clinical features include unilateral proptosis, globe displacement, ptosis, and eyelid edema. Pain is uncommon (approximately 10% of cases). Prompt orbital biopsy is required for confirmation of the diagnosis whenever rhabdomyosarcoma is suspected. Fine-needle aspiration biopsy should not be relied upon to make the diagnosis, because aggressive chemotherapy typically requires more definitive histologic confirmation and this may delay a proper biopsy. Patient management involves a multidisciplinary approach. The 4 types of rhabdomyosarcoma are embryonal, botryoid, pleomorphic, and alveolar. Of these, pleomorphic is the least common, with the best prognosis. The embryonal is the most common type. The alveolar type is the most malignant. A mnemonic for these 3 is: "embryonal everyone, pleomorphic please, alveolar awful."
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 3-month-old infant presents with constant tearing and occasional mucus discharge on the right side. What is the best course of action?

options.a: a course of oral antibiotics to prevent dacryocystitis
options.b: reassurance that in most cases, the tearing will resolve by 1 year of age
options.c: endonasal dacryocystorhinostomy with silicone intubation under general anesthesia
options.d: probing in the operating room to open the valve of Rosenmüller

pool.rationale:
This 3-month-old child most likely has congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO) because of an imperforate valve of Hasner in the inferior meatus. About 90% of congenital NLDO will resolve by 12 months of life.
Probing is typically delayed before age 6 to 12 months, depending on the study, with some studies showing lower efficacy if delayed longer than age 13 months. Probing prior to 6 months is reserved for those children who develop recurring dacryocystitis.
Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is reserved for those patients who have failed probing with silicone stent intubation (some experts also recommend balloon dacryoplasty before DCR).
Oral antibiotics are highly effective in managing active dacryocystitis, but they are not recommended for prophylaxis against infection. Topical antibiotics are sometimes prescribed for chronic mucoid discharge.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 70-year-old man has bilateral ptosis, as shown. He complains of decreased superior peripheral vision. What additional complaint is he most likely to report?
pool.rationale:
This patient has obvious dermatochalasis and brow ptosis, which are obstructing the visual axis. The most common compensatory maneuver in such cases is frontalis contraction, which then leads to brow ache, typically manifesting in the late afternoon or evening. Patients will also complain of worsening of ptosis in the evening because of frontalis fatigue. This complaint should not be misconstrued as suggestive for myasthenia: All ptosis becomes more symptomatic later in the day. Myasthenic ptosis will vary throughout the day in a more random fashion.
Dermatochalasis does not cause glare, itching, or diplopia. The presence of diplopia is a red flag for additional pathology (including myasthenia) and requires further evaluation.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 15-year-old patient with craniosynostosis has had numerous reconstructive surgeries to improve ocular alignment and proptosis. For what additional ophthalmic complication should this patient be periodically re-evaluated?
pool.rationale: Syndromic craniosynostosis is the premature closure of 1 or more of the sutures in the bones of the skull and results in various skeletal deformities, including orbital defects. Hypertelorism and proptosis are frequently observed in some craniosynostosis syndromes, such as Crouzon syndrome and Apert syndrome.   Proptosis can lead to dangerous corneal exposure issues. Early cataracts, glaucoma, and severe myopia are not associated with this condition, but other ophthalmic conditions associated with craniosynostosis syndromes include strabismus, astigmatism, ptosis, exophthalmos, nasal lacrimal duct obstruction, and amblyopia.

pool.q: What congenital eyelid condition, more common in Asian children, might contribute to mechanical entropion of the lower eyelid margin?
pool.rationale:
In epiblepharon, the lower eyelid pretarsal muscle and skin ride above the lower eyelid margin to form a horizontal fold of tissue that causes the cilia to assume a vertical position. The condition is most common in Asian children. With maturation of the facial bones, the epiblepharon might become less pronounced and the eyelash position might improve without surgical intervention.
Euryblepharon is associated with both vertical shortening and horizontal lengthening of the lower eyelids and may be associated with blepharophimosis–ptosis–epicanthus inversus syndrome (BPES). Congenital ectropion is caused by a vertical insufficiency of the anterior lamella of the eyelid and may give rise to chronic epiphora and exposure keratitis. Ankyloblepharon is a partial (ankyloblepharon filiforme adnatum) or complete fusion of the eyelid margins.

pool.q: In an adult with an acutely tender erythematous medial canthal mass that is inferior to the medial canthal tendon, what initial treatment should be considered?

options.a: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the orbit

pool.rationale: The location and findings suggest that this is an acute dacryocystitis, which is usually caused by oral or nasal derived bacteria. If there is no improvement with antibiotics or if relief of acute pain is necessary, incision and drainage can be performed. External DCR is generally performed after the acute infection resolves. CT scan is not indicated in acute dacryocystitis unless atypical features are present.

pool.q: An ophthalmologist receives a call from an emergency department regarding a patient who has a post-traumatic orbital compartment syndrome (OCS) and an orbital floor fracture noted on computed tomography (CT) scan. The ophthalmologist is over 90 minutes away from the emergency department. What is the best management for the patient until the ophthalmologist arrives?

options.b: lateral canthotomy and cantholysis performed by the emergency department physician
options.c: obtain CT to confirm an OCS
options.d: medically clear the patient for an urgent bony orbital decompression

pool.rationale: Orbital compartment syndrome (OCS) may occur in a variety of settings (eg, posttraumatic or postsurgical hemorrhage, abscess formation, noninfectious inflammation). Posttraumatic OCS usually results from hemorrhage. Large orbital fractures expand the orbital compartment into the adjacent paranasal sinuses, and this may be relatively protective against the development of OCS. However, if bleeding continues, blood will fill this larger compartment, resulting in OCS. Therefore, it is important not to discount the possibility of OCS in patients with orbital fractures. Prompt lateral canthotomy and cantholysis should be performed by the emergency department physician, particularly if the ophthalmologist is not able to perform the procedure in a timely fashion. Inadequate cantholysis will not relieve the OCS, and complete release should be verified once the ophthalmologist has arrived. Conservative management with IV fluids and pain management will only mask the pain noted in OCS. OCS is a clinical entity that can result in permanent visual loss if diagnosis is delayed. Therefore, definitive management should not be delayed by waiting for CT. OCS rarely manifests as a discrete hematoma on CT, but rather appears as an increased reticular signal in the intraconal fat. Posterior globe tenting may be seen on axial and parasagittal images, because the posterior sclera is distorted by proptosis and a stretched optic nerve. Bony orbital decompression is rarely needed in a patient with OCS. Use of intravenous mannitol may temporarily stabilize the OCS. If the OCS has not resolved, orbital surgery may be required.

pool.q: A 6-month-old child presents with constant tearing, moderate mucopurulent discharge, and a white eye. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Canalicular dysgenesis leads to impaired drainage of tears, resulting in epiphora without associated signs of dacryocystitis, such as redness, swelling, pain, or mucopurulence.
Infectious conjunctivitis typically causes a red eye and presents with tearing and irritation.
NLD obstruction, either as a primary congenital condition or secondary to edema of the nasal tissue during an upper respiratory illness, causes tearing. Presentation can range from minimal or no discharge to copious discharge and associated dacryocystitis. Dacryoadenitis is inflammation of the lacrimal gland.

pool.q: A mother is concerned that her newborn baby does not produce tears when he cries. The ophthalmologist reassures her and explains that the lacrimal gland is not yet fully developed. At approximately what age will the baby’s lacrimal gland be fully developed?
pool.rationale: The lacrimal gland is not fully functional until the infant is about 6 weeks old. Thus, newborn infants do not produce tears when crying.

pool.q: A 50-year-old patient is early in her course of docetaxel for breast cancer and presents complaining of tearing. What is the most appropriate response?

options.a: Perform early silicone intubation of the nasolacrimal duct.
options.b: Perform conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy with placement of a Jones tube.
options.c: Observe the patient for spontaneous resolution of tearing over the next 3 months.

pool.rationale: Docetaxel is known to cause inflammation and scarring of the canaliculi, which can result in permanent stenosis. In a patient who is early in the course of treatment and has tearing symptoms, early placement of silicone stents should be considered to avoid this complication. Observation is not appropriate, since the scarring can be irreversible. A Jones tube can be placed if the canaliculi are not salvageable, but this is rarely the case early in the course of treatment. Changing to another chemotherapy agent could be discussed with the oncologist, but it typically is most appropriate to continue the current therapy, with placement of silicone stents to avoid permanent stenosis of the canaliculi.

pool.q: The 59-year-old female presents with 6 months of irritation in the left eye. She has no past ocular history. Her presentation is shown in the figure. On examination, no symblepharon or forniceal shortening is observed. What is the underlying cause of the notable finding?

options.a: mechanical tethering of the lower eyelid
options.c: hypertrophy of the lower eyelid retractors
options.d: attenuation of the lower lid retractors

pool.rationale:
The figure shows involutional entropion of the left lower eyelid greater than the right lower eyelid. The right lower lid eyelashes are rotated upward. No eyelashes are observed on the left lower lid, because the lid has severe entropion. Involutional entropion usually affects the lower eyelids and is due to horizontal lid laxity, overriding orbicularis oculi, and attenuation/disinsertion of the lower eyelid retractors.
Surgical treatment typically consists of a horizontal shortening procedure, such as a lateral tarsal strip in conjunction with a Quickert suture. A Quickert suture is performed by placing a double-armed suture originating in the inferior fornix and with both ends exiting just below the eyelid margin and tied externally. Another successful surgical technique is direct exploration and reinsertion repair of the lower eyelid retractors.

pool.q: A 38-year-old patient is recently diagnosed with solitary fibrous tumor. From what embryologic origin is this tumor?
pool.rationale: Solitary fibrous tumor is composed of spindle-shaped cells that are strongly CD34-positive on immunohistochemical studies. They can occur anywhere in the orbit and may recur, undergo malignant degeneration, and metastasize if incompletely excised. The embryologic origin of this tumor is mesenchymal. Other mesenchymal tumors include rhabdomyosarcomas, fibrous histiocytoma, osteomas, and fibrous dysplasia.

pool.q: In patients with posterior lamellar eyelid deficiency, what is the primary principle of repair?
pool.rationale: In patients with posterior lamellar deficiency, the primary principle of repair is to augment the posterior lamellar tissue with a spacer graft. Anterior lamellar resection would not address the posterior issue and would be expected to cause retraction of the lid. Full-thickness skin grafting is not appropriate on the posterior surface of the lid. Lash excision is not an appropriate primary treatment for posterior lamellar deficiency and often does not alleviate eye irritation, because the stratified squamous epithelium of the anterior lamella continues to abrade the delicate ocular tissue, despite removal of the lashes.

pool.q: An obese 27-year-old woman with headaches and horizontal diplopia presents to the clinic. After thorough evaluation and testing, the ophthalmologist diagnoses her with pseudotumor cerebri and begins treatment with acetazolamide. She promptly develops Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) with ocular involvement, requiring a prolonged hospital stay. On her 6-month follow-up, this patient now has binocular vertical diplopia as well, with new limitation in supraduction on the right. What is the most likely cause of these findings?

options.a: new cranial nerve palsy from progression of pseudotumor cerebri
options.b: ocular surface disease from meibomian gland dysfunction

pool.rationale:
A symblepharon is an adhesion between conjunctival surfaces (bulbar and tarsal) which can occur as a result of inflammation, infection, trauma, or previous ocular or eyelid surgery. Symblepharon can be treated with conjunctival Z-plasty. If severe, a full-thickness conjunctival, buccal, or amniotic membrane graft may be required. SJS is a very common cause of symblepharon as well as dry eye from meibomian gland dysfunction.
Dry eye is present in almost all patients who have had ocular involvement of SJS, and it is a known cause of diplopia, but it is typically associated with monocular diplopia and would not cause restricted extraocular motility. Pseudotumor cerebri can cause cranial nerve VI palsy, which causes horizontal but not vertical deviations. Superior rectus hypertrophy can be seen in thyroid eye disease and is not usually found in SJS.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The occurrence of spastic entropion can usually be precipitated by what condition?
pool.rationale: Spastic entropion usually follows ocular surface inflammation (rather than exophthalmos, cicatricial changes in the conjunctiva, or Parkinson disease). It often occurs after intraocular surgery in a patient with pre-existing lid laxity. Orbicularis muscle contraction causes inward rotation of the eyelid margin. This then exacerbates the ocular surface irritation, creating a cycle of increasingly frequent corneal irritation and orbicular contraction. The cycle must be broken, and this can be achieved either by temporary taping of the eyelid or by surgery.

pool.q: A 50-year-old patient has biopsy-confirmed malignant melanoma originating in an area of lentigo maligna involving the majority of the lower eyelid. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.a: staged surgical excision using tissue expanders
options.b: wide surgical excision with evaluation of margins by permanent sections
options.d: total shave excision with healing by secondary intention

pool.rationale:
Lentigo maligna can spread in the vertical and horizontal plane and can eventually progress to become vertically invasive melanoma. This pattern of spread requires wide surgical excision with evaluation of margins by permanent sections. 
Staged surgical excision using tissue expanders and shave excision does not address the risk of missing a portion of malignant lesion. Cryotherapy plays a role in the treatment of acquired melanomas of the conjunctiva but is not a treatment modality for cutaneous melanoma.

pool.q: How can congenital myogenic ptosis be distinguished from acquired aponeurotic ptosis?
pool.rationale: Similar to acquired aponeurotic ptosis, congenital ptosis can present as severe ptosis, include an elevated eyelid crease, and be unilateral or bilateral. Patients with acquired aponeurotic ptosis have ptosis in all fields of gaze, while patients with congenital ptosis have eyelid lag on downgaze. Eyelid lag is present because the poorly developed and stiff levator muscle limits the relaxation of the eyelid in downgaze. Absent eyelid crease can be present in either. That is why it cannot be used to distinguish between the two.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 50-year-old man complains of a droopy left lid that seems to have gradually worsened. He reports a previous history of rigid gas-permeable (RGP) contact lens wear. What is the most likely etiology of his ptosis and the associated examination findings?

options.a: myasthenia gravis - ptosis improves with ice test
options.b: Horner syndrome - associated with miosis and anhidrosis
options.c: neurogenic - associated with motility abnormality limiting left eye adduction, supraduction, and infraduction
options.d: aponeurotic - high/indistinct lid crease, normal levator function, persistence/worsening of ptosis in downgaze

pool.rationale:
The differential diagnosis of ptosis includes several categories. Mechanical ptosis refers to a mass/lesion weighing down the lid. For instance, this can be seen with chalazia, lid swelling, or large tumors. Neurogenic ptosis refers to ptosis caused by interruption in innervation to the levator muscle. In CNIII palsy, the associated findings include a dilated pupil and a "down and out" eye position due to loss of innervation to the medial, superior, and inferior recti as well as the inferior oblique muscle. "Complete ptosis" with the eyelid covering the pupil is often seen.
Horner syndrome is another cause of neurogenic ptosis, affecting the sympathetically innervated Müller muscle. Müller muscle in isolation typically provides approximately 2 mm of eyelid elevation. Therefore, the ptosis associated with Horner syndrome is usually mild. Horner syndrome classic triad consists of ptosis, miosis (small pupil that fails to dilate in darkness) and anhidrosis (reduces sweating on affected side of face).
Interruption of signal at the neuromuscular junction is found in myasthenia gravis (MG). In a positive ice test, the ptosis improves (temporarily), suggesting the diagnosis of MG. Myogenic ptosis is the most common type of congenital ptosis, is characterized by reduced levator function, and often demonstrates lid lag in downgaze. This is due to a poorly developed, poorly functioning muscle.
Aponeurotic ptosis is the most common type of acquired ptosis. In aponeurotic ptosis, the levator aponeurosis is thinned out or dehisced from its attachment to the tarsal plate. It is associated with a high or indistinct lid crease, normal levator function, and persistence or worsening of ptosis in downgaze (compare to myogenic). Most commonly this is an involutional (aging) change. RGP wear, as well as long-term vigorous eye rubbing, can lead to levator dehiscence; this can be considered a type of (chronic) traumatic ptosis as well. Acute traumatic ptosis can be caused by both blunt and sharp trauma. For example, overstretching of an eyelid with some amount of preexisting levator dehiscence with an eyelid speculum during cataract surgery may worsen the ptosis.
Eyelid lacerations may involve the levator aponeurosis with sharp severing of the muscle as one of the sequelae of trauma. The presence of fat in an eyelid laceration is a classic indication for more extensive wound exploration and possible need for levator repair.

pool.q: A 67-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of left eye irritation. Examination shows a segmental area of pale, misdirected lashes. What technique would be most appropriate to achieve a lasting result?
pool.rationale: Trichiasis is an acquired misdirection of eyelashes. Mechanical epilation, removing misdirected lashes with forceps, can be used to treat solitary trichiasis. However, this is not a permanent solution, as recurrence is expected within 3 to 8 weeks after epilation. Cryotherapy is used for segmental trichiasis but does have potential side effects, including edema, skin hypopigmentation, eyelid margin notching, and possible interference with goblet cell function. Argon laser treatment, although not as effective as cryotherapy, is useful when only a few scattered lashes require ablation. Some pigment is required in the base of the lash for argon laser treatment to work, so it is sensitive to hair color and would not work in this patient. Nd:YAG laser is used to perform a laser capsulotomy and not used in the treatment of trichiasis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What eyelid neoplasm is associated with human papillomavirus (HPV)?
pool.rationale: Verruca vulgaris is caused by epidermal infection with human papillomavirus, and occurs rarely in the thin eyelid skin. The other neoplasms listed (seborrheic keratosis, molluscum contagiosum, syringoma) are not associated with human papillomavirus.

pool.q: The upper eyelid defect shown in the figure is best repaired with what surgical procedure?

options.a: layered closure of tarsus, subcutaneous tissue, and skin

pool.rationale:
The patient has a full-thickness marginal upper eyelid laceration. Although the eyelid laceration extends far superiorly, the eyelid margin defect is small (the lid is swollen and splayed open). With trauma, there is rarely tissue loss and therefore, primary closure of tarsus, subcutaneous tissue, and skin is the surgical procedure of choice.
A Cutler-Beard procedure is used to repair large upper eyelid margin defects greater than 50% of the eyelid margin. The procedure is performed by making an incision below the lower eyelid tarsus and creating a full-thickness lower eyelid skin graft that is advanced to the upper eyelid defect. Large lower eyelid margin defects involving more than 50% of the eyelid margin can be repaired by using a tarsoconjunctival flap from the upper eyelid into the posterior lamellae defect in the lower eyelid. The anterior lamellae is then reconstructed with either a skin advancement flap or a free-skin graft from the preauricular or postauricular region (modified Hughes procedure). With this procedure, the tarsoconjunctival flap is crossing the pupil for few weeks, which means this procedure should not be used in children in the amblyopic age ranges, as it can induce occlusion amblyopia. Advancement skin flap alone would only repair the anterior lamellae. With a full-thickness eyelid defect, repair of the posterior lamellae is also required for survival of the advancement skin flap.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Failure of what embryonal developmental process results in microphthalmia with orbital cyst?
pool.rationale: Microphthalmia with orbital cyst results from failure of the choroidal fissure to close in the embryo. Craniofacial clefts occur as a result of a developmental arrest or mechanical disruption of development. Etiologic theories include a failure of neural crest cell migration and a failure of fusion or movement of facial processes. Anophthalmia occurs when the primary optic vesicle fails to grow out from the cerebral vesicle at the 2-mm stage of embryonic development. Consecutive anophthalmia is thought to result from a secondary degeneration of the optic vesicle.

pool.q: What measurement assures that there will be sufficient tissue remaining after upper eyelid blepharoplasty?

options.a: 20 mm of skin between the inferior border of the brow and the upper eyelid margin

pool.rationale: To avoid excessive skin removal, the surgeon usually leaves at least 20 mm of skin remaining between the inferior border of the brow and the upper eyelid margin. The other measurements do not relate to having sufficient tissue.
