pool.q: A 20-year-old man is examined for ptosis of the right upper eyelid. His margin–reflex distance 1 (MRD1) is 2 mm greater when in downgaze than in primary gaze, and in upgaze the eyelid covers the pupil almost completely. There is symmetric retropulsion of each globe. What is the most likely etiology of his ptosis?
pool.rationale: Eyelid retraction in downgaze that causes an increase in the margin–reflex distance 1 (MRD1) is typical of congenital ptosis, in which the muscle is maldeveloped and is thus unable to relax and stretch in downgaze. However, this may also be true for infiltrative and compressive lesions involving the levator muscle, and in congenital ptosis, there should be normal retropulsion of the globes. Ocular myasthenia is associated with fluctuating ptosis, which is not discussed in this scenario. Finally, dehiscence of the aponeurosis is not associated with lid lag as noted in downgaze.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with a biopsy-proven, poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma of the medial canthus with aggressive growth. During definitive tumor extirpation, the medial canthus and canaliculi are removed. What would appropriate management include?

options.a: small margin excisions in order to minimize the degree of functional disruption to the surrounding tissues and lacrimal system
options.b: anchoring medial canthal attachments of the remaining eyelid margin firmly to the periosteum or bone with dissolvable suture to prevent postoperative ectropion and granuloma formation
options.c: a glabellar or forehead flap rotated to cover the defect
options.d: attempted repair of the canalicular system with either a dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) or conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) with Jones tube

pool.rationale:
Repair of medial canthal defects is often difficult because of the inherent complex 3-dimensional anatomy and the presence of the lacrimal drainage system. Since in this case the defect was created as a result of resection of a tumor, the patient may have to tolerate epiphora until recurrence of the tumor is no longer a risk. A glabellar or forehead rotational flap is a reasonable option, with the understanding that such flaps are often thick and may need subsequent debulking as a second stage procedure.
When full-thickness medial eyelid defects are present, the medial canthal attachments of the remaining eyelid margin must be fixed to firm periosteum or bone with heavy permanent suture, wire, or titanium miniplates.
Until tumor recurrence is ruled out, it is critical to avoid lacrimal surgery that could create a pathway for the tumor to spread into the nose or sinuses. Lacrimal surgery may be performed several years later, once the threat of recurrent disease has passed (5 years or based on clinical judgment).
Frozen sections and wide margins or Mohs micrographic resection techniques minimize the risk of recurrent medial canthal tumors and the risk of orbital or lacrimal extension of these tumors.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What are the mucin-secreting cells of the conjunctival fornices?
pool.rationale: Goblet cells are the mucin-secreting cells of the conjunctiva and are located in the fornices. The glands of Krause and Wolfring are accessory lacrimal glands found in the subconjunctival tissue, mainly in the upper and lower eyelids. The glands of Wolfring are found primarily along the nonmarginal tarsal borders, and the glands of Krause are found in the fornices. The meibomian glands are sebaceous glands located within the tarsal plate.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What prophylactic treatment is frequently used to prevent scarring after laser skin resurfacing?
pool.rationale: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) outbreaks may occur after laser skin resurfacing, which could lead to significant scarring. Most physicians prophylactically treat patients with perioperative oral antiviral agents. Oral, not topical, antivirals are necessary to suppress outbreaks of HSV. Selection of appropriate patients for laser skin resurfacing is imperative. Isotretinoin inhibits reepithelialization, and is therefore contraindicated in laser resurfacing if used within 12 months prior to laser treatment.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For 2 months, a 35-year-old man has had medial and inferior displacement of the right globe, with axial proptosis. Concurrently, he reports intermittent orbital pain. He claims that he had a "benign tumor of the lacrimal gland partially removed 2 years ago." An orbital computed tomography (CT) scan was done and demonstrated a large lacrimal gland tumor with some irregular bony remodeling in the lacrimal gland fossa. For this patient, what is the most probable diagnosis?

options.a: recurrent benign mixed tumor of the lacrimal gland
options.c: malignant mixed tumor of the lacrimal gland
options.d: adenoid cystic carcinoma of the lacrimal gland

pool.rationale: Malignant mixed tumors of the lacrimal gland typically arise from long-standing benign mixed tumors or from a benign mixed tumor that has recurred following initial incomplete excision or violation of the pseudocapsule. In this case, the history of a previously benign tumor, now with pain and proptosis, makes malignant mixed tumor the most likely diagnosis. Recurrent benign mixed tumor would not cause pain. Pseudotumor of the lacrimal gland and adenoid cystic carcinoma would both present in this way, but are less likely, given the history of a previous incompletely excised benign tumor.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the principal drawback to using a dermis-fat graft for acquired anophthalmos in adults?
pool.rationale: Dermis fat grafting is a useful method to restore volume in the anophthalmic socket. Dermis fat grafts may be implanted in the upper eyelid to fill out the sulcus in patients with a deep superior sulcus. They may also be used with exposure or extrusion of an implant when a limited amount of conjunctiva remains in the socket. The graft increases the amount of net conjunctiva available as the conjunctiva re-epithelializes over the front surface of the dermis. The main disadvantage compared to a synthetic implant is the unpredictable resorption of the fat, with resultant inadequate volume. Dermis fat grafts have minimal extrusion or infection rates, and the donor site morbidity is not typically a significant issue.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: For 5 days, a patient has had acute hordeola with no secondary cellulitis, and has not been treated. What management is recommended?

options.c: warm compresses, lesion massage, and topical antibiotics

pool.rationale:
Hordeola arise from impacted meibomian or Zeis glands. As the hordeolum expands, the sebaceous contents are extravasated into surrounding eyelid tissue and cause an inflammatory response. Secondary infection may also occur. The distinction between chalazion and hordeolum is admittedly vague, with some sources defining chalazion as noninfectious inflammation, whereas the term hordeolum connotes active bacterial infection.
For acute lesions without surrounding cellulitis, conservative management is a good initial therapy, including warm compresses, eyelid massage, and a topical antibiotic with or without a corticosteroid.
Intravenous antibiotics are rarely needed unless an infected hordeolum progresses to orbital cellulitis, a highly unlikely event. For management of acute lesions, oral antibiotics, especially doxycycline and minocycline, may be useful because of their antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory properties. Surgical drainage is reserved for larger lesions that do not respond to conservative therapy. Local corticosteroid injection may also allow for resolution. Observation alone is typically ineffective for management of hordeola.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What complication can be seen with botulinum toxin injection into the medial lower eyelid?
pool.rationale: Botulinum toxin injection into the medial aspect of the lower lid can diffuse posteriorly and affect the inferior oblique muscle, which originates in the anterior orbit near the lacrimal fossa. This can result in bothersome diplopia that is not permanent. Ptosis of the upper lid can occur, but is generally associated with injections in the central upper lid. Botulinum injections can be helpful in cases of spastic entropion, and can be used to decrease lacrimal gland secretion.

pool.q: What orbital condition will most likely benefit from the use of intravenous (IV) contrast-enhancing agents when imaged with computed tomography (CT)?

options.a: thyroid eye disease associated with hyperthyroidism with proptosis and preradioactive iodine treatment
options.b: paranasal sinus disease affecting the orbit

pool.rationale:
Tumors that are highly vascularized or that have altered vascular permeability may be better visualized by the use of intravenous contrast-enhancing agents. An orbital hemangioma will show a homogeneously enhancing, well-encapsulated mass.
A hyperthyroid patient with proptosis and preradioactive iodine treatment can be adversely affected with use of contrast, because patients with Graves disease and multinodular goiter are at increased risk of developing thyrotoxicosis following iodinated contrast injection.
Orbital fractures and paranasal sinus disease affecting the orbit do not require the use of IV contrast to make the diagnosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What procedure is used to treat tearing following chemotherapy with docetaxel?
pool.rationale: Canalicular obstruction resulting from chemotherapeutic agents such as docetaxel (or 5-fluorouracil) is treated with conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy, because a dacryocystorhinostomy procedure requires intact canaliculi through which the intubation tubes are placed. Intermittent irrigation is usually not sufficient to treat the tearing, and prophylactic intubation is best done prior to the onset of chronic tearing and structural canalicular stenosis. Punctal plugs are used to treat aqueous tear deficiency and are not appropriate in the setting of a canalicular obstruction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Following eyelid surgery, a patient develops an acute postoperative orbital hemorrhage with visual loss. What is the appropriate management of care in this setting?

options.d: evacuation of the clot after reopening the incision

pool.rationale: Vision loss in the clinical scenario described is secondary to a compressive effect from the orbital hemorrhage. Therefore, evacuation of the clot after reopening the incision is the appropriate next step. Intravenous steroids can be given to minimize edema; however, surgical intervention is the first step and more appropriate. Intravenous mannitol, acetazolamide, timolol, and anterior chamber paracentesis are all treatment modalities for nonhemorrhagic scenarios.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 60-year-old man has severe canalicular stenosis. Appropriate management would include what option?

options.d: dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) with intubation of the canalicular system

pool.rationale:
In cases of severe canalicular stenosis or frank canalicular obstructions, a conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) is indicated. In CDCR, a fistula is created between the conjunctiva in the area of the caruncle through the lacrimal sac and its bony fossa into the nasal cavity. A Pyrex Jones tube is inserted into this tract to maintain patency. For mild canalicular stenosis, probing and dilation, sometimes with silicone intubation, can be attempted.
A successful DCR requires patent canaliculi. A 3-snip punctoplasty is an excellent treatment option for punctal stenosis, but would fail in the face of more distal canalicular stenosis. Topical corticosteroids would also prove unsuccessful.

pool.q: What structure is involved in both Le Fort I and Le Fort II fractures?
pool.rationale: Le Fort I is a low transverse maxillary fracture above the teeth with no orbital involvement. Le Fort II fractures involve the nasal, lacrimal, and maxillary bones, as well as the medial orbital floor. Le Fort III fractures cause craniofacial disjunction and involve the orbital floor and medial and lateral orbital walls.

pool.q: Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphoma (EMZL, also termed mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue [MALT] lymphoma) of the gastrointestinal tract has been associated with what chronic infection?
pool.rationale:
Helicobacter pylori

Ocular adnexal lymphoma comprises approximately 6%–8% of orbital tumors. The vast majority are non-Hodgkin B-cell type with less than 3% T-cell types. Bilaterality is reported in 10%-20% of cases. The most common type is extranodal marginal zone lymphoma (EMZL), comprising 50%-90% of all cases of ocular adnexal lymphoma. H. pylori infections are found in 90% of cases of gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphomas, and some case series have identified H. pylori in cases of EMZL of the ocular adnexa.
Chlamydia psittaci is another suggested infectious cause of adnexal EMZL. Of the tumor types, EMZL, follicular, and lymphoplasmacytic are considered low-grade or indolent tumors while diffuse large B cell lymphoma and mantle cell lymphoma are considered high-grade tumors. Treatment typically involves surgery and radiation.

pool.q: What procedure would best correct a deep superior sulcus deformity following evisceration?

options.a: subperiosteal secondary implant on the orbital floor
options.b: dermis-fat graft to the upper lid
options.c: replacing prosthesis with a smaller prosthesis

pool.rationale:
A deep superior sulcus is a common deformity following evisceration or enucleation; it is best corrected by placement of a subperiosteal secondary implant on the orbital floor. This implant pushes the initial implant and superior orbital fat upward to fill out the superior sulcus.
Dermis-fat grafts may be implanted to the upper eyelid to fill out the sulcus, but eyelid contour and function may be damaged, and the graft may undergo resorption.
Enlargement of the ocular prosthesis may be helpful.
Horizontal lid shortening is helpful when the prosthesis is resting too low and generally does not have a large impact on the superior sulcus.

pool.q: What kind of assessment can help to rule out pseudoepiphora?
pool.rationale: In the evaluation of epiphora, the initial step is to distinguish patients with hypersecretion from those with lacrimal drainage obstruction. The evaluation of pseudoepiphora involves the assessment of the tear meniscus, the tear breakup time, and the ocular surface. The tear breakup time helps to evaluate the mucin layer of the tears. This is best evaluated with the use of fluorescein placed in the conjunctival cul-de-sac without anesthesia. The normal time before breakup should be at least 15 seconds. Rapid tear breakup (< 10 sec) may indicate poor function of the mucin layer despite a sufficient quantity of tears. Canalicular probing, lacrimal irrigation, and dye disappearance tests are all done to assess for lacrimal outflow obstruction, not pseudoepiphora. These tests may alter the evaluation of the tear breakup time, and therefore the pseudoepiphora evaluation, by creating normal reflex tearing.

pool.q: What sensory nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure?
pool.rationale: The ophthalmic division of cranial nerve V enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure. The optic nerve enters through the optic canal, and the maxillary division of cranial nerve V enters through the foramen rotundum. The facial nerve is a motor nerve and does not enter the orbit.

pool.q: What is the best initial step in management of suspected orbital lymphoma?

options.a: radiation without biopsy to avoid tumor seeding
options.d: total surgical removal of lymphoma to avoid radiation

pool.rationale:
Ocular adnexal lymphoma (OAL) consists of several subtypes elucidated by the World Health Organization's (WHO's) recent reclassification of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). Because the various NHL subtypes have different prognoses and different treatment paradigms, initial biopsy of suspected OAL is critical. Both fresh and formalin-fixed tissue is analyzed for morphology, immunohistochemistry, and flow cytometry. The subsequent treatment depends on the subtype of OAL identified.
The more indolent OAL subtypes, most frequently extranodal marginal zone lymphoma (EMZL, also known as mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue [MALT] lymphoma), can be treated with local radiation, corticosteroids, and long-term follow-up. More aggressive subtypes (which make up the minority of OAL), including diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and mantle-cell lymphoma, typically require systemic chemotherapy, even in cases of localized disease (stage IE).
Because of the WHO reclassification, it is important for the clinician to approach OAL with specific subtypes in mind rather than make sweeping assumptions about management based on older data, which tended to place all OAL together as one entity.

pool.q: Where is the most common site of obstruction in congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO)?

options.a: inferior aspect of the lacrimal fossa
options.b: inferior aspect of the nasolacrimal duct
options.c: junction of the lacrimal sac and nasolacrimal duct
options.d: junction of the common canaliculus and lacrimal sac

pool.rationale: NLDO is most commonly due to a failure of complete development and opening of the distal aspect of the nasolacrimal duct at the location of the valve of Hasner. Patency usually occurs spontaneously within a few months of life. The valve of Rosenmüller is located at the junction of the common canaliculus and the lacrimal sac. Obstruction is not usually present at the junction of the lacrimal sac and NLD. A mass palpated at the lacrimal fossa, which lies above the lacrimal sac, is concerning for malignancy.

pool.q: In non-Asians, where does the orbital septum of the upper eyelid fuse with the levator aponeurosis?

options.c: 2–5 mm above the superior tarsal border

pool.rationale: In non-Asians, the orbital septum fuses with the levator aponeurosis 2–5 mm above the superior tarsal border. The levator aponeurosis attaches to the tarsus at the inferior third of the tarsus. The fusion of the periosteum of the facial bones, the periorbita, and the orbital septum is the arcus marginalis. Whitnall ligament acts as a pulley for the force of the levator muscle and provides suspensory support for the upper eyelid and the superior orbital tissues.

pool.q: While performing a medial wall decompression, an ophthalmologist encounters clear fluid. The ophthalmologist suspects that it is cerebral spinal fluid. Identification of, and staying inferior to, what landmark could have minimized the chance of this complication?
pool.rationale:
The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries pass through the corresponding ethmoidal foramina in the medial orbital wall along the frontoethmoidal suture. This suture represents the level of the cribriform plate, the floor of the anterior cranial fossa. Trauma above this ethmoidal foramina can cause inadvertent entry into the cranial vault and subsequent cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) rhinorrhea.
The trochlea is located along the orbital roof and if penetrated can cause CSF rhinorrhea. However, it is unlikely to be involved during a medial wall decompression. The medial rectus muscle belly is not a landmark, as it would not allow for sufficient decompression to take place. Similarly, the lacrimal crest is a vertically oriented landmark that is too anterior to the plane of dissection during a medial wall decompression.

pool.q: The frontoethmoid suture is a clinically important landmark depicting the location of what structure?

options.c: superior aspect of the nasolacrimal fossa

pool.rationale: The frontoethmoid suture runs along the border of the medial wall and the roof. It marks the approximate location of the cribriform plate, which is superior and medial to the frontoethmoid suture line. The frontoethmoid suture is also the site of the anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries and veins. The nasolacrimal fossa along the medial wall is the attachment site of anterior and posterior limbs of medial canthal tendon. The ostium of the nasofrontal duct can be injured during frontal sinus fracture. The superior aspect of the nasolacrimal fossa houses the lacrimal sac.

pool.q: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presents to the emergency department with severe orbital pain, decreased vision, and proptosis. Computed tomography (CT) scan shows fulminant sinusitis with orbital invasion. Biopsy is performed, and Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver stain shows septate branching hyphae of uniform width. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
The clinical scenario described is a classic presentation of aspergillosis. On Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) stain, aspergillus is characterized by branching, septate hyphae.
Mucormycosis also would be on the differential diagnosis of acute sino-orbital disease in a patient with poorly controlled diabetes. However, GMS stain demonstrates broad, nonseptate hyphae in mucormycosis.
Echinococcosis is caused by a dog tapeworm; it can sometimes cause progressive inflammation and a severe immune response if there is rupture of an orbital cyst. It is not associated with sinus disease.
Cysticercosis is caused by the Taenia solium parasite and may rarely cause orbital infection. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for serum antibodies may aid in diagnosis.

pool.q: The patient below presents after recently immigrating from South America. A complete examination is performed and is normal other than the findings shown in the image. What is the appropriate recommendation with regard to follow-up for this patient?

options.b: The patient should have regular ophthalmology follow-up for ocular hypotony due to ciliary body shutdown.
options.c: The patient should have regular ophthalmology follow-up appointments to screen for uveal melanomas.
options.d: Schedule a follow-up appointment with dermatology to check for skin melanoma.

pool.rationale:
The patient exhibits the typical slate-grey pigmentation of the skin and sclera seen in oculodermal melanocytosis (OM, nevus of Ota). Note the distribution along the maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve. OM is more prevalent in Asian, African, and Hispanic populations.
OM is a congenital lesion, in contradistinction to primary acquired melanosis (PAM), an acquired condition of older white populations. Unlike PAM, which may progress to skin melanoma, patients with OM are at risk for choroidal (0.25%) and meningeal melanoma. Routine screening by dilated fundus examination may be difficult: Patients with OM have a thickened uvea, and as a result have poor pupillary dilation. B-scan ultrasonography may be necessary to definitively rule out an intraocular mass.
Patients with OM should also be monitored for glaucoma development due to involvement of the trabecular meshwork.

pool.q: What is the preferred management of lipodermoids?
pool.rationale: Lipodermoids, also referred to as dermolipomas, are benign lesions most commonly found in the superotemporal quadrant, but they may extend deeper to the levator and extraocular muscles. They are solid tumors, distinguished from dermoids by their significant adipose tissue component. No treatment is required for these tumors. However, if they are large or cosmetically bothersome, resection of the anterior visible portion can be performed, with careful preservation of the overlying conjunctiva.

pool.q: What osseous orbital feature is associated with the annulus of Zinn?
pool.rationale: The annulus of Zinn is a fibrous structure in the apex of the orbit that is formed by the common origin of the 4 rectus muscles. It separates the superior orbital fissure into 2 compartments, with associated nerves and blood vessels entering the orbit in a predictable fashion within these 2 spaces. The infraorbital fissure, ethmoidal foramen, and inferior orbital groove are not associated with this structure.

pool.q: What is the best management for most cases of primary sebaceous gland carcinoma?
pool.rationale: Management of sebaceous gland carcinoma includes excision of the lesion, with tumor-free margins. This procedure can be done with wide excision, frozen-sections, or Mohs micrographic surgery. Because of the nature of the malignancy, which may have skip lesions and pagetoid spread, map biopsies are also often done at the same time, to ensure that no residual tumor is left behind. Although adjunctive cryotherapy, radiotherapy, or chemotherapy may be considered, they are not used as primary therapy. Orbital exenteration is considered in the case of invasive or recurrent neoplasia and may be needed in cases of sebaceous cell carcinoma that are recurrent, large, or invade through the orbital septum.

pool.q: What is a characteristic finding of involutional ptosis?
pool.rationale: Involutional or aponeurotic ptosis is characterized by a higher than normal eyelid crease, normally functioning levator muscle (> 15 mm) and often ipsilateral compensatory eyebrow elevation. The eyelid crease is often found at a higher level than normal secondary to levator attenuation or frank disinsertion. Aponeurotic disinsertion also results in superior migration of the orbital septum and underlying preaponeurotic fat, which in turn results in hollowing of the upper eyelid (deep superior sulcus). An absent or poorly formed eyelid crease is a characteristic finding in congenital ptosis.

pool.q: What type of tumor is an orbital dermoid?
pool.rationale:
Dermoid and epidermoid cysts are among the most common benign orbital tumors of childhood. These cysts are present congenitally and enlarge progressively. The more superficial cysts usually become symptomatic in childhood, but deeper orbital dermoids may not become clinically evident until adulthood. Both dermoid and epidermoid cysts are lined by keratinizing epithelium; however, dermoids may contain dermal appendages such as hair follicles and sebaceous glands, while epidermoids do not.
Both epidermoids and dermoids represent choristomas. These are tissue anomalies characterized by normal cells that are not normally found at the involved site. Other choristomas include dermolipomas and teratomas.
Hamartomas are anomalous growths of tissue consisting only of mature cells that are normally found at the involved site. Examples of these are infantile (capillary) hemangiomas and the characteristic lesions of neurofibromatosis.

pool.q: How is notching of the eyelid minimized during the repair of a marginal eyelid laceration?

options.a: precise suture placement and critical suture tension
options.c: placement of square knot at the eyelashes
options.d: tarsal sutures that extend through the conjunctiva

pool.rationale: Repair of eyelid margin lacerations requires precise suture placement and critical suture tension to minimize notching of the eyelid margin. It is important that the tarsal approximation be made in a meticulous direct manner and that the eyelid margin be precisely anatomically aligned. Surgeons differ as to whether they place the tarsal or the eyelid margin sutures first, and many variations of suturing techniques are acceptable. To prevent corneal epithelial disruption, the tarsal sutures should not extend through the conjunctival surface.

pool.q: A patient with recent orbital surgery has decreased vision, an afferent pupillary defect, and an intraocular pressure (IOP) of 60. What is the preferred management?

options.a: open incision, drain any hematoma, explore for active bleeding

pool.rationale:
The orbit has a fixed volume, and there is limited room to accommodate any expansion of its contents. An acute rise in orbital pressure from hemorrhage or introduction of air into the orbit causes orbital compartment syndrome (OCS), which is manifested by decreased vision, afferent pupillary defect, and increased IOP. Vision loss can occur rapidly from compression of the central retinal artery, compression of the optic nerve or its vasculature, or ischemic optic neuropathy from stretching of nutrient vessels.
OCS can be caused by trauma, surgery, retrobulbar injections, or pre-existing orbital disease. Decompression of the orbit is the treatment of OCS. For patients who have had recent orbital surgery, the wound should be opened, the hematoma should be evacuated, and active bleeding should be cauterized. In OCS caused by trauma or injections, decompression is usually achieved by lateral canthotomy and cantholysis. Elevated IOP is due to increased orbital pressure, not glaucoma. Therefore, glaucoma treatments such as acetazolamide or tube shunts are not indicated.

pool.q: A 54-year-old non-smoking woman complains of 2 weeks of rapid-onset right-gaze pain, proptosis, and diplopia. Other than remission of breast carcinoma following mastectomy 5 years ago, her medical history is negative. The results of her thyroid function tests, including the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) test, are normal. Orbital computed tomography (CT) scan reveals a 12 mm diameter irregular infiltrating mass within the body of the lateral rectus muscle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale: The presence of pain, proptosis, and early ophthalmoplegia suggests the possibility of metastatic carcinoma. The most common primary source of orbital metastases in women is breast cancer, which may occur many years after the breast has been removed. The extraocular muscles are frequently involved because of their abundant blood supply. The irregular infiltrating mass noted on CT is most consistent with metastatic disease. Lymphoma does not typically cause pain. Cavernous hemangioma would be well-circumscribed on CT scan, and would not typically appear within an extraocular muscle. Graves orbitopathy typically causes fusiform enlargement of the extraocular muscles, sparing the tendon insertion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: From what cell type does orbital rhabdomyosarcoma arise?
pool.rationale:
Rhabdomyosarcoma arises from pleuripotent mesenchymal cells, not from extraocular muscles. The average age of onset is 5-7 years, and patients typically present with rapidly progressive, unilateral painless proptosis. There are 4 different variants of rhabdomyosarcoma.
Alveolar accounts for only 9% of orbital rhabdomyosarcomas and is the most malignant form. It has a tendency to develop in the inferior orbit. Embryonal is the most common type and accounts for more than 80% of cases. It has a predilection for a superonasal location in the orbit and has a very high survival rate (94%). Pleomorphic is the rarest form. It is also the most well-differentiated form and consequently has the highest survival rate (97%). The botryoid variant of rhabdomyosarcoma is quite rare. It is unique in that it does not occur as a primary orbital tumor, but rather invades the orbit from the adjacent paranasal sinuses or from the conjunctiva. Treatment of rhabdomyosarcoma requires surgical debulking, chemotherapy, and radiation.

pool.q: A 47-year-old obese man presents with complaints of chronic mucus discharge, especially in the morning. Examination demonstrates the findings in the figure.  What is the best initial step in managing this patient's condition?

options.a: Obtain corneal topography for possible keratoconus.
options.b: Dissuade him from any eyelid surgery because there would be poor wound healing, owing to an abnormality in his collagen and elastin fibers.
options.c: Refer him to a rheumatologist for a workup, looking for collagen vascular disease.
options.d: Refer him for sleep studies to rule out sleep apnea.

pool.rationale:
The clinical scenario is consistent with floppy eyelid syndrome (FES), a disorder that has a predilection for overweight males. Clinical findings include those listed as well as possible keratoconus. Patients with FES have a high incidence of concomitant sleep apnea, which may have significant systemic ramifications; therefore, a referral for sleep studies should be part of the initial management schema.
Patients with FES have been shown histopathologically to have abnormal collagen and elastin in their eyelids, although it is unclear whether this is the cause of or an effect from FES. Regardless, this finding results in a higher than average rate of wound dehiscence with attempted surgical correction of FES by horizontal tightening procedures. Despite this, such surgery can be highly successful in the appropriate patient.
FES has no known association with collagen vascular diseases. Corneal topography may be obtained in select patients with FES and suspected keratoconus, but the most important initial step is to rule out potentially dangerous episodes of prolonged sleep apnea.

pool.q: A neonate presents with a bluish mass in the medial canthal area below the medial canthal tendon. What is the most likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
Mucoceles may form within the lacrimal sac or within the nasal cavity as a consequence of congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO). When the mucocele is within the lacrimal sac it is termed a dacryocystocele. These may be present at birth or may develop within 1-4 weeks after birth. A dacryocystocele occurs when mucus is trapped in the tear sac because of a functional block above the sac (valve of Rosenmüller) and obstruction at the distal end (valve of Hasner) of the NLD. The dacryocystocele is initially sterile and may respond to conservative management with prophylactic topical antibiotics and digital compression of the lacrimal sac. When there is minimal improvement or infection develops, probing of the lacrimal drainage system may be necessary to address the disorder. Extension of the dacryocystocele cyst into the nasal cavity at the level of an occluded valve of Hasner may also occur. The intranasal cystic portion often extends inferiorly under the inferior turbinate, where it can be observed during nasal examination. Intranasal examination and urgent treatment are needed if the condition is bilateral and causes airway obstruction, as infants are obligate nasal breathers.
Causes of swelling above the medial canthal tendon may be a result of meningoencephaloceles or dermoid cysts. Imaging with computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is useful in differentiating these better.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common reason for failure of internal (endonasal) dacryocystorhinostomy?

options.a: silicone tube removal later than 6 months

pool.rationale:
Inadequate ostium size is the most common reason for failure of endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy. Other reasons include fibrosis and occlusion of the osteotomy, common canalicular obstruction, or inappropriate placement of the bony ostium.
Silicone tube removal later than 6 months has not been shown to cause failure. A deviated nasal septum and middle hypertrophy can cause the surgical procedure to be more challenging, but independently they are not primary reasons for endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy failure.

pool.q: A patient sustains a low transverse fracture in the maxilla above the teeth without any orbital involvement. What type of fracture is this?
pool.rationale:
Le Fort described a series of 3 facial fracture patterns following blunt trauma. Put simply, the fractures progress from the palate to the skull base across the medial buttresses of the face in a pyramidal fashion.
A Le Fort I fracture is a transverse fracture of the maxilla just above the teeth and has no orbital involvement.
A Le Fort II fracture involves the midface. It typically involves the maxilla and may extend to the lacrimal drainage system, resulting in posttraumatic epiphora.
A Le Fort III fracture is most easily described as complete craniofacial disjunction: The fracture extends across both orbits and the skull base (involving the sphenoid bone). In short, the face is fractured away from its attachments to the skull. Le Fort III fractures may involve the optic canals and result in traumatic optic neuropathy.
Naso-orbital ethmoidal or nasoethmoidal complex involve the bones in the area of the medial canthal tendon and lacrimal sac. They may result in telecanthus, medial canthal rounding, and epiphora.
A zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture, also known as a tripod or cheekbone fracture, involves the horizontal and vertical buttresses of the maxilla and zygoma. The inferior and lateral orbital rims are usually involved, and an orbital floor fracture is an associated finding.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What procedure is likely to be preferred for the treatment of ptosis related to Horner syndrome?
pool.rationale: Transconjunctival levator-Müller muscle resection is a technique performed for correction of minimal (2 mm) ptosis. The Müller muscle, which contributes about 2 mm of eyelid elevation, is innervated by the sympathetic nervous system. Testing patients for ptosis improvement after instillation of 2.5% phenylephrine drops can help to identify ideal candidates for this surgical approach. Horner syndrome is a constellation of clinical signs resulting from a deficiency of sympathetic activity. These patients experience a mild ptosis secondary to disruption in the sympathetic innervation to the Müller muscle. Therefore, this surgical technique would be preferred for patients with mild ptosis from Horner syndrome.

pool.q: A newborn has a difference between her lower lids. The pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated, and the parent denies any symptoms. Clinical examination shows the presence of a punctum on the right lower lid, but punctal agenesis on the left lower lid. What symptom is most likely to develop?
pool.rationale: Agenesis of the lacrimal punctum can result in epiphora, since it represents a blockage of the lacrimal outflow system. It would not cause mucopurulent discharge, redness, or dry eye. Punctal hypoplasia or stenosis is encountered more frequently than true aplasia. Tearing associated with minimal mucopurulence suggests blockage caused by punctal or canalicular dysgenesis. Tearing associated with frequent mucopurulence and matting suggests complete obstruction of the nasal lacrimal duct.

pool.q: A 48-year-old woman has a well-circumscribed, intraconal, midorbital mass with progressive vision loss. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals heterogenous gadolinium enhancement consistent with a cavernous hemangioma. What is the next step in managing this patient?
pool.rationale:
Cavernous hemangioma is a common orbital lesion of young to middle-aged adults, with a female predilection. On MRI, a characteristic heterogeneous enhancement pattern is often seen during initial gadolinium infusion that becomes homogeneous as the study progresses; this feature greatly narrows the differential diagnosis. In atypical cases, specific MRI and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) sequences may be very helpful in differentiating cavernous hemangioma from active venolymphatic or arteriovenous malformations, usually abrogating the need for and inherent risks of cerebral arteriography.
Computed tomography has less-specific patterns: longstanding lesions may exhibit areas of calcification. Although a cavernous hemangioma is usually slowly enlarging, the presence of a compressive optic neuropathy typically requires intervention.
Although some patients with early optic neuropathy may opt for observation to at least temporarily avoid the risks of treatment, surgical intervention should be offered. While stereotactic radiotherapy, including gamma knife radiosurgery, may be an option for lesions that are difficult to access in the orbital apex, anterior or mid-orbital lesions typically do well with excisional surgery.
Observation with serial examinations and imaging is certainly a reasonable option if a cavernous hemangioma is found incidentally and the patient is asymptomatic.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with unilateral brow ptosis secondary to facial paralysis. What muscle is most likely responsible for the brow ptosis?
pool.rationale: The orbicularis oculi, procerus, corrugator supercilii, and frontalis muscles receive their motor supply by way of branches of CN VII (the facial nerve). The nerve penetrates the muscle through the undersurface of each muscle. The frontalis elevates the eyebrows and so would be the cause of the brow ptosis in this case.

pool.q: A 23-year-old soldier was injured by an improvised explosive device (IED), sustaining severe facial burns and requiring enucleation of the right eye. At enucleation, a small implant was placed in the orbit and a large conformer was placed in the socket. Six weeks later, the socket is clean and there is some mild redundant conjunctiva. The ophthalmologist orders a permanent prosthesis for the patient. What risk factor does this patient have for future socket contracture?
pool.rationale: A severe initial injury, such as burns or extensive lacerations, is a risk factor for socket contracture. The presence of redundant conjunctiva is the opposite issue to that of contracture, and is not a risk factor. Placement of a small implant or of a large conformer are not risk factors. On the contrary, placement of a small implant and a large conformer can help maintain the fornices in situations where there is a high risk of contracture.

pool.q: A 45-year-old man was leaning over a railing trimming a bush with metal clippers when he fell over the railing and developed sudden pain and vision loss in the left eye. Imaging of the orbit is shown in the figure. What is the cause of the orbital finding?

options.b: air from a medial orbital floor fracture

pool.rationale:
The figure shows a soft tissue window of an orbital computed tomography (CT) image of the left orbit. Within the medial orbit, a large linear hypodensity is observed almost to the orbital apex. The degree of hypodensity is similar to that seen in the nearby ethmoid sinuses, suggesting that the hypodensity is either air or wood. Given the well-defined borders of the hypodensity and no observed medial wall fracture, wood is the most likely cause. In this case, a wooden branch was removed from the orbit. An embedded intraorbital wooden foreign body poses a high risk for infection and should be removed and cultured. The wound should also be irrigated. Prophylactic antibiotics should be strongly considered.
A metallic foreign body appears as a hyperdense lesion on CT imaging. The appearance of a hematoma on CT has a range of hypo-, iso-, hyper-, and mixed-density, depending on the age and characteristics of the hematoma. However, it would be unlikely for a hematoma to have this degree of hypodensity seen in this example.

pool.q: What orbital inflammatory disease commonly affects the respiratory system and kidneys?
pool.rationale: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (formerly Wegener granulomatosis) is a necrotizing small-vessel granulomatous vasculitis of unknown etiology, classically affecting the upper and lower respiratory system and the kidneys. Upper respiratory symptoms include sinusitis, chronic sinusitis, otitis, epistaxis, and ulcerations of the nasal mucosa. Lower respiratory symptoms include cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, pleurisy, and cavitary pneumonitis. Renal symptoms may be limited to microscopic hematuria. Other symptoms include arthralgia, fever, malaise, and weight loss. Idiopathic orbital inflammation (pseudotumor) sometimes occurs after upper respiratory infection, especially in children, but is otherwise not typically associated with systemic involvement. Sarcoidosis most commonly affects the lungs, but the orbit may be affected. Although sarcoidosis may affect any organ system, renal involvement is not a common presentation. Sjögren syndrome is associated with dry eyes and dry mouth. This syndrome may coexist with rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and scleroderma, which rarely involve the respiratory system.

pool.q: A patient presents with persistent tearing after a herpes zoster infection affecting the V1 and V2 distribution. On examination, he has outward turning of the affected lower eyelid margin. What type of ectropion is likely is causing his symptoms?
pool.rationale:
Cicatricial ectropion results from contracture or loss of anterior lamella tissue, which can occur in the setting of herpes zoster that affects the eyelid skin.
Involutional ectropion occurs secondary to horizontal eyelid laxity. Paralytic ectropion occurs in the setting of facial nerve palsy. Mechanical ectropion occurs due to gravitational effect from an eyelid mass, fluid accumulation, or herniated orbital fat. Determination of the cause of ectropion is important for planning of surgical repair.

pool.q: A 2-year-old child has a mass above the medial canthal tendon that has been increasing in size over the past several months. The mass is painless and was discovered incidentally during a routine eye examination. What is the recommended management?

options.c: magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the skull base

pool.rationale:
The main concern in a patient presenting with a slowly progressive, superomedial (above the medial canthal tendon) orbital mass is an expanding skull base process. In children, this is typically due to encephalocele (inferior herniation of brain tissue), meningocele (herniation of the meninges), or meningoencephalocele (herniation of both); these lesions are especially common in congenital clefting syndromes. Dermoid cysts may also occur in this region. Dacryocystoceles often form below the medial canthal tendon, but if there is any concern for encephalocele, consider imaging before probing and irrigation.
In adults, the most common cause is an expanding frontoethmoidal mucocele, which may have eroded through bone into the orbit and anterior cranial fossa (Fig. 1). It is crucial to obtain imaging of the area before proceeding with any type of surgical intervention in this clinical situation, in order to avoid any potential intracranial complications.
In children, an MRI is preferred to computed tomography (CT) for 2 reasons: 1. It will provide better imaging of the skull base soft tissue than CT; 2. MRI avoids radiation exposure to a young child's brain.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What eyelid malignancy is prone to invade locally by spreading along nerves?
pool.rationale:
Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the eyelid is less common than basal cell carcinoma but is more aggressive. SCC can metastasize through lymphatic transmission, blood-borne transmission, or direct extension, often along nerves.
There are 4 clinicopathologic forms of cutaneous melanoma: lentigo maligna melanoma, nodular melanoma, superficial spreading melanoma, and acrolentiginous melanoma. The eyelid is most often involved by lentigo maligna melanoma via secondary extension from the malar region or by nodular melanoma.
Sebaceous adenocarcinoma is highly malignant and potentially lethal. The tumor arises from the meibomian glands of the tarsal plate, glands of Zeis, or sebaceous glands of the caruncle, eyebrow, or facial skin. These tumors usually metastasize to regional lymph nodes and rarely spread hematogenously or through direct extension.
Kaposi sarcoma is a frequent manifestation of AIDS and presents as a chronic reddish dermal mass. It is composed of spindle cells of endothelial origin.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What bone forms the anterior portion of the nasolacrimal fossa?
pool.rationale:
The medial wall of the orbit is composed of 4 bones from anterior to posterior: maxilla, lacrimal, ethmoid, and the body and lesser wing of the sphenoid bone. The lacrimal sac fossa is bounded anteriorly by the ascending process of the maxilla, which forms the anterior lacrimal crest.
The maxillary bone fuses with the lacrimal bone within the fossa, and the lacrimal bone goes on to form the posterior lacrimal crest.
A small portion of the palatine bone juts up in the posterior orbit to form a portion of the orbital floor.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 76-year-old woman presents for evaluation of bilateral droopy upper lids. She has a 30-year history of bilateral hard contact lens use. She has good levator function, thin eyelid skin, and a high lid crease. What is the most likely explanation for her eyelid ptosis?
pool.rationale:
Characteristics of aponeurotic ptosis include older age, long-standing hard contact lens use, good levator function, thin eyelid skin, and a high lid crease. Additional history that may be associated with aponeurotic ptosis includes post-trauma, long-standing edema as in thyroid-related orbitopathy and blepharochalasis, and chronic allergies, with associated eye-rubbing.
Neurogenic ptosis, such as Horner syndrome or cranial nerve (CN) III palsy, is often associated with other clinical findings, including pupillary changes. Previously unrecognized congenital ptosis does not usually have normal levator function.
Acquired myogenic ptosis is uncommon and results from localized or diffuse muscular disease such as muscular dystrophy, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, myasthenia gravis, or oculopharyngeal dystrophy.
Mechanical ptosis usually refers to the condition in which an eyelid or orbital mass weighs or pulls down the upper eyelid, resulting in inferior displacement. It may be caused by a congenital abnormality, such as a plexiform neurofibroma or hemangioma, or by an acquired neoplasm, such as a large chalazion or skin carcinoma. Postsurgical or posttraumatic edema may also cause temporary mechanical ptosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What brow lift procedure is used for treatment of mild brow ptosis and is performed through an upper eyelid blepharoplasty incision?
pool.rationale:
Browpexy treats mild brow ptosis and is performed through an upper eyelid blepharoplasty incision. During a blepharoplasty procedure, the tissues below the brow are resuspended with sutures to the frontal bone periosteum above the orbital rim.
Larger amounts of brow ptosis can be treated with a direct brow elevation, performed with incisions placed at the upper edge of the brow hairs; endoscopic brow and forehead lift, performed through small incisions approximately 1cm behind the hairline; or a pretrichial brow and forehead lift, performed through an incision just below the hairline.

pool.q: What lesion characteristics should raise one's index of suspicion for malignant melanoma of the eyelid?

options.a: new nodule formation in a previously flat, pigmented lesion

pool.rationale:
Nodule formation, growth, irregular borders, and irregular pigmentation in a previously pigmented eyelid lesion are risk factors for the development of melanoma. Racial pigmentation does not increase the risk for melanoma.
A uniformly pigmented stable lesion can be followed conservatively with serial examination, but the patient should be warned about findings suspicious for melanoma, including surrounding oculodermal melanocytosis (nevus of Ota), sharply demarcated lesion borders, and a uniformly pigmented lesion.
Oculodermal melanocytosis (nevus of Ota) is a congenital disorder typified by pigmentation of periocular skin, a "slate-gray" pigmentation of the sclera, and increased pigmentation and thickening of the iris, resulting in poor pupillary dilation. Patients with nevus of Ota are at increased risk for uveal, not eyelid, melanoma (1 in 400). Orbital and dural melanomas have also been reported with this condition.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What treatment would be recommended for a 52-year-old man interested in nonsurgical treatment of prominent nasolabial folds?
pool.rationale: Deep nasolabial folds are best treated with filler materials. Bovine collagen has declined because it requires skin testing for allergic reaction to bovine-derived collagen. Botulinum toxin may temporarily paralyze the lower facial musculature, potentially resulting in difficulty with smiling, speaking, and chewing. Laser resurfacing would not reach the depth of the nasolabial fold without first causing unacceptable damage to surrounding tissue.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An ophthalmologist is called to evaluate a patient in the emergency department who was transferred from another hospital. The patient has had progressive swelling of the right eyelid for the past several days. He has also had fevers, malaise, anorexia, and altered mental status. On examination, he has pronounced violaceous swelling of the right orbit, with areas of necrosis. The orbit is tight and requires immediate canthotomy/cantholysis. The right pupil is amaurotic and vision in that eye is no light perception (NLP). His left eye has a reactive pupil with vision of 20/25. Blood cultures sent from the outside hospital are positive for Group A beta hemolytic streptococcus. What is the next step in management?

options.c: intravenous antibiotics and surgical debridement in the operating room

pool.rationale:
The photo and clinical presentation are concerning for necrotizing fasciitis (NF). Given the high mortality rate, and the fact that NF patients can clinically decline very rapidly, all patients with NF should be admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for monitoring, as opposed to a general medical floor. Although starting immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics is a correct measure to take, plans to go to the operating room (OR) should not be delayed to watch for improvement. Prompt surgical treatment is one of the most important factors to decrease mortality in NF. This patient should be taken to the OR to debride necrotic tissue as expeditiously as possible (ideally within no more than a few hours of presentation).
Group A beta hemolytic streptococcus is the usual culprit in the etiology of NF. The aggressive nature of NF is determined in large part by how invasive that particular strain of the bacteria is. Virulence factors for this bacteria include the M protein and pyrogenic exotoxins (not endotoxins). M protein is an antiphagocytic virulence factor that renders the bacteria resistant to attack by host leukocytes. Pyrogenic exotoxins that are released cause fever, shock, and widespread tissue injury, potentially precipitating multiorgan failure.
Although risk factors for necrotizing fasciitis include conditions that can cause some degree of immunosuppression (diabetes mellitus, alcoholism, malignancy, rheumatologic disease), one study showed that 52% of NF patients were healthy and had no risk factors. Therefore, patients with NF do not automatically warrant an immunosuppressive workup or HIV screening. NF has also been reported following minor trauma (including after blepharoplasty and dacryocystorhinostomy [DCR] procedures).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Perineural invasion, bone destruction, and pain are associated with what lacrimal gland mass?
pool.rationale:
Adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC) is the most common malignant epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland. This highly malignant carcinoma may cause pain because of perineural invasion and bone destruction. The relatively rapid course, with a history of generally less than 1 year, and early onset of pain help differentiate ACC from pleomorphic adenoma, which is painless and characteristically exhibits progressive proptosis for more than a year. The tumor usually extends into the posterior orbit because of its capacity to infiltrate and its lack of true encapsulation.
Most lacrimal gland masses represent nonspecific inflammation (dacryoadenitis). They present with acute inflammatory signs and usually respond to anti-inflammatory medication. They do not cause bony destruction or exhibit perineural invasion.
The vast majority of orbital lymphoproliferative lesions are non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). The typical lymphoproliferative lesion presents as a gradually progressive, painless mass, resulting in proptosis, a visible periocular mass, or ptosis. These tumors are often located anteriorly in the orbit or beneath the conjunctiva, where they may show the typical salmon-patch appearance. Lymphoproliferative lesions, whether benign or malignant, usually mold to surrounding orbital structures rather than invade them; consequently, disturbances of extraocular motility or visual function are unusual.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When operating in the region of the temporal fossa, in what tissue layer is the temporal (frontal) branch of cranial nerve VII found?
pool.rationale:
In the temporal area, the temporal (frontal) branch of cranial nerve VII crosses the zygomatic arch and courses superomedially in the deep layers of the temporoparietal fascia (also called the superficial temporalis fascia), often near branches of the temporal artery.
Figures: A, Superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS). Note that the facial nerve branches inferior to the zygomatic arch are deep to the SMAS. B, The SMAS exposed during a face-lift procedure. The horizontal surgical markings indicate the border of the zygomatic arch, and the oblique lines mark the area of planned excision of the SMAS during the procedure. C, Coronal section of the face. The temporal branch of the facial nerve is found within the superficial portion of the temporoparietal fascia (extension of the SMAS).

pool.q: What structure is most easily damaged by surgical dissection in the superolateral conjunctival cul-de-sac?
pool.rationale:
The lacrimal sac ductules consist of 2 to 6 ductules that extend from the orbital lobe of the lacrimal gland, into the palpebral lobe, and join the palpebral lobe ducts. From there, 8 to 12 major palpebral lobe ductules drain into the lateral superior fornix cul-de-sac. They are located 4-5 mm above the superior margin of the upper tarsus. Therefore, dissection in this area can cause injury and, potentially, secondary dry eye. Whitnall ligament attaches laterally with septa transversing through the stroma of the lacrimal gland and attaches to the inner aspect of the lateral orbital wall. The horns of the levator aponeurosis differ from Whitnall in that they lie more inferior and toward the canthi. The lateral horn inserts onto the lateral orbital tubercle, and it divides the lacrimal gland into orbital and palpebral lobes, attaching firmly to the orbital tubercle.
The lacrimal artery lies within the stroma of the lacrimal gland and is unlikely to be injured during surgery within the conjunctival cul-de-sac.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: How does the presence of ipsilateral orbital pain and paresthesia affect the examiner's determination of the likelihood that the patient has adenoid cystic carcinoma versus benign mixed tumor of the lacrimal gland?

options.a: Pain implicates adenoid cystic carcinoma and paresthesia implicates benign mixed tumor.
options.b: Pain and paresthesia implicate adenoid cystic carcinoma.
options.c: Pain implicates benign mixed tumor and paresthesia implicates adenoid cystic carcinoma.
options.d: Pain and paresthesia implicate benign mixed tumor.

pool.rationale: The historical factors of significance, which help to differentiate adenoid cystic carcinoma from benign mixed tumor, are pain, progression (signs and symptoms present less than 1 year), paresthesia (perineural invasion), and ptosis, especially temporally. Benign mixed tumor does not usually result in marked pain or paresthesia.

pool.q: An older woman has epiphora from associated lower lid laxity. What is the appropriate procedure for this patient?
pool.rationale: Adjusting the horizontal tension on the lower lid will improve the position of the lower lid and better appose the punctum to the tear film. Rotational sutures, either temporary or medial spindle, may improve the anterior-posterior position of the punctum but do not help with the pump function of the lacrimal drainage system. Intubation of the lacrimal system does not address the underlying problem of vertical tension.

pool.q: Swelling or distention of the lacrimal sac extending above the medial canthal tendon is suggestive of what condition?
pool.rationale:
Swelling or distention of the lacrimal sac extending above the medial canthal tendon should raise concern for a primary lacrimal sac tumor, which may be associated with epiphora or chronic dacryocystitis. Reflux of blood from the punctum on irrigation, as well as spontaneous bleeding, are also highly concerning for a tumor.
Canaliculitis typically presents with persistent weeping and discharge, sometimes accompanied by a follicular conjunctivitis centered in the medial canthus, and the punctum is often erythematous and dilated, or “pouting.” Dacryoliths, or concretions formed within the lacrimal sac, can obstruct the nasolacrimal duct and cause lacrimal sac distention and dacryocystitis, but these conditions should not cause distention above the medial canthal tendon.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 34-year-old man has an esotropia of 30 PD in primary gaze, which increases in right and left gaze. Abduction and elevation are bilaterally reduced. He has right greater than left upper eyelid retraction. What is the likely diagnosis?
pool.rationale:
This case describes esotropia and eyelid retraction in a young adult male, with both abduction and elevation deficits. These findings are most likely due to thyroid eye disease. Early signs of thyroid eye disease include upper eyelid retraction with lateral flare, and thickening of the inferior and medial recti first. Presentation can be unilateral or bilateral.
While bilateral sixth nerve palsies would cause an esotropia and abduction deficits, they would not produce eyelid retraction. Idiopathic orbital inflammatory syndrome usually is a unilateral process. Carotid cavernous fistula also would not cause eyelid retraction, although it could produce ptosis if the third cranial nerve were affected.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Where is the marginal arterial arcade of the upper eyelid?

options.a: superior to the tarsus between the orbicularis oculi and the levator muscle
options.b: along the eyelid margin just anterior to the tarsus
options.c: superior to the tarsus between the levator aponeurosis and the Müller muscle
options.d: 2 mm superior to the eyelid margin just anterior to the tarsus

pool.rationale: The arterial supply to the eyelids originates from both the internal carotid artery ([ICA] to ophthalmic artery to supraorbital and lacrimal artery) and external carotid artery ([ECA] to angular and temporal artery). The anastomosis between these 2 circulations forms the 2 arterial arcades in the upper eyelid (marginal and peripheral arcade) and 1 arterial arcade in the lower eyelid. In the upper eyelid, the marginal arcade is found 2 mm superior to the eyelid margin just anterior to the tarsus. The peripheral arcade in the upper eyelid is located superior to the tarsus, between the levator aponeurosis and the Müller muscle. The arterial arcade of the lower eyelid is found just inferior to the tarsus.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In what direction is the globe most likely to be displaced when a child with a congenital orbital cleft cries?
pool.rationale: Craniofacial clefting syndromes are theorized to be a result of failure of neural crest cell migration and failure of fusion of facial processes. Examples include Treacher Collins-Franceschetti syndrome and Goldenhar syndrome. In these patients, the bones of the skull or orbit may have congenital clefts through which intracranial contents can herniate. These protruding contents can be meninges (meningocele), brain tissue (encephalocele), or both meninges and brain (meningoencephalocele). When these herniations involve the orbit, they most commonly present anteriorly with a protrusion subcutaneously near the medial canthus or over the bridge of the nose. Straining or crying may increase the size of the mass and the globe may be displaced temporally and downward (inferolaterally). Treatment is surgical and should be done in collaboration with a neurosurgeon.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Dacryocystorhinostomy is a useful and preferred intervention for what condition?
pool.rationale:
Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) through an external or internal (transnasal) approach is the treatment of choice for most patients with acquired nasolacrimal duct obstruction (NLDO).  Recent data have demonstrated higher success rates for internal DCR than were previously reported.
Dacryocystitis indicating total NLDO requires a DCR in most cases because of inevitable persistent epiphora and recurrence. DCR requires the presence of a patent canalicular system.
Epiphora from severe canalicular obstruction, when the canalicular system cannot be used or reconstructed, would be managed by conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) with Jones tube placement.
Congenital NLDO is most commonly caused by failure of complete development and opening of the distal end of the duct. Obstruction of the valve of Hasner in the inferior meatus is symptomatic in 5% of infants at birth. It either resolves spontaneously or responds to passage of a probe into the nasolacrimal duct, with or without silicone intubation.
A lacrimal sac malignancy is best managed by external dacryocystectomy and possible lateral rhinotomy and medial maxillectomy, sometimes performed in concert with an otolaryngologist.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What histologic characteristic of conjunctival melanoma is most predictive of a poor prognosis?
pool.rationale:
Conjunctival melanoma is a rare tumor, accounting for only 2% of all eye tumors. The risk factors for development are unknown. They occur most commonly in non-Hispanic whites, and there is an association with primary acquired melanosis and nevi.
An important histologic feature to help determine prognosis is depth of invasion of the lesion. Other factors that increase the risk of metastatic disease are incomplete resection, local recurrence, and a non-limbal location.
The other factors listed do not influence prognosis. Oil red O staining is a technique used for sebaceous adenocarcinoma of the eyelid, and not melanoma. S-100 protein staining is used to help identify melanoma histopathologically, as it is present in over 95% of malignant melanomas, but it does not offer prognostic value.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What orbital or adnexal structure is commonly involved in and/or is the nidus of preseptal cellulitis in adults?
pool.rationale:
Preseptal cellulitis is cellulitis anterior to the orbital septum. The lacrimal sac is the only preseptal structure of the answer choices (lacrimal gland - orbital lobe, lacrimal gland - palpebral lobe, trochlea). The most common causes of preseptal cellulitis in adults are dacryocystitis and superficial skin trauma from scrapes, wounds, and insect bites. In children, superficial skin trauma, as well as underlying sinusitis, are common causes. The vast majority of preseptal cellulitis is secondary to gram-positive bacteria, particularly Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species. S aureus is the most common trauma-related organism. Additionally, methicillin-resistant S aureus (MRSA) is a common pathogen, both in the hospital-acquired setting and in community-acquired cases in the 21st century. Haemophilus influenzae was a common cause in the 20th century, but is less so now because the practice of flu vaccination is widespread.
Abscesses can be drained and direct inoculations treated with topical antibiotic ointment. Preseptal cellulitis is usually treated with oral antibiotics on an outpatient basis, with hospitalization and intravenous (IV) antibiotics for particularly worrisome cases or failed outpatient therapy. Post-septal cellulitis is typically referred to as "orbital cellulitis," and most commonly results from sinusitis. Computed tomography (CT) imaging of the orbits and sinuses may be obtained to confirm clinical suspicions. Orbital cellulitis is treated on an inpatient basis, with IV antibiotics and oftentimes with surgical debridement and drainage.
The other answer choices all involve post-septal structures. Thus, none are correct, because infection of the lacrimal gland or the trochlea would constitute orbital cellulitis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When removing bone from the medial wall in an orbital decompression, where can the surgeon locate the posterior ethmoidal arteries?
pool.rationale:
The anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries are critical anatomic landmarks to identify during orbital decompression. Their foramina both lie along the line of the frontoethmoidal suture (FES). The FES usually defines the level of the cribriform plate and fovea ethmoidalis, which separate the skull base from the ethmoid sinuses. As a general statement, penetration of the medial wall below this level is safe, because it decompresses the orbit into the sinuses; penetration of the orbit above this level is fraught with potential neurologic complications, since the surgeon would enter the intracranial space. That said, many pathologic conditions (craniofacial anomalies such as Crouzon syndrome, etc.) are characterized by a low-lying skull base, and not infrequently, otherwise normal patients will present with a low skull base; review of preoperative imaging is therefore crucial in all patients.
The sphenoethmoidal recess, superior orbital fissure, and infraorbital canal do not involve the ethmoidal foramina and the posterior ethmoidal arteries.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What procedure is used during the surgical repair of most forms of ectropion?

options.d: horizontal incision of lower lid anterior lamella

pool.rationale: Lateral canthal tendon tightening via the lateral tarsal strip procedure is the most frequently used procedure to correct ectropion from any cause, typically in conjunction with additional procedures more specific to the etiology of the lid malposition. The spindle procedure is used for punctal ectropion, creating an incision in the conjunctiva inferior to the puncta, and is sutured, thereby creating a rotational scar in the conjunctiva turning the puncta towards the globe. Incising the lid skin horizontally would be effective only if there were a cicatricial or mechanical pull inferiorly pulling down on the lid. Regardless of the etiology, lateral tightening is usually necessary, in addition to addressing the specific cause of the malposition. Medial canthus tightening is technically complicated and thus less often used.
