pool.q: Where is the ostium of the nasolacrimal duct (NLD)?
pool.rationale: The NLD terminates at the valve of Hasner and drains in the meatus beneath the inferior turbinate. The maxillary sinus, frontal sinus, and anterior ethmoidal sinus drain in the middle meatus. The posterior ethmoidal sinus drains into the superior meatus. The sphenoid sinus drains above the superior turbinate in the area called the sphenoethmoidal recess.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Following excision of a large dermolipoma, a patient reports experiencing severe dry eye. What structure is most likely to have been injured during the procedure?
pool.rationale: During resection of a dermolipoma, the overlying conjunctiva should be preserved. Care must be taken to avoid damage to the lacrimal gland ducts, the extraocular muscles, and the levator aponeurosis. Although the glands of Wolfring are salivary excretory glands, these are fewer in quantity and distribution along the conjunctiva. The meibomian glands and the glands of Zeis are sebaceous glands that contribute to the tear film on the eyelid margin and on the lash cilia, respectively, and neither would likely be involved during the excision of a dermolipoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 60-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes presents with progressively worsening double vision and severe periorbital pain that began 2 days ago. One day prior, she noted that the double vision resolved. Severe vision loss to no light perception is noted on the left, along with a fundus examination consistent with an ophthalmic artery occlusion. Computed tomography (CT) of orbits shows extensive opacification of the left maxillary sinus extending into the orbital apex. What would a biopsy most likely show?
pool.rationale:
Few orbital and paranasal sinus processes progress to rapid and profound visual loss. Chief among these is zygomycosis (mucormycosis), a fungus with a propensity to invade blood vessel walls, producing thrombosing vasculitis. Tissue necrosis then promotes further fungal invasion. Predisposing factors include systemic disease or treatments associated with metabolic acidosis and immunosuppression (diabetes, malignancy, chemotherapy, and corticosteroids). Tissue is usually obtained to confirm the diagnosis. Histology shows nonseptate, large branching hyphae that stain with hematoxylin-eosin.
Presenting signs often include proptosis and orbital apex syndrome (internal/external ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, decreased corneal sensation, and profound and rapidly progressive visual loss. Pain is also a hallmark of the disease, presumably due to soft tissue ischemia (“orbital angina”).
Treatment is aimed at control of underlying metabolic or immunologic abnormality and local surgical debridement. Antifungal therapy is given via intravenous administration of amphotericin B or liposomal amphotericin B.
Bacterial infection rarely presents with this tempo of clinical progression, with one major exception being odontogenic orbital cellulitis (orbital infection from an infected tooth), which can rapidly spread into the orbit and skull base via the paranasal sinuses and venous plexuses. Necrotizing fasciitis, an extremely aggressive infection from the skin, typically involves more superficial layers of the lids and perhaps anterior orbit, but infrequently spreads to the orbital apex early in the disease course.
Orbital lymphoproliferative disease has a fairly indolent presentation in the vast majority of cases. On occasion, an aggressive primary or secondary (from an adjacent paranasal sinus) diffuse large B-cell or mantle cell lymphoma can present with sudden visual loss, but histopathology would not show a pleomorphic infiltrate. Similarly, metastatic disease to the orbital apex would only rarely present with rapidly progressive visual loss and would typically not present with concomitant maxillary sinus involvement.
In the case presented, the primary concern for the clinician must be mucormycosis, and it requires urgent work-up and management.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 70-year-old patient presents with slowly progressive unilateral ptosis with a high lid crease, a deep superior sulcus, and normal levator function. Following instillation of phenylephrine, his lid position does not change. What is the preferred method of ptosis repair?
pool.rationale:
This patient presents with classic findings of involutional ptosis. As described, the levator muscle itself is normal, but the levator aponeurosis is stretched or disinserted, thus requiring advancement.
Phenylephrine stimulates Müller muscle contraction and is a reasonable predictor of the effect that a Müller muscle-conjunctival resection will have on the upper eyelid. Because phenylephrine did not elevate the eyelid effectively in this patient, an external levator advancement is indicated.
Frontalis sling is not indicated, because levator function is normal; frontalis slings are generally reserved for ptosis with poor levator function, which is classically congenital, traumatic, or neurogenic (chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia [CPEO], myasthenia gravis). A brow lift would correct brow ptosis but not ptosis from levator dehiscence.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The anterior and posterior origins of the medial canthal tendon fuse just temporal to what structure?
pool.rationale: The anterior and posterior origins of the medial canthal tendon fuse just temporal to the lacrimal sac. The anterior limb inserts on the anterior lacrimal crest, the posterior limb on the posterior crest. The Whitnall ligament (superior transverse ligament) is located where the levator muscle transitions into the levator aponeurosis.

pool.q: A 50-year-old patient has a mass in the left upper eyelid. Examination shows an enlarged, nontender lacrimal gland without periorbital edema. What echographic characteristic would support a diagnosis of lymphoma rather than pleomorphic adenoma?
pool.rationale:
Low internal reflectivity indicates that the lesion is homogeneous, consistent with the histology of lymphoma. Other ultrasound features of orbital lymphoma include variable shape, regular internal structure, weak attenuation, and firm consistency.
In contrast, pleomorphic adenoma of the lacrimal gland orbital lobe demonstrates medium-to-high internal reflectivity on orbital ultrasound. Other features are ovoid or round shape, high pulsatility, moderate sound attenuation, and firm consistency. Pleomorphic adenomas may contain cysts.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with a chronic reddish dermal mass of the lower eyelid. Biopsy shows spindle cells without malignant features. What is the most appropriate next step?
pool.rationale: Kaposi sarcoma is a frequent manifestation of AIDS, and should prompt workup for HIV if it is seen in an individual without a known immunodeficiency disorder. Wide excision, cryotherapy, and intralesional chemotherapy are all appropriate treatment modalities, but the lesion may also regress with adequate antiviral treatment of the HIV infection.

pool.q: A child presents with pulsatile proptosis. What phakomatosis is suspected?
pool.rationale:
Orbital pulsations can result from the transition of normal intracranial pulsations through a bony defect or from abnormal vascular flow within the orbit. Bony defects can occur from trauma, surgical removal of bone, mucoceles, or congenital defects.
Neurofibromatosis type 1 is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by hamartomas of skin, eye, central nervous system, and viscera. Aplasia of the sphenoid wing also is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1, and these patients may present with pulsatile proptosis due to this bony defect. The other phakomatoses (neurofibromatosis type 2, von Hippel-Lindau disease, tuberous sclerosis) listed are not associated with pulsatile proptosis.

pool.q: A 55-year-old patient presents with lower lid entropion. The examination suggests a cicatricial process. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.a: repair of disinserted lower lid retractors
options.d: skin grafts to the anterior lamella

pool.rationale: Ocular cicatricial pemphigoid is one of the more common causes of cicatricial entropion in the US. Stevens-Johnson syndrome may also result in posterior lamellar scarring. If an inflammatory etiology of the cicatricial process is suspected, initial management should be directed toward accurate diagnosis and anti-inflammatory or other medical treatment to prevent worsening of the cicatricial process. Trachoma is a common cause of upper eyelid entropion. In general, cicatricial eyelid malpositions are treated by lengthening the affected lamella. For cicatricial entropion, posterior lamellar lengthening (conjunctiva and tarsus) would be the appropriate therapy; skin grafts are a good option for cicatricial ectropion. Repair of lower eyelid retractor disinsertion is typically performed in involution (noncicatricial) eyelid malpositions. Epilation does not address the cause of the entropion.

pool.q: A 38-year-old patient undergoes lateral orbitotomy to excise an intraconal cavernous hemangioma located in the inferior, posterior lateral orbit. The patient reports trouble reading. What is the most likely cause of the patient's postoperative reading difficulties?

options.a: disruption of the posterior ciliary arteries
options.b: hemorrhage within the optic nerve sheath

pool.rationale:
The ciliary ganglion is at risk for injury in lateral approaches to the intraconal space. The parasympathetic innervation, which controls accommodation and pupillary constriction, synapses within the ciliary ganglion. With injury to the ciliary ganglion, parasympathetic innervation is disrupted, causing postoperative accommodative difficulty.
Inflammatory occlusion of the short posterior ciliary arteries occurs in giant cell arteritis and can result in vision loss. Superior oblique muscle weakness can result in diplopia that is worse in downgaze (rather than result in accommodation problems), but that muscle would be unlikely to be damaged in the surgery described. Hemorrhage within the optic nerve sheath can cause visual dysfunction, but this would limit both distance and reading vision.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What causes acute spastic entropion?
pool.rationale: Acute spastic entropion is caused by ocular irritation or inflammation. Disinsertion of eyelid retractors and horizontal eyelid laxity contribute to involutional entropion. Deficiency of eyelid skin is a cause of cicatricial ectropion.

pool.q: An 8-year-old child who has had constant tearing from the left eye since birth is brought to the clinic. Palpation of the lacrimal sac does not reveal mucopurulent discharge. There is a heightened tear film and epiphora. There does not appear to be an inferior or superior punctum. A medial eyelid cut down does not reveal patent canaliculi. What is the next step?
pool.rationale: Symptomatic tearing in a patient with absence of the lacrimal system requires a CDCR, which includes the placement of a Jones tube to connect the tear film to the nasal cavity. A DCR requires intact puncta, canaliculi, and lacrimal sac in order to join the tear film with the nasal cavity. Probe and intubation also require an established lacrimal system. Turbinate infracture is reserved for cases in which the inferior turbinate appears to be lateralized against the nasolacrimal duct at the time of probing and irrigation. This procedure enlarges the inferior meatus.

pool.q: Primary closure of a small lower eyelid defect is attempted, but excessive tension is noted during the closure. What is the best way to proceed?

options.a: Release the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon.
options.b: Use a tarsoconjunctival flap developed from the upper eyelid.
options.d: Perform a 3-layer closure using permanent sutures for all layers.

pool.rationale:
Small defects of the lower eyelid can be repaired by primary closure. In addition, the inferior crus of the lateral canthal tendon can be internally or externally released so that there is an additional 3 mm to 5 mm of medial mobilization of the remaining lateral eyelid margin.
Performing a 3-layer closure using permanent sutures for all layers does not address the need to decrease horizontal tension. Creating a free skin graft for reconstruction of the anterior lamella and using a tarsoconjunctival flap are generally reserved for larger lower eyelid defects; this defect is described as small.

pool.q: What is the most common eyelid finding associated with naso-orbital-ethmoid fractures?

options.a: widening of the vertical palpebral fissure
options.b: widening of the horizontal palpebral fissure

pool.rationale:
Naso-orbital-ethmoid fractures usually result from the face striking solid surfaces. Patients characteristically have a depressed bridge of the nose and traumatic telecanthus. Treatment includes repair of the nasal bone fracture, and plate stabilization, such as with microplate fixation, because it allows precise bony reduction.  Transnasal wiring of the medial canthus is less commonly done.
These injuries do not result in rounding of the lateral canthus or changes in the size of the palpebral fissure.

pool.q: A patient with chronic discharge, eyelid swelling, and erythema medial to the punctum is unresponsive to oral cephalexin and topical erythromycin. What is the most appropriate next course of action?

options.a: computed tomography (CT) scan of the orbits to rule out a tumor
options.c: broad-spectrum oral antibiotics with anaerobic coverage

pool.rationale:
A variety of bacteria, viruses, and mycotic organisms can cause infection within the canaliculus, causing canaliculitis. The most common pathogen is a filamentous gram-positive rod, Actinomyces israelii.
The patient presents with persistent weeping and discharge, sometimes accompanied by a follicular conjunctivitis centered in the medial canthus. The punctum is often erythematous and dilated, or “pouting.” A cotton-tipped applicator can be used to apply pressure to the canaliculus (“milking”). Expression of purulent discharge confirms the diagnosis.
Canaliculitis can be difficult to eradicate. Culture of the discharge may be useful in identifying the organism. Conservative management consists of warm compresses, digital massage, and topical and sometimes oral antibiotic therapy. Many patients require more aggressive treatment, particularly those with A israelii infection, which has a tendency to form concretions, or “stones.” Within these stones, organisms are protected from lethal antibiotic concentrations. Curettage through the punctum is sometimes successful at removing multiple stones.
Should more aggressive surgery be required, a canaliculotomy can be performed through the horizontal canaliculus and approached from the conjunctival surface. The incision is left open to heal by second intention and does not require stenting. Irrigating the canaliculus with povidone-iodine or penicillin-fortified drops perioperatively may be of benefit as well. Care must be taken to remove any intraluminal foreign bodies, such as punctal plugs, to prevent recurrence.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What orbital tumor is associated with Kasabach-Merritt syndrome and thrombocytopenia?
pool.rationale:
Infantile (capillary) hemangiomas are common primary benign tumors of the orbit in children. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of these lesions demonstrates characteristic fine intralesional vascular channels and high blood flow. Kasabach-Merritt syndrome refers to multiple large visceral capillary hemangiomas producing thrombocytopenia. The other lesions listed are not associated with thrombocytopenia.
Cavernous hemangiomas are also benign orbital tumors, but typically present in adults.  MRI demonstrates small, intralesional vascular channels containing slowly flowing blood.
Lymphangiomas are believed to represent vascular dysgenesis. They are serum-filled channels, and because their endothelial cells do not proliferate, they are not neoplasms.
Dermoid cysts are lined by keratinizing epithelium and contain dermal appendages, such as hair follicles and sebaceous glands.

pool.q: What is the term for an extra row of eyelashes that emerge from the meibomian glands?
pool.rationale: Distichiasis, which can be acquired or congenital, is defined as accessory eyelashes growing posterior to the normal row of eyelashes (from the meibomian glands or tarsus). Trichiasis is defined as an acquired misdirection of eyelashes that curve toward the ocular surface. Madarosis is the absence or loss of the eyelashes. Poliosis refers to a decrease or absence of melanin in the eyelashes.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What sequela associated with a cavernous-carotid fistula is an indication for urgent surgical intervention?
pool.rationale:
Arteriovenous fistulas are acquired lesions caused by abnormal direct communication between an artery and a vein. This may be secondary to trauma or degeneration. The 2 forms are carotid cavernous fistula and dural cavernous fistula. The carotid cavernous fistula is typically associated with trauma such as basal skull fracture, whereas the dural fistula occurs more often in older patients with systemic hypertension and atherosclerosis.
Proptosis and compressive optic neuropathy can occur in both and are considered an indication for urgent intervention. Exophthalmos, arterialization of episcleral venules, elevated cavernous sinus pressure with III, IV, or VI nerve palsy, and elevated intraocular pressure may occur, but they do not require urgent intervention.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What clinical feature is most consistent with necrotizing fasciitis?
pool.rationale:
Necrotizing fasciitis is a deep, subdermal infection that rapidly spreads along the fascial layers of the body. It is classically due to group-A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus, but other organisms may cause similar infection. The hallmark of the disease is rapid progression over hours and pain secondary to necrosis. Prior to eschar formation (a sign of tissue infarction), clinical examination may show a deep, violaceous hue to the affected skin. Subcutaneous tissue demonstrates a hardened wooden feel rather than fluctuance.
Studies have shown that periorbital necrotizing fasciitis may carry a lower mortality rate than necrotizing fasciitis in other anatomic locations, and may respond to conservative therapy with intravenous antibiotics alone, rather than aggressive debridement. Involvement of the lower face and neck appears to increase mortality and morbidity. If periorbital debridement is necessary, it is important to spare the epidermal and dermal layers as much as possible to minimize postoperative scarring (which can result in very severe lagophthalmos and exposure keratopathy). Histopathologic studies have shown that the infection is usually limited to deeper fascial layers and that skin-sparing debridement is effective.
Of note, certain streptococcal species also produce exotoxin, which may result in pulmonary and renal shutdown, with subsequent multi-organ failure. Patients with suspected necrotizing fasciitis should be monitored closely, in consultation with internal medicine and infectious disease physicians.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 47-year-old woman presents with unilateral right proptosis and eyelid retraction. Her visual acuity is 20/40 in the right eye, which has limitation in right abduction and upgaze. There is moderate staining of her ocular surface on the right side. Aside from imaging the orbit, what is the most appropriate next step in management?
pool.rationale: The clinical scenario presented is new-onset thyroid eye disease. Although the patient’s symptoms are moderate, the next appropriate step is to complete the workup to establish the diagnosis and the stage of the disease process. Her surface disease should be managed nonsurgically for now, and her response to treatment should be reevaluated prior to proceeding with surgical intervention. Surgery may be required, but the typical pattern of management is orbital decompression, followed by strabismus surgery, and then eyelid retraction repair.

pool.q: A young girl who is in the emergency department with an orbital fracture presents with bradycardia and nausea. What does this most likely result from?

options.a: air trapped in the orbit compressing the cavernous sinus
options.b: unrecognized penetrating trauma to the cavernous sinus

pool.rationale: When the inferior rectus muscle becomes entrapped within an orbital fracture, attempted ocular excursions can stimulate the oculocardiac reflex, causing pain, nausea, and bradycardia. Urgent repair should be undertaken in these cases. Release of the entrapped muscle without delay can limit ultimate restriction and fibrosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 75-year-old patient has lower lid laxity, a preseptal orbicularis muscle that overrides the pretarsal orbicularis muscle, and disinserted lower lid retractors. This constellation of clinical features predisposes the patient to what condition?
pool.rationale:
Horizontal lower eyelid laxity destabilizes the eyelid margin and predisposes the patient to involutional ectropion or entropion. Once the lower eyelid retractors become disinserted, vertical laxity occurs, typically manifesting as entropion. A vicious cycle begins as the lashes rub and irritate the cornea, which then causes inner contracture and spasm of the orbicularis oculi muscle as a protective mechanism. Because of the vertical instability, the preseptal orbicularis "overrides" the pretarsal orbicularis, causing even more inturning of the lid margin and lashes. Orbicularis override is also referred to as spastic entropion.
Cicatricial entropion and ectropion are defined by shortening of either the anterior or posterior lamella. The anterior lamella consists of skin and orbicularis oculi muscle and any cicatrix in this layer (skin scarring from trauma, burns, surgery, etc.) will result in out-turning of the eyelid (ectropion). The posterior lamella is composed of tarsus and conjunctiva, and shortening (ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, etc.) will result in cicatricial entropion.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the most common type of malignant melanoma to affect the eyelid?
pool.rationale: There are 4 clinicopathologic forms of cutaneous melanoma: lentigo maligna melanoma, nodular melanoma, superficial spreading melanoma, and acrolentiginous melanoma. The eyelid is most often involved by either lentigo maligna melanoma, which accounts for 90% of all head and neck melanomas, or nodular melanoma, which accounts for 10% of cutaneous melanomas but is rare on the eyelids. Lentigo maligna melanoma is the invasive vertical malignant growth phase that occurs in around 2% of patients with lentigo maligna.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient has a unilateral supraduction deficit and positive forced ductions. He also has upper eyelid retraction. What is the most likely etiology?
pool.rationale:
Graves ophthalmopathy is the most common cause of eyelid retraction (and eyelid retraction is the most common clinical feature of Graves ophthalmopathy). Neither progressive supranuclear palsy, nor third nerve palsy, nor orbital trauma would produce eyelid retraction.
Although progressive supranuclear palsy, orbital trauma, and third cranial nerve palsy are conceivable etiologies for a supraduction deficit, only orbital trauma and Graves ophthalmopathy would have positive forced ductions.
Positive forced ductions indicate a restrictive extraocular muscle problem and can be found in traumatic orbital fracture with entrapment of the inferior rectus or surrounding connective tissue, Graves disease, postsurgical strabismus, and Brown syndrome in the adducting position.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Radioactive iodine treatment of thyroid cancer can cause epiphora via what mechanism?
pool.rationale: Therapeutic radioactive iodine for the treatment of thyroid cancer may lead to closure of the lacrimal apparatus as a result of sodium/iodide symporter in the mucosa of the sac and duct. This is not seen with the lower dosage used to treat the thyroid gland in patients with Graves hyperthyroidism.

pool.q: A 6-year-old child has had painless proptosis for 2 weeks and has undergone a computed tomography (CT) scan, which is shown in the figure. What diagnosis is most likely?

options.b: retention of an orbital foreign body

pool.rationale:
Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) should always be high on the differential diagnosis list of painless proptosis occurring in a child. The average age of orbital RMS presentation is 5 to 7 years, but RMS may also occur in younger or older children. Recognition of the possibility of orbital RMS is important because urgent biopsy for histopathologic confirmation is important in successful management; spread of tumor into the paranasal sinuses or cranial vault worsens prognosis. Of note, a minority of orbital RMS cases may present with pain and other inflammatory signs that may be difficult to differentiate from idiopathic orbital inflammatory syndrome (IOIS).
The most common cause of unilateral proptosis in a child is orbital cellulitis. However, orbital cellulitis typically presents clinically with pain and erythema, and radiographically with significant sinus opacification. Neither is seen in the photographs. Similarly, IOIS presents with sudden onset of pain. A retained orbital foreign body should also present with symptoms of pain and erythema, either from sterile or infectious inflammation. Of note, a retained orbital foreign body should always be considered in the differential diagnosis of a pediatric orbital mass, even without a clear history of trauma.

pool.q: What structure is the tarsal strip secured to during a lateral tarsal strip procedure?

options.a: superior crus of the lateral canthal tendon
options.b: periosteum inside the lateral orbital rim
options.d: periosteum external to the lateral orbital rim

pool.rationale: The lateral tarsal strip procedure is used for horizontal tightening of the eyelid. The strip of lateral tarsus is secured to the internal aspect of the lateral orbital rim periosteum to restore the normal anteroposterior curvature of the lid margin. Securing the strip outside the lateral orbital rim would create a gap between the lid and the globe. This procedure does not involve securing the strip to the lid margin or superior crus of the lateral canthal tendon.

pool.q: Why are orbital roof fractures more likely to occur in young children than in adults?

options.a: There is better pneumatization of frontal sinuses in young children.
options.b: The frontal lobe is underdeveloped in young children.
options.c: There is over-projection of the midface in young children.
options.d: There is a larger cranial vault-to-midface ratio in young children.

pool.rationale: Orbital roof fractures occur much more commonly in young children than adults for 2 main reasons. First, pneumatized frontal sinuses, the structures that absorb much of the force of a frontal blow in adults, are not yet developed in children. This absence of pneumatized frontal sinuses allows force to be transferred directly to the orbital roof, resulting in fracture. Second, an infant or toddler has a much higher cranial vault-to-face ratio than an adult (8:1 vs 2:1, respectively) along with a flatter face, lacking the midfacial and nasal projection of adults. This results in a larger and more prominent forehead that is more susceptible to injury. The frontal lobe is not underdeveloped in young children.

pool.q: A 48-year-old man presents with diplopia and left-sided head pain. Three years ago he had a frontal sinus fracture. On magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), he has a mass compressing the superior left globe and extending intracranially (see Fig. 1). Today he has 5 mm left eye hypoglobus. What is the best management option?

options.c: endoscopic drainage and reestablishment of sinus drainage
options.d: orbital biopsy through an upper eyelid crease incision

pool.rationale:
The history, clinical findings, and radiographic description are highly suspicious for a frontal sinus mucocele extending into the orbit and anterior cranial fossa. Mucoceles are essentially mucosally lined balloons that slowly expand as mucus is produced but that have no egress into the nose. These lesions can erode bone and on occasion are misdiagnosed as malignancy, although the radiographic appearance is diagnostic in most cases.
Mucoceles most frequently occur in the frontal sinus region because of the anatomically narrow area of the frontoethmoidal recess. Frontal sinus trauma greatly increases the probability of mucocele formation.
Mucoceles are best treated by transnasal endoscopic drainage and re-establishment of frontal sinus drainage into the nose. The mucosa is typically left intact to minimize any seeding and subsequent loculation of the problem.
Orbital biopsy should be avoided to minimize injury to the sinus mucosa. Craniotomy would be reserved for those cases that require ablation or cranialization of the frontal sinus. Empiric radiotherapy is not indicated for mucoceles.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What anatomic relationship of the periorbita contributes to the formation of a subperiosteal abscess?

options.a: The periorbita is permeable to inflammatory and infectious cells, which pass from the orbit to the subperiosteal space.
options.b: The periorbita is firmly attached to the entire length of orbital bones.
options.c: The periorbita is firmly attached to the arcus marginalis anteriorly and the dura mater covering the optic nerve at the apex.
options.d: The periorbita contains vascular and lymph structures that allow for inflammatory cells to collect in the subperiosteal space.

pool.rationale:
The periorbita is simply another name for the periosteum of the orbit. As periosteum travels toward the orbit along the facial bones, it fuses at the orbital rim to form the arcus marginalis, which is firmly tethered to the underlying bone and serves as the take-off point for the orbital septum (which may be considered an extension of the periosteum).
The periorbita extends posteriorly into the orbit from the arcus marginalis as an avascular layer that is loosely attached to underlying bone except at the major orbital ostia (superior and inferior orbital fissures, optic canal). The loose attachment allows for a potential subperiosteal space for pus or blood (subperiosteal abscess or hematoma). The periorbita is relatively impermeable, sequestering blood or pus.
Posteriorly, periorbita fuses with the dura of the optic nerve at the optic canal.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What treatment has the highest success rate in eliminating epiphora in patients with total obstruction at the common canaliculus?
pool.rationale: Although it is preferable to use the native anatomy when possible, a CDCR has the highest likelihood of creating an intact lacrimal drainage system.  For a canaliculorhinostomy, the scarred canalicular segment is removed and the remaining patent canalicular system is anastomosed to the lacrimal sac mucosa or the lateral nasal wall mucosa. When successful, a canaliculorhinostomy results in the most natural anatomy. Unfortunately, the success rate for this procedure is lower with common canalicular obstruction. Silicone intubation will be insufficient to relieve the obstruction. A DCR will not address an obstruction at the canaliculus.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When performing an endoscopic brow lift, the incision in each temporal region can result in what complication?
pool.rationale:
The temporal pocket is created in the plane of the deep temporalis fascia. Dissection in this plane spares the frontal branch of the facial nerve in the overlying superficial temporalis fascia. However, if the dissection is carried out in the incorrect plane, damage to CN VII can occur. Additionally, during the temporal dissection, the temporal artery can also be encountered, which can result in hemorrhage and/or hematoma. Another complication of the scalp incisions is alopecia.
Eyelid ptosis would result from a CN III injury, which is not encountered during an endoscopic brow lift. Dissection leading to the periosteal release at the medial aspect of the orbital rim can lead to CN V damage.  A Horner syndrome would result from damage to the sympathetic nerve chain, which is not encountered during this surgery.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient arrives in the trauma bay after a motor vehicle crash in which he hit his face on the dashboard. He has ecchymosis and significant swelling to his right eye. The eyelids are "rock hard" to the touch. He complains of blurry vision in the right eye. His visual acuity is 20/80 OD and 20/20 OS. He can see 6/11 color plates OD and 11/11 OS. IOP is 35 OD and 22 OS. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.a: Obtain computed tomography (CT) of the orbits
options.c: Start maximum topical ocular antihypertensive drops and recheck the pressure in 30 minutes,
options.d: Perform an immediate lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis.

pool.rationale: To preserve visual function, immediate canthotomy and cantholysis should be performed to release the retrobulbar hemorrhage. The compartment syndrome effect caused by hemorrhage in the orbit leads to optic nerve compression and compromised arterial perfusion. This patient is experiencing increased intraocular pressure as well as decreased visual acuity and color vision, which suggests optic nerve involvement. The most appropriate next step is to intervene with a canthotomy and cantholysis. The other options would only delay definitive treatment.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What technique is used to evaluate the stability of the tear film?
pool.rationale:
Tear breakup time is a way of assessing the stability of the tear film. This can be observed after fluorescein has been placed in the conjunctival cul-de-sac. The patient is asked to open his or her eyes and refrain from blinking. The ophthalmologist then examines the tear film using a broad beam of the slit lamp. The time before breakup should be at least 10 seconds.

An enlarged tear film meniscus may suggest deficiency of lacrimal outflow, and observation of the lacrimal lake may demonstrate precipitated proteins or debris that may indicate an abnormal tear film. The basal tear secretion test is used to measure tear secretion. The dye disappearance test is useful for assessing the presence or absence of adequate lacrimal outflow.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the preferred surgical intervention for symptomatic upper and lower canalicular obstruction?
pool.rationale: Both dacryocystorhinostomy and balloon dacryocystoplasty require an intact canalicular system for success. Probing and dilation cannot be performed without patent canaliculi. The only widely accepted method to treat bicanalicular obstruction is to bypass the blockage with a conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) and a Jones tube.

pool.q: What is a modifiable risk factor for thyroid eye disease (TED)?
pool.rationale: Development of thyroid eye disease (TED) is up to 7 times more likely for smokers than nonsmokers. Non-modifiable risk factors include female gender, Graves hyperthyroidism, and age group: 40-44 years and 60-64 years in women, and 45-49 years and 65-69 years in men. Obesity, alcohol consumption, and hypertension are not risk factors for TED.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What congenital condition is associated with hypoplasia of the orbit, eyelids, and adnexal structures?
pool.rationale: Orbital development is partially dependent upon the size and growth of the globe. In anophthalmia, there is a total absence of tissues of the eye, which leads to poor orbital development. Ankyloblepharon and eyelid colobomas have abnormal eyelid development, but orbital development is usually normal. Telecanthus is an increased distance between the medial canthi, while inter-pupillary distance remains normal.

pool.q: A 45-year-old woman who experienced blunt trauma to her right orbit 1 week ago presents with a droopy right lid. On examination, she has an MRD-1 of 1.5 mm and levator function of 5 mm. Visual acuity is 20/20 OU and there are no pupillary abnormalities. There is no evidence of orbital hemorrhage, exophthalmos, or ophthalmoplegia. The remainder of her ocular examination is normal. What is the best assessment of her injury and approach to treatment?

options.a: She has traumatic ptosis, and observation for at least 6 months should be allowed to assess for spontaneous recovery before surgical intervention.
options.b: She has paralytic lagophthalmos due to a facial nerve injury. She should allow for 3 months of observation to assess for spontaneous recovery before surgical intervention.
options.c: She has paralytic ptosis due to a levator injury and should have frontalis sling surgery if there is no spontaneous improvement in the next 2 months.
options.d: She has an injury to the facial nerve resulting in traumatic ptosis. She should undergo frontalis sling ptosis repair if there is no improvement within 6 months.

pool.rationale:
The clinical scenario describes a traumatic ptosis from blunt trauma. Traumatic ptosis can result from a number of etiologies, including damage to the oculomotor nerve, carotid dissection with a secondary Horner syndrome, blunt or lacerating injury to the levator muscle, or eyelid edema.
Injury to the facial nerve would cause brow ptosis or lagophthalmos due to orbicularis oculi weakness. However, the levator muscle would remain intact, allowing the patient to open her eyelid.
Traumatic ptosis from blunt injury should be followed conservatively for at least 6 months. The majority of patients will experience either partial or complete spontaneous recovery of eyelid function. If the levator muscle does not recover after that time, surgical intervention can be considered.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The lateral canthal tendon attaches to what structure?
pool.rationale: The lateral canthal tendon attaches at the lateral orbital tubercle, also known as the Whitnall tubercle. The Whitnall ligament is a separate fascial band that does not insert on the tubercle of the same name. The lateral orbital tubercle is posterior to the orbicularis oculi muscle and lateral orbital rim.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An external dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) is an effective treatment for what finding?
pool.rationale:
Dacryoliths often involve not only the canaliculi (causing chronic canaliculitis), but also the lacrimal sac. Lacrimal sac dacryoliths are often associated with nasolacrimal obstruction. A DCR would thus allow for removal of the lacrimal stones and re-establishment of lacrimal outflow.
If a lacrimal sac tumor is suspected, a dacryocystectomy is indicated. If preoperative imaging shows tumor growth more inferiorly, then extirpation of the nasolacrimal duct should also be performed. In cases of lacrimal sac malignancy, a DCR is contraindicated, because there is a need to maintain the integrity of the lacrimal sac mucosa, to allow for complete tumor removal. Furthermore, an intact bony lacrimal sac fossa acts as a potential anatomic barrier against intranasal spread. Anterior ethmoiditis on occasion mimics dacryocystitis. When surgery is necessary, it is best managed by transnasal endoscopic technique. A DCR requires patency of the canaliculi for success. The procedure will simply not work in a patient with complete canalicular obstruction; in such cases, a conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) with placement of a Jones tube is indicated.

pool.q: What is an indication for emergent surgery to repair an orbital floor fracture?

options.a: indirect traumatic optic neuropathy in an adult
options.b: restriction of extraocular motility and vasovagal symptoms in a child
options.c: inferior globe dystopia > 5 mm in an adult

pool.rationale:
Orbital floor fractures (blowout fractures) are rarely an emergent or urgent pathology. Large fractures that cause significant globe dystopia (enophthalmos and/or hypoglobus) can be repaired successfully 1-3 weeks after injury.
The one major exception is the so-called "white-eyed blowout fracture" that occurs primarily in children. Because the pediatric orbital skeleton has not fully calcified, the bones are pliable and can "greenstick" (wherein one side of a bone is broken and the other is bent), rather than break cleanly. This results in a trapdoor effect along the orbital floor or, less commonly, the medial wall: A narrow fracture opens, allowing fat and/or rectus muscle to herniate into the maxillary/ethmoid sinus, and then the trapdoor fracture snaps shut, tightly entrapping soft tissue and potentially causing significant muscle ischemia. The fracture is termed "white-eyed" because the patient has few if any of the usual signs of orbital trauma: There is almost no ecchymosis or eyelid edema. The tightly entrapped muscle typically causes a severe vasovagal reaction from the oculocardiac reflex when the child tries to move his/her eyes, resulting in nausea, vomiting, poor oral intake, and bradycardia.
There is no known effective treatment for the classic indirect traumatic optic neuropathy (TON) seen in a deceleration injury. The only TONs that may respond to treatment are those secondary to compression: orbital hemorrhage or optic nerve impingement (from a foreign body or bone fragment).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What movement of the jaw most commonly causes elevation of the ptotic eyelid in Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome?

options.a: mandibular movement to the contralateral side
options.b: mandibular movement to the unilateral side

pool.rationale:
The Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome (also known as the Marcus Gunn phenomenon) is a trigemino-oculomotor synkinesis. Strabismus and amblyopia are common associations, occurring in about half of patients. The strabismus may be comitant, but noncomitant forms are also frequently encountered, including double-elevator palsy and superior rectus palsy.
Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant, but with incomplete penetrance.
The movement that most commonly causes elevation of the ptotic eyelid is lateral mandibular movement to the contralateral side. This phenomenon is usually first noticed by the mother when she is feeding the baby.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the preferred treatment for a benign mixed tumor of the lacrimal gland (pleomorphic adenoma)?

options.a: incisional biopsy of the tumor followed by external beam irradiation
options.d: incisional biopsy of the tumor followed by complete excision

pool.rationale: Benign mixed tumor (pleomorphic adenoma) is the most common epithelial tumor of the lacrimal gland. It has a varied cellular structure, consisting primarily of a proliferation of benign epithelial cells and a stroma composed of spindle-shaped cells with occasional cartilaginous, mucinous, or even osteoid degeneration or metaplasia. The lesion is circumscribed by a pseudocapsule, and thus a complete removal of tumor with its pseudocapsule and surrounding margin of orbital tissue is the preferred treatment of choice for the lowest risk of dissemination. Biopsy will disrupt the mass and its capsule, which has been shown to increase recurrence rate.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What cutaneous malignancy is associated with actinic keratosis?
pool.rationale: Actinic keratosis is the most common precancerous skin lesion, often affecting people with fair complexion and a history of chronic sun exposure. Over extended follow-up, a patient with multiple actinic keratoses has a 12%-16% incidence of squamous cell carcinoma. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignant neoplasm of the eyelid. Sebaceous carcinoma and malignant melanoma are less common.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with stable thyroid disease has new horizontal and vertical diplopia, which worsens at the end of the day. Lid retraction is less obvious than in the past. What would best explain these findings?
pool.rationale: A variable strabismus that worsens later in the day or with fatigue and is associated with ptosis is indicative of myasthenia gravis, in which acetylcholine receptor antibodies cause muscle weakness and strabismus. It can occur in patients with thyroid eye disease. Worsening thyroid eye disease can cause a worsening strabismus, but it should be stable throughout the day and associated with worsening lid retraction. Third nerve palsy can cause ptosis and new-onset diplopia, but it would be stable over the day. A decompensated phoria should not affect the lid position.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the surgical procedure of choice for complete obstruction of both canaliculi due to scarring?
pool.rationale:
Complete canalicular obstruction is a contraindication for DCR, regardless of the approach (external or endonasal). DCR requires a patent canalicular system. If the canaliculi are scarred, then conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy (CDCR) with Jones tube placement is indicated.
Probing and irrigation can be used for congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction. Punctoplasty is used for punctal stenosis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient has eversion of the lower eyelid margin. There is actinic damage on the patient's cheeks and a scar along the inferior eyelash line from previous excision of a squamous cell carcinoma. What procedure would be preferred to combine with horizontal eyelid tightening to repair the ectropion?
pool.rationale:
Cicatricial ectropion occurs when there is a deficiency of skin secondary to trauma (including from prior surgery), burns, and/or chronic actinic skin damage. Repair of cicatricial ectropion usually requires a 3-step approach:
  1. Surgical release of vertical traction via anterior approach
  2. Horizontal eyelid tightening
  3. Vertical augmentation of the anterior lamella, which can be accomplished with full-thickness skin graft, midface lift, or adjacent tissue transfer
In cases of eyelid marginal malposition, the "two lamella" concept should be applied to choose the best procedure. Put simply, the eyelid along the height of the tarsal plate consists of an anterior lamella (skin and orbicularis oculi muscle) and a posterior lamella (conjunctiva and tarsus). Each lamella can be surgically manipulated to achieve the desired final eyelid position.
In this case, the abnormality lies in the anterior lamella shortened through actinic damage and surgical scarring. Surgery to the posterior lamella with either a lengthening or shortening procedure (eg, conjunctivoplasty) would not help in lengthening the anterior lamella. Blepharoplasty would only exacerbate an already shortened anterior lamella.
The best answer is to lengthen the anterior lamella with a full-thickness skin graft. Since full-thickness skin grafts contract less than split-thickness grafts, this is the correct answer.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What branch of the facial nerve most commonly innervates the corrugator supercilii muscle?
pool.rationale: The facial nerve divides into 5 branches. From superior to inferior, they are: temporal (frontal), zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical. The temporal (frontal) branch innervates the superior part of the facial mimetic muscles, including the corrugator supercilii.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A transnasal endoscopic orbitotomy would be most effective in what procedure?

options.b: removal of a lateral orbital apical lesion
options.c: biopsy of a ciliary ganglion tumor
options.d: excision of a superomedial dermoid cyst

pool.rationale: A transnasal endoscopic approach to the orbit is useful in managing disease in the medial orbit. One of the most common uses of the transnasal approach is for removal of the lamina papyracea during medial orbital wall decompression for thyroid eye disease. The technique provides an excellent view of the medial orbital wall, optic canal, and skull base. Additionally, it has the theoretical advantage of minimizing iatrogenic compression of orbital soft tissue in an already congested orbit, since bone is removed from “outside in,” as opposed to the transcaruncular approach. This technique should not be used in accessing lesions lateral to the optic nerve (lateral orbital apex and ciliary ganglion). A superomedial dermoid cyst is usually located relatively anteriorly within the orbit and requires wide dissection for complete excision to avoid rupture; this is best achieved using standard anterior orbitotomy techniques.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: When evaluating an eyelid specimen for possible sebaceous cell carcinoma, what histopathologic evaluation should be performed?
pool.rationale: Lipid stains are useful for accurate diagnosis of sebaceous cell carcinoma of the eyelid. The other pathologic studies are useful to diagnose other conditions (eg, Congo red for amyloidosis), but are not helpful when evaluating for sebaceous cell carcinoma.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What condition is likely to present with a palpable, smooth, painless mass in the superolateral orbit with pulsating proptosis upon mastication?
pool.rationale: Orbital dermoids present as palpable, smooth, painless, ovoid masses that enlarge slowly. They are either freely mobile or adhere to the underlying periosteum. They typically occur in the area of the lateral brow adjacent to the frontozygomatic suture or in the upper medial eyelid adjacent to the frontoethmoidal suture. In the temporal fossa, dumbbell extension through the suture and into the underlying orbit should be ruled out with computed tomography. Pulsing proptosis with mastication is a highly specific feature of dumbbell extension. Surgical removal of a dermoid cyst should include meticulous removal of all of the cyst wall and contents, or an acute inflammatory response can result.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the goal of orbital decompression surgery for Graves disease-related ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease)?

options.a: reduction of stare from lid retraction
options.b: expansion of the orbital volume to accommodate enlarged extraocular muscles
options.d: improvement of ocular misalignment and diplopia

pool.rationale: Orbital decompression often, and in particular in the chronic stage of thyroid eye disease, does not affect the orbital inflammatory process or its sequelae but simply expands orbital volume for the large muscles. It often does not have any effect on lid retraction, even when proptosis is reduced, and it can in fact exacerbate diplopia.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 58-year-old female presents with unilateral eyelid thickening and focal loss of eyelashes. What is the most appropriate management?
pool.rationale:
Eyelid thickening in the setting of eyelash loss should raise suspicion for an infiltrative process. In this setting, one should be concerned about the possibility of a neoplasm, especially sebaceous gland carcinoma, which can be mistaken for chronic asymmetric blepharitis. This presentation warrants biopsy.
Serial photography would not be appropriate, with the significant possibility of a cancerous process. Warm compresses would be indicated for posterior blepharitis, but that condition would not be the cause of focal eyelash loss. A Fox shield can be useful for some patients with floppy eyelid syndrome, a condition that also would not produce eyelash loss.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What accessory lacrimal glands are located along the margin of the tarsus?
pool.rationale: The glands of Wolfring and Krause are accessory lacrimal glands and are structurally identical to the main lacrimal gland. They account for roughly 10% of the total lacrimal secretory volume. The glands of Wolfring are located along the proximal margin of the tarsus, while the glands of Krause are located primarily in the upper fornix. The glands of Moll and Zeis are apocrine sweat glands and modified sebaceous glands, respectively.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with a history of Stevens-Johnson syndrome presents for entropion evaluation and is noted to have vertical conjunctival shortening. What type of entropion best accounts for this clinical picture?
pool.rationale: Cicatricial entropion refers to an inward-turning of the lid margin due to scarring of the posterior lamella. This results in irritation of the globe from inturned cilia. Various conditions may lead to cicatricial entropion, including autoimmune, inflammatory (such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome), infectious, surgical, and traumatic conditions and long-term use of medications that induce chronic conjunctivitis, such as topical glaucoma medications.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What eyelid lesion is most appropriately managed with Mohs micrographic surgery?
pool.rationale: Mohs micrographic surgery can be useful in the management of skin malignancy. Basal cell carcinoma is a perfect candidate for Mohs micrographic surgery because it exhibits contiguous spread without skip lesions or metastasis, and interpretation of the histopathology on frozen sections is reliable. Malignant melanoma and Merkel cell carcinoma require wide resection with metastatic workup. Actinic keratosis is a pre-malignant lesion that can often be treated with topical liquid nitrogen therapy and does not warrant Mohs excision.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient who previously underwent a medial orbitotomy for a cavernous hemangioma presents with a complaint of epiphora. What structure is most likely to have been damaged during the surgical procedure?
pool.rationale: When dissecting in the medial orbit, the surgeon must be careful to avoid damaging the medial canthal tendon, lacrimal canaliculi and sac, trochlea, superior oblique tendon and muscle, and inferior oblique muscle, as well as the  sensory nerves and vessels along the medial aspect of the superior orbital rim.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The "tram-track" sign (parallel radiodense lines) on plain x-ray or computed tomography (CT) imaging suggests what orbital lesion?
pool.rationale: The appearance of calcification of a meningioma on plain x-ray or CT is referred to as tram-tracking. Both CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans show diffuse tubular enlargement of the optic nerve with contrast enhancements, as well as parallel radiodense lines representing lesion edge calcification. Fibrous dysplasia characteristically has a ground-glass appearance on imaging with sparing of the soft tissues. Retinoblastoma usually shows calcifications as well, but without the parallel radiodense lines. Cavernous hemangiomas are usually well encapsulated and intraconal.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What fat pad is traversed when performing a browpexy?
pool.rationale:
The retro-orbicularis oculi fat pad (ROOF) is suspended during a browpexy procedure. It is accessed through the upper eyelid incision during a blepharoplasty. Postseptal superior dissection is carried out to identify the ROOF. This fat pad is usually suspended with a 4-0 Vicryl suture to the frontal periosteum to achieve an internal brow fixation/elevation.
Medial preaponeurotic and central aponeurotic fat pads are located within the eyelid and do not achieve brow elevation when manipulated. The sub-orbicularis oculi fat pad is located within the lower eyelid.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 28-year-old patient sustains fractures of the medial orbital wall and roof near the orbital apex, but does not require any surgical intervention. What is appropriate advice in the conservative management of this patient?

options.a: for 2 weeks, wear eye shield over involved eye when sleeping
options.b: for 2 weeks, head up and bed rest
options.c: for 2 weeks, no blowing the nose
options.d: for 2 weeks, no extended periods of reading

pool.rationale: Orbit fractures create connections between the paranasal sinuses and the orbit, introducing the possibility of retrograde passage of air into the orbit with maneuvers that create positive pressure in the sinuses, such as nose blowing. This can be painful, and in severe cases could cause significant increased orbital pressure with compressive optic neuropathy. For this reason, patients with orbital fractures are instructed not to blow their nose for 2 weeks following the injury. Bed rest, wearing a protective shield when sleeping, and avoiding prolonged reading are not necessary following an orbital fracture. If the patient's computed tomography (CT) scan shows sinusitis, antibiotics are sometimes recommended. Some practitioners also recommend steroids to decrease edema, but this is controversial.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What method is typically used to repair a large lower eyelid defect involving more than 50% of the eyelid?
pool.rationale:
The eyelid-sharing technique of a Hughes flap combined with skin grafting of the anterior lamella would be an ideal repair technique for a large defect of the lower eyelid. Note that repair of a large full-thickness eyelid defect requires reconstruction of the mucosa-lined posterior lamella and the cutaneous anterior lamella. At least one of the lamellae should be a vascularized flap; free grafts of both lamellae will not survive. Thus another option in this case would be a free tarsoconjunctival graft from the contralateral upper eyelid with vascular supply from a pedicled skin–muscle flap.
The Cutler-Beard procedure is an eyelid-sharing technique in which a full-thickness lower eyelid flap is moved into the defect of the upper eyelid by advancement of the flap behind the remaining lower eyelid margin. Primary closure of a large defect involving more than 50% of the lower lid is unlikely to be possible, and granulation alone would lead to a poor functional and cosmetic result.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: An 8-year-old girl is being evaluated for precocious puberty and acromegaly. She also has hearing loss and has had multiple broken bones. During the examination, the ophthalmologist finds unilateral proptosis. What is the preferred initial imaging study to define the expected lesion?
pool.rationale: Fibrous dysplasia is a developmental bone disorder where normal bone is replaced with fibrous bone tissue involving one or multiple regions. It is best appreciated on computed tomography (CT), which shows characteristic hyperostotic bone. Despite the patient's young age, CT is the best initial imaging of choice for diagnosis. Fibrous dysplasia associated with cutaneous pigmentation and endocrine disorders is a condition known as Albright syndrome. Fibrous dysplasia is also associated with neurofibromatosis type II.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A 33-year-old female patient developed acute swelling, redness, and mild tenderness of the right upper eyelid, as shown. There was no palpable pretarsal mass or tarsal abnormality on eversion of the eyelid. What is the most likely cause for her swelling?
pool.rationale:
The image depicts an inflamed nodule in the central portion of the right upper eyelid. Dacryoadenitis can certainly present with acute onset and inflammatory signs, but it affects the lateral portion of the upper lid in the area of the lacrimal gland.
Plexiform neurofibroma classically presents with an "S-shaped" eyelid deformity, but may also present as an isolated nodule. However, neurofibroma rarely causes inflammation.
Molluscum contagiosum is a viral infection of the eyelid that presents as one or more pearly white, well-circumscribed nodules on the eyelid. Again, inflammation is not a typical feature.
Chalazion frequently presents as an inflamed nodule. Oily secretions of the meibomian glands extrude into the surrounding eyelid soft tissue, inciting an inflammatory response that presents as swelling, redness, and tenderness. A secondary bacterial infection may also contribute to the inflammation. Chalazion is considered by some professionals to be an all-encompassing term that describes inflammation from one of the oil glands of the eyelid. Other experts divide these lesions into external hordeola (arising from the glands of Zeis) and internal hordeola (from the meibomian glands).
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The frontal sinuses begin to develop during what time?
pool.rationale: The ethmoid air cells are the only truly aerated sinuses at birth. Pneumatization of the remaining sinuses takes years to occur. The next to pneumatize are the maxillary sinuses. The frontal and sphenoid sinuses may begin to aerate in early childhood, and the frontal sinuses begin to be seen radiographically when the child is around 6 years old. This process will continue until the sinuses are fully aerated in the late teenage years or early adulthood.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: The mucocutaneous junction represents an important demarcation of the ocular surface. In a normal eye, the mucocutaneous junction colocalizes with what portion of the lid margin?

options.a: between the meibomian gland orifices and the lash follicle
options.b: anterior to the meibomian gland orifices
options.d: posterior to the meibomian gland orifices

pool.rationale: The mucocutaneous junction of the eyelid margin is often confused with the gray line. The gray line is a section of pretarsal orbicularis (Riolan) muscle just anterior to the tarsus. The mucocutaneous junction is located posterior to the meibomian gland orifices on the eyelid margin.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: After workup for new-onset diplopia, a man had an orbitotomy to remove a painful orbital mass. The pathologic specimen was a solitary fibrous tumor. What is the main risk factor for metastasis?
pool.rationale:
The term solitary fibrous tumor (SFT) describes a group of mesenchymal tumors that, until recently, were called by a variety of names (eg, hemangiopericytoma, fibrous histiocytoma) and considered to be separate entities.
SFT has a propensity for malignant transformation and subsequent metastasis, although the chance of this happening depends on the subtype of SFT and the amount of atypia on initial histopathology. The single most important factor in decreasing the risk of metastasis is complete excision of the tumor. The remaining choices (pain, presence for 3 months, scleral involvement) do not play a role in metastatic potential.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What is the typical time course for a capillary hemangioma of the eyelid?

options.c: rapid growth from 6 to 12 months of life
options.d: complete regression by 2 years of age

pool.rationale: Capillary hemangiomas are hamartomatous growths of proliferating capillary endothelial cells. They have a characteristic growth pattern of rapid growth in the first 12 months of life, with a subsequent period of regression and involution, with complete regression common around 5 years of age. Growth in puberty would be extremely uncommon, as would spontaneous involution shortly after birth or complete regression by 2 years of age.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: What would be the preferred management for a large, flat eyelid lesion with irregular borders and varied pigmentation?

options.a: total surgical excision with margin evaluation

pool.rationale: The most likely diagnosis for this lesion is a melanoma. Lentigo maligna accounts for 90% of head and neck melanomas. Management consists of total surgical excision utilizing permanent sections to assure complete removal. Biopsy is not preferred for a flat lesion and, if performed, would not be done on the margin, because the examiner could miss seeing the tumor. Observation is an option only for small, well-defined macular lesions. Radiation therapy is not indicated, as melanomas are radiation resistant.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: In a patient with asymmetric ptosis, how is ptosis unmasked in the "better" eye?

options.b: careful measurement of the margin–reflex distance (MRD)
options.c: lifting of the more ptotic eyelid

pool.rationale:
In a patient with asymmetric ptosis, lifting the worse lid may unmask ptosis in the contralateral eye. This is because of Hering's law of equal innervation.
Measurement of the MRD helps to document the amount of ptosis and plan for repair, but does not unmask a hidden ptosis. Phenylephrine can be used to determine who is a candidate for an internal approach to ptosis repair (Müller muscle resection). An icepack test can be used to evaluate suspected cases of myasthenia gravis.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A newborn was recently diagnosed with blepharophimosis syndrome. What is the most common epicanthal finding in this condition?
pool.rationale:
Epicanthus is a medial canthal fold that may result from immature midfacial bones or a fold of skin and subcutaneous tissue. The condition is usually bilateral and a cause of "pseudostrabismus," wherein the child may appear esotropic because of decreased scleral exposure nasally. There are 4 types:
  • epicanthus tarsalis, in which the fold is most prominent in the upper eyelid (normal variation of Asian eyelids)
  • epicanthus inversus, in which the fold is most prominent in the lower eyelid
  • epicanthus palpebralis, in which the fold involves the upper and lower eyelids equally
  • epicanthus supraciliaris, in which the fold arises from the eyebrow region and runs to the lacrimal sac
Blepharophimosis syndrome is another name for blepharophimosis-ptosis-epicanthus inversus syndrome (BPES). It is an autosomal dominantly inherited blepharophimosis that usually presents with telecanthus, epicanthus inversus (a fold of skin extending from the lower to upper eyelid), and severe ptosis. It is caused by mutations in the FOXL2 gene, located on chromosome 3. There are 2 types ( I and II), which both involve abnormalities of the eyelids, but type I also includes an early loss of ovarian function in women.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient with cicatricial entropion (as shown) is being evaluated by an ophthalmologist. What clinical finding is a contraindication to surgical repair?
pool.rationale:
Various conditions may lead to cicatricial entropion, including autoimmune (mucous membrane [ocular cicatricial] pemphigoid), inflammatory (Stevens-Johnson syndrome), infectious (trachoma, herpes zoster), surgical (enucleation, posterior-approach ptosis correction, transconjunctival surgery), and traumatic (thermal or chemical burns, scarring) conditions. The long-term use of topical glaucoma medications, especially miotics, can cause chronic conjunctivitis with vertical conjunctival shortening and secondary cicatricial entropion.
Successful management of cicatricial entropion depends on thoughtful preoperative evaluation to determine the cause, severity, and prominent features in each patient. Surgical repair is contraindicated during the acute phase of autoimmune diseases, and topical and systemic medications are more appropriate until the disease stabilizes.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Periorbital edema and crepitus following endoscopic sinus surgery suggests what clinical condition?
pool.rationale:
Any fracture that extends into a sinus may allow air to escape into the subcutaneous tissues, causing crepitus, and is commonly associated with fractures of the medial orbital wall. During endoscopic sinus surgery, the lamina papyracea may be breached, resulting in medial wall fracture.
Mucoceles of the sinuses are cystic structures resulting from obstruction of the sinus excretory ducts. These lesions may invade the orbit by expansion and erosion of the bones of the orbital walls and cause globe displacement. Silent sinus syndrome occurs when subclinical sinusitis causes thinning of the bones of the maxillary sinus, leading to collapse of the orbital floor and enophthalmos. Retrobulbar hemorrhage can occur as a complication of endoscopic sinus surgery, but it would not cause crepitus.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient has severe cicatricial entropion, which leads to corneal irritation and abrasions. The ophthalmologist recommends surgical entropion repair with conjunctival reconstruction. The patient has poor oral hygiene and is therefore not a candidate for an autologous mucous-membrane graft. What would be the preferred alternative graft?
pool.rationale:
Cicatricial entropion can be caused by conditions such as cicatricial pemphigoid, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, trachoma, herpes zoster virus, enucleation, posterior-approach ptosis correction, thermal or chemical burns, and other scarring conditions. The vertical tarsoconjunctival contracture and internal rotation of the eyelid margins causes irritation to the globe and requires correction. The goal of treatment is to eliminate the chronic ocular irritation by removing the lashes and keratinized tissue from contact with the globe and cornea. Minor inversion of the eyelid can be corrected by resection of anterior lamellar tissue with or without mucous membrane grafting. More extensive forniceal shortening and distortion of eyelid structures requires grafting to reconstruct the conjunctiva.
Most commonly used and successful grafts are either a buccal mucous membrane graft or an amniotic membrane graft. In this case, the patient is not a candidate for buccal mucous membrane grafting, so the preferred graft would be amniotic membrane. Skin grafts would not be used for conjunctival reconstruction, but rather for anterior lamellar reconstruction.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Three weeks ago, a 23-year-old man had blunt trauma to the left upper lid. Examination shows he has 3 mm of left ptosis, which does not change throughout the day. He also has an elevated lid crease and normal levator function, ocular motility, and pupillary responses. What is the most likely type of ptosis in this patient?
pool.rationale: Aponeurotic ptosis occurs when levator muscle is disinserted from the tarsal plate attachment and can occur secondary to age-related dehiscence (most common) or, less commonly, from trauma or intraocular surgery. Characteristics of aponeurotic ptosis include normal levator function, higher than normal eyelid crease (high-riding levator aponeurosis), and eyelid droop on downward gaze. Mechanical ptosis is from mass effect that weighs or pulls down the upper eyelid. Myogenic ptosis has absent upper lid crease and absent-to-poor levator function. When acquired, myogenic ptosis results from localized or diffuse muscular disease, such as muscular dystrophy, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, myasthenia gravis, or oculopharyngeal dystrophy. Neurogenic ptosis when acquired results from interruption of innervation and is often seen with other features, such as cranial nerve III palsy, Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome or Horner syndrome.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: A patient presents with intermittent diplopia that changes in every clinic visit and variable amounts of ptosis. What is the target of the antibody responsible for this condition?
pool.rationale:
Myasthenia gravis (MG) is an autoimmune disease characterized by antibody production against the acetylcholine receptor on the motor end plate of the muscle. Serologic testing for MG typically involves obtaining acetylcholine receptor antibodies, of which there are 3 types: blocking, binding, and modulating, named after their perceived mechanism of action. The first 2 antibody tests are the more important.
The remaining 3 answer choices (antibodies to acetylcholine, thyroid-stimulating antibodies, and fibroblast growth factor receptor) do not fit for MG. However, there is a known association between MG and thyroid dysfunction, and the thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI) test, along with more conventional tests for thyroid abnormality, are sometimes ordered in patients with MG. The utility of TSI in the management of thyroid dysfunction and thyroid eye disease is not completely understood.
pool.ref: Ophthalmology BCSC Question Bank — Oculofacial Plastic & Orbital Surgery — chapter/edition not encoded in source, confirm

pool.q: Where on the eye does the inferior oblique muscle insert?
pool.rationale:
The inferior oblique muscle originates in the anterior orbital floor lateral to the lacrimal sac and travels posterolaterally within the lower eyelid retractors to insert inferolateral to the macula.
The ora serrata, the ciliary body, and the inferior vortex vein are not the appropriate insertion locations of the inferior oblique muscle.

pool.q: A 60-year-old man presents with a palpable mass superior to the medial canthal tendon. What is the suspected diagnosis and appropriate management after obtaining imaging to rule out meningocele?

options.a: incisional biopsy of lacrimal gland tumor
options.b: external beam radiation therapy for sphenoid wing meningioma
options.d: excisional biopsy of a lacrimal sac tumor

pool.rationale:
A palpable mass in the medial canthal area superior to the medial canthal tendon is suspicious for a lacrimal sac malignancy or a nonlacrimal-based mass such as a meningocele or mucocele.
Distention of the lacrimal sac associated with chronic dacryocystitis would typically cause a palpable mass inferior to the medial canthal tendon.
A lacrimal gland tumor would be located in the temporal aspect of the upper lid and superior orbit, not in the medial canthal area. While rare, lacrimal sac tumors are benign 45% of the time and malignant 55% of the time. Squamous cell papillomas and carcinomas are the most common tumors of the sac.
A sphenoid wing meningioma would cause a mass in the temporal fossa.
